title: Buffalo Beskar, Part 9: I’m gonna need more protection
summary: If you’re following me on this journey of turning cat litter buckets into a reasonable cosplay approximation of Mandalorian armor inspired by the Buffalo Bills, you’ve likely seen how the breastplate shape has come into its own. Mandalorians need more armor than just their chest though, so let’s build spaulders and tassets! What are those, […]
full_text: If you’re following me on this journey of turning cat litter buckets into a reasonable cosplay approximation of Mandalorian armor inspired by the Buffalo Bills, you’ve likely seen how the breastplate shape has come into its own. Mandalorians need more armor than just their chest though, so let’s build spaulders and tassets! What are those, you ask? Well, you’re in luck if you read on below! Spaulders and Tassets huh? Yep. At least I think I have the terms correct, but there are a lot of words for armor types and I’m not an expert by any means. Spaulders, per the internet, are shoulder plates. While the Armorer in The Mandalorian refers to Din Djarin’s shoulder armor as pauldrons, I’m not convinced. And mine for sure are not. Pauldrops typically are larger and provide more coverage, including accounting for the armpit. The shoulder armor in most Star Wars sets don’t provide that same coverage and to me look like the smaller spaulders. Why the boring language lesson? I keep saying I’ve been overthinking things and my armor isn’t haphazard. I formerly was a pretty avid martial artist and have some firearm experience, so if I’m designing armor for me, it’s going to work for me. That means getting details right, including mobility and use cases. Let’s get a first glimpse at my spaulders and tassets. This is my left shoulder spaulder. I’ve marked a line down the center and I’m holding it over something with a long flat edge (dehumidifier if you’re interested). Once the center line is heated, I was able to bend it down the line, creating something like a crease rather than just a smooth curve. Either would work, but I liked how the crease looked. The piece with rivets and layers at the top is for my right thigh and I think this would be best called a “tasset.” You can see the spaulder from above thanks to the line. We’ll come back to that one in a moment as there’s another piece that needs to be attached to it. The two simpler pieces are the other tasset (left leg) and spaulder (right shoulder). Don’t worry, I will be making vambraces to cover my forearms, but those will be a different story entirely when it comes to build and I’m saving those for later. How much thought went into this armor? Let’s discuss the term “haute-piece.” This is the left spaulder, that if you looked closely had a second piece laying on it in the picture we just looked at. Here I am inserting a support piece to reinforce the attachment of it to the main piece of the spaulder. It kinda looks like a little wing jutting off the side. What’s the point of that? That’s a haute-piece. Imagine a weapon like a sword or lightsaber hitting my shoulder. Let’s say it hit me right in the “with glade” logo. Let’s further imagine that the blow was not perfectly perpendicular to the armor. Perhaps my arm was raised a bit. What would happen in that instance? Well, the lightsaber might glance off the smooth spaulder and… into my neck. I’d prefer not to go out like Jango Fett. Yes, I know Mace Windu’s lightsaber didn’t hit the spaulder first, but the point still remains. Lightsaber + neck = bad time. The haute-piece catches the blade before it slides up. Only my left side has a haute-piece, which is again deliberate. For reasons I’ll go into more details on later, my right and left side are built differently for different situations. As a potential spoiler, the strongest melee attacks will generally come at your left side as most people are right-handed. Therefore, left side haute-piece. Once I had the basic shape of everything, it was time to refine a little. Little things can aesthetically make a big difference. Here’s one line that changed with final shaping. This is the right thigh’s tasset, the upper segment. You can see the before and after final shaping to get my lines right. The other pic is the pile of plastic shavings that collectively came off these to get them right. Y’all wanna see some paint? With the final shape coming into form and plenty of nice painting weather, I was eager to get the first coats on. I know this edition of the Buffalo Beskar project is focused on the other armor, but let’s get a closeup of the breastplate in “beskar pewter.” Have I mentioned how much I love this paint? It was very tempting to just leave this, but we’re a Bills site, and this is a Bills project. Before you see what this looks like in metallic blue, let’s have a glimpse of the set in pewter. And here’s the full set. The piece I’ve yet to mention (between the tassets, and below the breastplate) is a lightweight back plate that was needed so I could make this wearable. On the right side spaulder, you can see the way those will go on, but I’ll spare those details until later. Right now, let’s take a look at the color coat for each of these. Each one will have “story” elements added in, but that’s not for this article to dive into. For now, I leave you with this…

title: Plays That Defined 2025: Buffalo Bills at New England Patriots, Week 15
summary: The 2025 Buffalo Bills season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - DECEMBER 14: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills in action against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on December 14, 2025 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Sarah Stier/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2025 Buffalo Bills season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to the “rules” of this exercise, we’re not voting for our favorite highlight necessarily, but the one that best captures the essence of the game. Put differently, if you had to choose just one play to show someone to explain as much of the contest as possible, which would you choose? Week 15; Buffalo Bills at New England Patriots After a thrilling come-from-behind win against the Cincinnati Bengals at home in the snow, the Buffalo Bills prepared to head a little East to take on the New England Patriots. Behind the Patriots in the division, and already having dropped a game to them, the Bills were looking to close the gap while getting some revenge. Now the darlings of the NFL, New England hadn’t dropped a game since Week 3, two weeks before taking down Buffalo. Down 21 – 0 early, it looked like Bills fans would have to wait for revenge. Entering halftime, a Buffalo touchdown was fun, but the Bills were still down by 17. Buffalo took a hell of a deep breath during the break and came back with a stampede of points while allowing just one more score to New England. A late lead seemed tenuous, but the defense held on for the final two drives by the Patriots to secure the victory. James Cook touchdown (Q3; 3:51) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 15 – James Cook touchdown pic.twitter.com/WyiIAUQyTu — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 25, 2026 In the second half, the Bills battled back to get into the game. A touchdown by Dawson Knox brought them to “just” ten points down from the Pats. This touchdown from James Cook was the definition of “hard fought,” needing to be reviewed to confirm he got in. Hard fought was the name of the game here, with 37 rushing attempts by Buffalo for just 168 yards. This helped control the clock and the pace of the game, which ended up being major factors in the Buffalo win. This was the first of two rushing touchdowns by Cook (the second being the game winner) to go with a first half receiving one. Now down by just three, it was suddenly anyone’s ball game. Tre’Davious White interception (Q3; 1:39) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 15 – Tre'Davious White interception pic.twitter.com/8cD1rjyzax — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 25, 2026 The second half defense was (mostly) a different beast from the first half. New England was pushed off their game, for instance being faced with 3rd & 25. Needing to pass deep, not Drake Maye’s strong suit, the ball arced high and drifted wide. Tre’Davious White was in better position to track the ball and came away with the arm punt. Dawson Knox touchdown (Q4; 10:10) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 15 – Dawson Knox touchdown pic.twitter.com/qrP289TwdW — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 25, 2026 Contributing in a big way alongside James Cook was tight end Dawson Knox. Knox’s three catches weren’t anything wild, but it was a day for spreading the ball around with Khalil Shakir being the only target with a higher catch total at five. Making Knox’s game special was mostly the timing. Two of this three catches went for scores. This one seemed unlikely not only because of Josh Allen running like a madman while throwing, but the down and distance thanks to being set back by an offensive holding penalty the play before. That penalty had negated an Allen rushing touchdown as well, setting up for a nailbiter attempt on this down. And oh yeah, with this score the Bills had a lead for the first time in the contest. Bills allow rushing touchdown… again (Q4; 10:03) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 15 – Rushing touchdown allowed pic.twitter.com/zS6vgMZ0l7 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 25, 2026 That lead was short-lived as the very next play was this nonsense. This 65-yarder was the second extremely long rushing touchdown and the fourth rushing touchdown total. The two shorter ones were being ran in by Drake Maye. For those of you reading this who might be comparing Maye and Allen, that put the tally of passing touchdowns for zero from Maye against three from Allen. Fourth-down stop (Q4; 1:54) Plays That Defined 2025 – Week 15 – Fourth down stop pic.twitter.com/kvIFgsUyj3 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) June 25, 2026 After taking the lead again thanks to another James Cook rushing touchdown Buffalo needed to hang on. New England ended up with two drives to try to retake the lead. The Patriots, feeling pressured to pass, only called one run play on these final two drives. Buffalo’s pass defense forced a three-and-out and then a four-and-out seen here with Joey Bosa tipping the ball. Buffalo was able to run out the clock for the win. Which play best defines the Bills’ win?
author: Skarekrow

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: quarterback Kyle Allen
summary: The Buffalo Bills have an elite quarterback. That’s not just me rambling; the good folks over at ESPN recently released their quarterback rankings, and they had Josh Allen at No. 1 among all NFL signal-callers. Our own top-dog, Chris Trapasso, wrote that Allen is the best player in the NFL before that ESPN piece published. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JUNE 9: Kyle Allen meets with the media following the Buffalo Bills mandatory minicamp at Kaleida Health Performance Center on June 9, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have an elite quarterback. That’s not just me rambling; the good folks over at ESPN recently released their quarterback rankings, and they had Josh Allen at No. 1 among all NFL signal-callers. Our own top-dog, Chris Trapasso, wrote that Allen is the best player in the NFL before that ESPN piece published. Any discussion of the backup quarterback spot, then, is tainted a bit with the knowledge that none of us want to see that backup in the game for an extended period of time. Whether we’re talking about Case Keenum, Mitchell Trubisky, Matt Barkley, or the subject of today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we know that the backup quarterback is nowhere near as good as the starting quarterback. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Kyle Allen Number: 11 Position: QB Height/Weight: 6’3” 210 lbs. Age: 30 (31 on 3/8/2027) Experience/Draft: 8; signed with the Carolina Panthers following the 2018 NFL Draft College: Houston Acquired: Signed with Bills on 3/12/2026 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Allen signed a two-year deal worth $4.1 million overall this spring. For the 2026 season, his cap hit if he makes the 53-man roster is $1.9 million. If he’s released, the Bills will carry a dead cap charge of $1.8 million this season. 2025 Recap: Allen spent last year with the Detroit Lions as the backup to Jared Goff. He played just sixteen offensive snaps in the regular season, throwing two incomplete passes and kneeling three times for -3 rushing yards. He had plenty of action in the preseason, though, completing 79.5% of his pass attempts (35-of-44) for 401 yards, five touchdowns, and two interceptions. He rushed five times for 16 yards, as well. Positional outlook: Allen is one of three quarterbacks on the current roster. Josh Allen and Shane Buechele are the others. 2026 Offseason: Allen is healthy and he participated in offseason workouts. He’s likely to see lots of action in the preseason. 2026 Season outlook: In some places, the starting quarterback is weak enough where fans and pundits clamor for the backup quarterback to take the field. With the Bills, it’s the exact opposite: The starting quarterback is elite, so absolutely no one hopes that the backup sees a snap that doesn’t involve garbage-time kneel-downs this season. If Kyle Allen does have to play for an extended time, it likely spells curtains for the Bills. He hasn’t had any extended playing time in the NFL since the 2022 season when he started two games for the Houston Texans. He was mildly successful in his one season starting with the Carolina Panthers, throwing 17 touchdowns and 16 interceptions in 13 games back in 2019, but let’s be realistic here: Josh Allen is one of one. Kyle Allen, while he might be a great locker room guy and a serviceable veteran to hold the clipboard on Sundays, isn’t the man we want taking snaps. With all of that said, Allen is worlds better than Shane Buechele, the only other person vying for a role on the sidelines on Sundays. Kyle Allen will be Josh Allen’s backup this season.

title: First-read targets a metric to watch with Buffalo Bills with Joe Brady as head coach
summary: How much the offense will look different in 2026 versus 2025 has been a significant topic if discussion ever since former offensive coordinator Joe Brady was announced as the new Buffalo Bills head coach following the dismissal of former head coach Sean McDermott. How much the offense was influenced by McDermott’s desires, and in what […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: DJ Moore #2 of the Chicago Bears stands on the field prior to an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images How much the offense will look different in 2026 versus 2025 has been a significant topic if discussion ever since former offensive coordinator Joe Brady was announced as the new Buffalo Bills head coach following the dismissal of former head coach Sean McDermott. How much the offense was influenced by McDermott’s desires, and in what ways, is a largely speculative topic. And while the truth is that we’ll won’t really know until the bullets start flying in week one what is true, the next logical question after “how much will be different” is “how will we know”? Apart from diving into route concepts and outlining on film new or unfamiliar pieces of the offense in 2026 versus 2025, run/pass ratio is likely to be a hot topic early in the regular season. With the Bills being at the top of the league in overall run rate over the last few seasons, how pass happy the team is or is not out of the gate will likely be an easy barometer for many people when seeking to find the differential between a “Brady-envisioned offense” and a “McDermott-envisioned offense run by Brady.” But allow me, if you would, to offer an additional (not alternative) metric for us to keep an eye on early in 2026 that may show some departure from previous years and could help show a departure from the offense of the past: first read targets. In 2025, these were the Bills’ leaders in first-read (or designed) targets, sorted by first read/designed targets per game, per Fantasy Points: Khalil Shakir – 69 first read targets (4.21 per game, 23.5% of team’s total) Keon Coleman – 46 (3.54, 19.3%) Dalton Kincaid – 38 (3.16, 17.3%) Gabe Davis – 14 (2.33, 12.3%) Joshua Palmer – 27 (2.25, 11.7%) Brandin Cooks – 10 (1.43, 11.2%) Dawson Knox – 34 (2.00, 10.8%) Elijah Moore – 12 (1.33, 7.1%) Tyrell Shavers – 13 (0.76, 4.1%) Curtis Samuel – 4 (0.67, 3.8%) Mecole Hardman – 1 (0.50, 3.1%) Keleki Latu – 2 (0.40, 2.1%) Jackson Hawes – 5 (0.29, 1.6%) The “spam the screen to Shakir button” narrative was completely justified as it became a story of the 2025 season, but these numbers could look very different even earlier in the season. For one, the Bills have a healthy Dalton Kincaid (and yes, part of that is wishful thinking and aligning myself with the tight end himself saying he’s never felt better). The numbers above are sorted by first read/designed targets per game , which means we’re controlling for the time Kincaid missed, but we’re not controlling for any limiting the Bills may have had to do with him due to lingering knee issues. Games where his overall snap count wasn’t what it otherwise would have been if not for load management are included (Kincaid didn’t play a game with more than 35 snaps from Week 6 all the way until the end of the regular season). He would have ended the season No. 2 on this list if not for the injury issues? We can never know for sure, but given his team-leading 0.27 targets per route run, that feels probable. The second consideration to this list looking different is, of course, the addition of wide receiver DJ Moore, brought to the team early in the offseason with via a trade with the Chicago Bears. Moore not only slots in as the team’s likely top wide receiver target overall, but also provides a screen presence the Bills funneled almost exclusively through Shakir previously. So by all accounts, the list should look markedly different this year than last. Moore and Kincaid will likely be No. 1/No. 2 in some order, and Shakir and Coleman will likely see their gold and silver spots vacated. How much of a delta there is between the top two or three and the remainder of the team will help determine if the “everybody eats” era of the Bills passing attack is officially over. Was it there out of necessity because the Bills lacked a top target and their first-round hyper-efficient tight end was injured? Was it a McDermott thing? Or is that just who they are and will always be under Joe Brady? The Bills had six players with 10% or greater first read/designed target percentage in their offensive in 2025. The only other teams that had six players in that category were the Las Vegas Raiders and the Miami Dolphins. Only one team (the Green Bay Packers) had seven players with 10% or more first read/designed targets. The team did truly spread the focus of their offense around in 2025. I’ll be keeping an eye on what this looks like to open 2026. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!

summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: ATLANTA - DECEMBER 18: Punter Todd Sauerbrun #10 of the Carolina Panthers looks on against the Atlanta Falcons on December 18, 2004 at the Georgia Dome in Atlanta, Georgia. The Falcons defeated the Panthers 34-31 in overtime.(Photo by Streeter Lecka/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #53. Todd Sauerbrun One of the most fun things in football is when a player that should not be the center of attention makes themselves the center of attention. The Carolina Panthers had that with punter Todd Sauerbrun, for better or for worse. He was the best punter in franchise history, but he might be more remembered for his antics and personality than his actual play on the field. Sauerbrun came into the NFL as a second ( 2nd! ) round pick of the Chicago Bears. He spent five years there before playing one year in Kansas City. He signed with the Panthers in 2001, and boy did he time in perfectly. The Panthers had an absolutely abysmal offense in Sauerbrun’s first two seasons, which gave the burly punter plenty of opportunities to bomb punts. He was top three in the league in total punts (sick brag) and led the league in total punt yards in both seasons. He was a first team all pro in both of those seasons, then followed that up with a second team all pro in the following season. The 2004 season saw his production dip just a smidge while the off field issues start to become too much to deal with. He departed after that season and went on to be other people’s problem. In 2004, Panthers kicker John Kasay got hurt, which set off a whole host of problems with Sauerbrun. First, Sauerbrun pressured the team to not sign their preferred replacement Bill Gramatica because he disliked the entire Gramatica family. Then, he offered to pull double duty, but only on the condition that the Panthers forgive some of the money they had fined him for being overweight. That obviously didn’t go over well. Then, to make matters worse, he was arrested for driving while intoxicated late in the season. He was also linked to the Panthers steroid scandal a couple months later. You can’t have that many distractions from your punter, no matter how he good he is. While Sauerbrun had more than his fair share of troubles and controversies, he was still the best punter the Panthers have ever had. Being the best ever at your position earns you a spot in the Panthers’ top 100, even if you’re kind of a jerk.

title: OT Taylor Moton will miss time due to blood clots, CB Jaycee Horn joins him on NFI list for the Panthers
summary: This afternoon, we found out OT Taylor Moton will likely miss time due to being diagnosed and treated due to blood clots in his lungs. Reportedly, Taylor Moton was diagnosed in June and is currently receiving treatment. He will likely miss the early part of the season as he’s placed on the NFI list. This […]
full_text: NFL Carolina Panthers offensive tackle Taylor Moton | Bob Donnan-Imagn Images This afternoon, we found out OT Taylor Moton will likely miss time due to being diagnosed and treated due to blood clots in his lungs. #Panthers starters CB Jaycee Horn and RT Taylor Moton will be placed on the reserve/NFI list. Moton is dealing with blood clots and he likely will miss the start of the season. Meanwhile, Horn recently had stitches on his foot and should be back soon. — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) July 21, 2026 Reportedly, Taylor Moton was diagnosed in June and is currently receiving treatment. He will likely miss the early part of the season as he’s placed on the NFI list. This news isn’t great for a Panthers squad that will already be missing OT Ikem Ekwonu for likely at least the first half of the season, if not more. The development now means Rasheed Walker, whom the Panthers signed to a one year deal in free agency, will likely be manning the left tackle spot, where 1st round pick from this past draft Monroe Freeling will take on duties as the starting right tackle very early. Freeling was expected to compete with Walker for the left tackle spot, his more natural position. However, with two good offensive tackles on the shelf, Freeling’s timetable to be playing has moved up one way or the other. The Panthers also signed OL Brady Christensen this past week to a one year deal, and he has experience at basically every position along the offensive line, including a few starts at right tackle. He could very well be tasked with starting if Freeling isn’t ready right away, though his timetable is also up in the air due to recovering from a torn Achilles mid way through 2025. The Panthers also announced CB Jaycee Horn will be joining him on said NFI list, though the current speculation is he will be ready for the start of the season. He reportedly suffered a cut on his foot that required stitches, so that situation is much less concerning. Sound off down below on this news in the comments!

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 54 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - FEBRUARY 1: Receiver Ricky Proehl #81 of the Carolina Panthers catches a 12 yard touchdown pass in front of cornerback Asante Samuel #22 of the New England Patriots in the fourth quarter of Super Bowl XXXVIII at Reliant Stadium on February 1, 2004 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Ronald Martinez/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #54. Ricky Proehl Ricky Proehl was a semi-local product, having attended Wake Forest University just a couple hours outside of Charlotte. He had a very good junior season and followed that up with an even better senior campaign, leading him to be selected in the third round of the 1990 NFL Draft by the Phoenix (now Arizona) Cardinals. He immediately was a major factor in the Cardinals offense, getting 99 targets his rookie year despite only starting two games. The following four years saw his targets increase year over year, topping out at 110 in his final season in Arizona. His production matched the targets, averaging about 800 yards and four touchdowns per season. Following the 1994 season, the Cardinals traded Proehl to the Seattle Seahawks for a fourth round pick. Proehl’s Seattle tenure started horribly as he suffered a broken foot in their season opener in 1995. He did return, but ultimately only played eight games that year. The following season was a healthy one for Proehl but a disappointing one, so the Seahawks released him. He signed a one year deal with the Chicago Bears and had a pretty good year, leading to a career changing contract with the then St Louis Rams. Proehl’s first year with the Rams saw him reach a career high in targets opposite Isaac Bruce. The 1999 offseason saw the Rams add Torry Holt via the Draft and Marshall Faulk via trade with the Colts, leading to the legendary Greatest Show on Turf years. Proehl went from borderline top option to fourth option in one offseason but made the most of his now limited opportunities. He posted career highs in first down percentage (the percentage of receptions that resulted in a first down) and yards per target, while also boasting career highs in catch percentage as he truly became Kurt Warner’s reliable “got to have it” target. With a Super Bowl ring in tow and five memorable years in St Louis, Proehl signed on with a young up and coming team out of Charlotte. It was just the second year into John Fox’s tenure as head coach, and the team looked to be headed in the right direction despite being full of youth. The wide receiver room, in particular, had some promising but unseasoned players in Muhsin Muhammad and Steve Smith, and Proehl took on the grizzled veteran mentor role while maintaining his security blanket role for unheralded quarterback Jake Delhomme. Evidence of this limited but immensely important connection came in the very first game of Proehl’s Panthers tenure when Delhomme, the backup at the time who was inserted at half time, found Proehl with just 16 seconds left for a 12 yard game winning touchdown. That game launched the Panthers first Super Bowl run, and Proehl was at the center of many important moments. He had a couple major first down receptions late in the fourth quarter of Week 2 against the Bucs that led to an eventual overtime win. Proehl also hauled in one of the most iconic passes of the Panthers short history in Super Bowl XXXVIII. Trailing the Patriots with just over a minute to go in regulation, Delhomme again found his “ole reliable” receiver in the endzone from 12 yards out, tying the game at 29. While the Panthers would end up losing the game, Proehl’s performance would cement him in Panthers lore. He spent two more seasons with the Panthers before retiring after the 2005 season. Though his statistical impact pales in comparison to other short-tenured Panthers, his role on one of the most successful Panthers teams in franchise history is undeniable. He also returned to coach the wide receivers from 2011-2017, helping a ragtag group of busts and no-name receivers become a corps helped the team reach the Super Bowl in 2015. Hopeful future Hall of Famer Steve Smith credits Proehl for a large part of his own success due to Proehl’s mentorship helping Smith focus his infamous fiery play style. From his clutch plays on a Super Bowl bound team to his mentorship of younger receivers as a veteran player and as a coach, Proehl has no doubt earned his spot at No. 54 on our countdown of the Top 100 Panthers.

title: Chicago Bears’ Tight Ends Coach Jim Dray is a Breakout Candidate
summary: Well-coached and successful teams, which the Chicago Bears now appear to be, always run the risk of their assistant coaches being hired away. The Ben Johnson era was just a season old, and the Bears lost offensive coordinator Declan Doyle to the Baltimore Ravens and running backs coach Eric Bieniemy to the Kansas City Chiefs. […]
full_text: Nov 3, 2024; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Chicago Bears tight ends coach Jim Dray against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images Well-coached and successful teams, which the Chicago Bears now appear to be, always run the risk of their assistant coaches being hired away. The Ben Johnson era was just a season old, and the Bears lost offensive coordinator Declan Doyle to the Baltimore Ravens and running backs coach Eric Bieniemy to the Kansas City Chiefs. If Johnson’s offense is among the league’s best again in 2026, the other 31 teams will certainly be sniffing around his coaching staff. In a recent article by The Athletic’s Jourdan Rodrigue , she identified Bears tight ends coach Jim Dray as an assistant coach who could break out in 2026. “Other than the quarterback, Bears coach Ben Johnson has made it clear that tight end is the most important element of his layered, explosive offensive system,” Rodrique wrote. “That especially highlights Dray, whom Johnson retained from the Matt Eberflus-era staff. Dray will be coaching one of the most talented position rooms in the NFL, featuring Cole Kmet, Colston Loveland, and rookie third-rounder Sam Roush.” Johnson was a tight ends coach for two years in Detroit before the Lions promoted him to offensive coordinator. The aforementioned Declan Doyle was the tight ends coach in Denver for two years under Sean Payton before Johnson hired him away last year. After an eight-year playing career, Dray has been coaching in the NFL since 2018 and has been coaching tight ends in Chicago since 2022. He was one of two offensive assistants retained when offensive coordinator Luke Getsy was fired in 2024, and the only offensive assistant retained when Ben Johnson took over in 2025. Besides Dray, do you think any other Chicago assistants could be poached in 2027?

title: Five Questions Surrounding The Chicago Bears Heading Into Training Camp
summary: Fresh off their first NFC North title in seven seasons, the Chicago Bears are entering training camp with a sense of continuity. Head coach Ben Johnson enters his second year as the head man, and aside from a few minor shuffles, his coaching staff remains largely intact. Coupled with a roster that should be close […]
full_text: Fresh off their first NFC North title in seven seasons, the Chicago Bears are entering training camp with a sense of continuity. Head coach Ben Johnson enters his second year as the head man, and aside from a few minor shuffles, his coaching staff remains largely intact. Coupled with a roster that should be close to 70% of last season’s starters, this offseason has felt much calmer than in past seasons. Despite a high level of continuity and the optimism coming off their first postseason victory in 15 seasons, there are still plenty of unanswered questions heading into the regular season. While it’s fair to say the Bears arrived a year early last year, the hunter has now become the hunted, and the league will be on notice. We’ve seen iterations of this team making the playoffs before, but it’s been two decades since they’ve had back-to-back seasons with playoff appearances. With more pressure and higher expectations, we’ll dive into five pressing questions surrounding the Bears as they head into training camp ahead of the 2026 regular season. 1. Will quarterback Caleb Williams and the offense finally hit the ground running? If we’re talking about the start of training camp, this is likely to be the topic on everyone’s mind. For too long, fans have been subjected to a struggling offense early in camp that will show flashes of “good days” but ultimately never catch up to the defense. Then the regular season rolls around, and it’s as bad as most feared. Last year’s struggles were a little more understandable. Still, although they finished as a Top 10 offense by season’s end, they opened the regular season looking disjointed, minor the Week 3 explosion against the Cowboys. While it’s probably unfair to expect the offense to dominate the defense in every practice completely, a more even affair, without constant penalties and with the ball hitting the ground, is what most fans will be looking for. On paper, the offense is returning all but three starters from last season. We’ll get to some of those battles later on, but in terms of continuity, this has been the most stability the offense has seen in quite some time. Early struggles may occur, but ultimately, this offense needs to hit the ground running without the same avoidable mistakes we heard about last August. Here’s to hoping the nonchalant pre-season preparation will remain just that. 2. Sorting out the offensive line: Who wins out at left tackle and center? There won’t be many open competitions for starting jobs once camp opens. Still, thanks to a playoff injury to Ozzy Trapilo and a surprise retirement from Drew Dalman, two openings on the starting offensive line will be up for grabs. In an ideal world, both competitions will be wrapped up quickly, and the team will have plenty of time to get their starting five together. As we learned with last year’s left tackle competition, that perfect world rarely exists in football. We’ll first start at center, where it’s a two-player race to see who gets the Week 1 nod. By all accounts, veteran Garrett Bradbury, for whom the Bears traded a 2027 fifth-round selection, holds the edge. Johnson has never hidden that he values a veteran presence at the position, which is why they splurged on Dalman during last year’s free-agent period. Although Bradbury is far from the overall player that Dalman was, he provides a level of stability that would be hard for any rookie to match. That said, Jones is an experienced player on the older side compared to most early-round draft prospects. He started 38 games over the last three seasons and comes from a school that is known for churning out NFL-ready offensive linemen. There’s no doubt that Jones will be viewed as the long-term replacement for Dalman, but with questions still lingering at left tackle, don’t be surprised to see the coaching staff default to the veteran early in the season. Even if that happens, last year was a prime example of how this staff is not afraid to shake things up as the season goes along. At left tackle, three of the four names are extremely familiar. That said, this feels like a two-man competition, headlined by fifth-year veteran Braxton Jones and recently signed Jedrick Wills. While it’s possible that Theo Benedet or Kiran Amegadjie could end up in the mix, a healthy Jones comfortably wins this competition. To take it a step further, I’d say it’s more likely that Amegadjie isn’t on the 53-man roster than that he outright wins the starting job. The biggest unknown in this group is Wills, and not due to ability. Health will be a sizable factor for him heading into camp. When healthy, his ceiling is the highest on the roster. The issue is that he has not been healthy in a few years. With Trapilo not expected to play this season, getting average-quality left tackle play would be a big win for this entire unit. Outside of the two starting spots, how the depth shakes out will be interesting to watch. For the first time in a while, the Bears have more depth than roster spots along the offensive line. Call it the Ben Johnson effect, but it’s a great “problem” to have. One would believe that the “loser” of the left tackle competition will earn a spot, as well as whoever loses out at center. Add in Luke Newman, and you’re already at eight. Benedet seems like a lock too, which makes nine, barring a trade of Bradbury if Jones wins the job. The biggest question in this particular situation is how many bodies they’ll keep. Teams typically keep between eight and 10, and it wouldn’t be a shock if Chicago kept 10. Assuming that 10 is the final number, that leaves one spot for Jordan McFadden, Amegadjie, or any of the undrafted free agents they signed in May. Suffice it to say, there will be a few rosterable players who won’t be on the Bears’ final 53-man roster. 3. How quickly does an extension for right tackle Darnell Wright come together? I’ve written about this a few times, and frankly, until it happens, the storyline won’t go away. That’s not to say this is something to be concerned about by any means, but rather that it will happen sooner rather than later. Last month, in my 10 Bears takes, I covered the different paths his market might take. While some will point to Lane Johnson’s one-year $25 million extension as a baseline, I don’t believe that will be the case. More realistically, the deals that both Tristan Wirfs and Penei Sewell signed (while playing right tackle) are more in line with what fans should expect: anywhere from four to five years and an average value of right around $28 million per season. Simply put, it won’t be cheap, but it has been well earned, and Wright is still a rising talent with an All-Pro level ceiling. Given how quickly the cap continues to rise, establishing a “new” market at right tackle makes sense. It’s also worth mentioning that, because he has this year and next year’s fifth-year option in terms of control, the Bears can spread some of his new money over these two cheaper years to ultimately lower the cap hit once the extension kicks in. Now, getting to a timeline for when a deal could be struck. Former general manager Ryan Pace tended to get deals done before training camp, but current general manager Ryan Poles has been a little less predictable. While a deal could be struck before the end of July, don’t be surprised to see things drag out until August or early September. Part of that could simply be cap manipulation to see if they can swing a deal for someone (more on that in a few), and some of it could be to see if any other extensions come through that change the dynamic of their negotiations. One way or another, Wright is under contract for at least two seasons, and it’s clear that, of all their starting offensive linemen, he’s the future of this group. I fully expect a deal to get done, and when it does, fans can expect it to eat anywhere from $2-3.5 million from this year’s cap space. With that in mind, Poles has been extremely conservative with his…

(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re starting on the d-line with our Chicago Bears’ training camp positional preview articles, and after looking at EDGE yesterday, today is all about the interior. While the Bears didn’t add any defensive ends this offseason (not a single one!), they did add some tackles to compete. Roster Locks Grady Jarrett fought through an early injury last year and played better in the second half. He was DT3 most of last season, which is a perfect role for him, but it should come with a decrease in playing time in 2026. He played the third-most snaps on the entire d-line in 2025, and that’s with missing three games. He’s at that age (33) where even a minor setback could derail his season, so keeping him fresh and healthy should be a priority for the Bears. Gervon Dexter Sr. is entering his contract year, and thus far, there has been no reported movement on an extension. His sacks have increased each of the past three years, but I get the feeling the Bears may let him walk after this season, unless he improves his overall play and consistency. The Bears added Neville Gallimore on a two-year deal worth about $10 million, and the 29-year-old will look to build off his career-best 2025, where he had 38 tackles and 3.5 sacks. “The interior of the Bears defensive line, headlined in 2025 by Gervon Dexter Sr., Grady Jarrett and Andrew Billings, was not good enough,” NFL.com’s Matt Okada wrote in a recent article detailing every team’s biggest remaining roster issue. “Chicago struggled mightily against the run and logged the sixth-lowest QB pressure rate. This spring, they replaced Billings with the equally average Neville Gallimore and added a few more depth pieces. In other words: zero improvement, as I see it. In a competitive division — where weak trenches could be a death knell — this feels like a potentially major issue.” Either these three need to play at a much higher level in 2026, or one of the remaining d-tackles needs to step up and surprise, because this position could be a problem. A Good Bet To Make It Someone needs to win the fourth spot in the rotation, but the rest of the roster is made up of rookies and league minimum-type players, so there should be a spirited battle. Roster Bubble/Practice Squad The Bears traded two seventh-round picks to get into the sixth round for Jordan ven den Berg from Georgia Tech. He’s a fantastic athlete who plays with power, but he was a day-three pick for a reason. He needs to tighten up his technique and become more consistent. Jayden Loving was a 2026 UDFA from Wake Forrest, and much like ven den Berg, he needs to hone his technique and become more consistent. But that athletic upside is intriguing. NFL scouts timed 308 LB DT Jayden Loving between a 4.68-4.78 in the 40 yard dash at the Wake Forest Pro Day. He also jumped 35 inches on the vertical. He bench pressed 225 LBS 33 reps. His agility drills would rank #1 at the NFL Combine among all DTs. Hopefully NFL teams will go… https://t.co/xcAU7ncIGT pic.twitter.com/6MabpRzpxo — Coach Clif Marshall (@ClifMarshall) March 25, 2026 James Lynch has played in 71 games in his career (2020 to 2025) with 4 starts. He missed the 2023 season with a torn ACL, but played in every game the last two years for the Titans, including a career-high 334 defensive snaps in 2025. Kentavius Street played for Dennis Allen in New Orleans in 2022, and that familiarity could give him a leg up as the DT4. The 30-year-old spent the first half of last year on the Falcons’ practice squad, but was added to their 53-man roster and played 216 defensive snaps in seven games. Who do you think makes the 53 at defensive tackle for the Bears?

title: Answering Dan Hoard’s 5 questions entering Bengals Training Camp 2026
summary: Bengals Training Camp is a week away from getting underway on the Kettering Health Practice Fields behind Paycor Stadium. Storylines abound, and there are many questions going into camp and about the Bengals’ 2026 season. For the second straight season, the Voice of the Bengals, Dan Hoard, released an episode of the Bengals Booth Podcast […]
full_text: Oct 16, 2025; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals center Ted Karras (64) reacts after Cincinnati defeated the Pittsburgh Steelers on a late-game field goal by placekicker Evan McPherson (2) (not pictured) during the fourth quarter at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | Katie Stratman-Imagn Images Bengals Training Camp is a week away from getting underway on the Kettering Health Practice Fields behind Paycor Stadium. Storylines abound, and there are many questions going into camp and about the Bengals’ 2026 season. For the second straight season, the Voice of the Bengals, Dan Hoard, released an episode of the Bengals Booth Podcast where he asked five identical questions to seven Bengals beat writers as we get ready for the grind of Training Camp. Richard Skinner (retired Local12 columnist), James Rapien (host of First Word on The Crown, host of Enter the Jungle on Cincinnati Bengals Talk, publisher/writer for All Bengals at Sports Illustrated), Mike Petraglia (columnist for CLNS Media), Jay Morrison (writer for All Bengals and Sports Illustrated), Paul Dehner Jr. (columnist for The Athletic, host of The Growler Podcast), Kelsey Conway (writer for the Cincinnati Enquirer), and Ben Baby (writer for ESPN.com) all joined Dan Hoard on the latest Bengals Booth Podcast episode to share their answers to Dan’s five questions. After all seven members of the beat shared their answers, Dan shared his own. Now, I’m giving you my answers to Dan’s questions. You can listen to this full episode of the Bengals Booth Podcast below. View Link 1. What is your biggest question going into Training Camp? I actually have three big storylines going into Bengals Training Camp this year. First, how good is the Bengals’ interior offensive line? Orlando Brown Jr. and Amarius Mims are rock solid at the tackles, but what about the inside of the Bengals’ offensive line? Can Dylan Fairchild build on a solid rookie season? Will Ted Karras still be that rock-solid guy at center in his age-33 season? Is Dalton Risner the long-term answer at right guard? It’s going to be fascinating to see these three go up against a completely remade Bengals’ interior defensive line, with the likes of Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, B.J. Hill, and the second wave of T.J. Slaton, Kris Jenkins Jr., and McKinnley Jackson. Iron sharpens iron, and that will hopefully be the case for the Bengals’ interior offensive line and the Bengals’ defensive line in Training Camp. Second, who is this team’s WR3? Is Andrei Ioisvas going to break out like we kept hearing that he could in each of the last two seasons? What’s Colbie Young’s role going to be? Depth is thin behind Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. Sure, there are some fun pieces in Charlie Jones and Mitchell Tinsley. But who steps up behind Chase and Higgins is a major question. Third, are the Bengals’ edge rushers going to be a difference-maker on this team? If they are, even after Trey Hendrickson left in free agency this offseason, that would be a major accomplishment. But with Boye Mafe, Myles Murphy, Shemar Stewart, and Cassius Howell in the fold, there is an infusion of talent at a position that’s a huge value and difference-maker in the NFL. Is Stewart going to rewrite an early narrative on his career? Is Mafe entering the prime of his career? Does Murphy build on a strong second half last year? What’s Howell’s role going to be? The edge rushers on this team are fascinating because they’re not getting a lot of attention, but they could. 2. Who is this year’s breakout player? I so wanted to go Jack Endries for this one because he’s, low-key, my favorite draft pick on the Bengals this season. But I’ll save him for another question. For this year’s breakout, I’m going Boye Mafe. Look at who Mafe played with on the Seattle Seahawks’ defense last year, a defense that led the Seahawks to the Super Bowl LX title. If you’re wondering why Mafe’s numbers were down in 2025, that’s why. But it was his ability to pressure the quarterback that impacted Leonard Williams, Uchenna Nwosu, DeMarcus Lawrence, Byron Murphy II, and Jarran Reed and all of their abilities to finish at the quarterback. Now in Cincinnati, Mafe has a greater chance to have bigger numbers this season. While the Bengals’ defensive line is retooled on paper, we still haven’t seen it on the field yet. We know what Mafe can do, and he’s only three seasons removed from a nine-sack season. We saw how great Trey Hendrickson became in his five seasons with the Bengals, and his career took off after signing with them in free agency. Maybe Mafe will have a similar trajectory. 3. Who is this year’s Mitchell Tinsley? Jack Endries. I’m a big fan of the Bengals’ seventh-round pick. He had a really good college career at both California and Texas, and he’s coming in with a chip on his shoulder. The sure-handed pass-catcher could be an asset to the Bengals in short-yardage situations, the red zone, goal-to-go scenarios, and even in between the 40s where a conversion could nullify having to make a decision on whether to punt, go for it, or kick a long field goal. 4. The Bengals win the AFC North if… what? Well, first of all, they need to sweep the Browns. Seriously. Myles Garrett isn’t even in Cleveland anymore. But I’ll echo something Paul Dehner Jr. said, and that’s this Bengals’ offense needs to come out swinging against their division rivals. Remember 2021, when the Bengals swept both the Steelers and Ravens? The Bengals put up 41 points in both games against the Ravens and once against the Steelers. Joe Burrow threw for 941 yards in two games against the Ravens, and Ja’Marr Chase had 326 receiving yards in those two games. Can the Bengals counter the counters the Ravens, Steelers, and Browns showed over the last four seasons? I want to see the Bengals’ offense just come out and unleash an aerial attack that decimates all three teams, whether at home or on the road. Yeah, the Bengals may be constructed differently than the other three teams in the AFC North. But in those division games, screw that. Play your game, and make them beat you. 5. Give a sizzling hot take about the 2026 Bengals I hope you’re ready for this one. For clarity, I don’t 100% believe this will happen. But the point of a hot take, at least in my opinion, is to predict something that could happen but you may not necessarily believe will. This is a two-part hot take. Here goes. The Bengals will HOST the AFC Championship Game against the Pittsburgh Steelers. What an environment that would be if it happens: A night game in The Jungle against the Steelers, with a trip to the Super Bowl on the line. But wait, let’s add something to this. Part two is that Joe Flacco will have to come in for a significant play or drive in the fourth quarter because of something that happens to Joe Burrow. Whether it be a stinger, cramps, or being evaluated for a concussion, Flacco will have to come in for a play or drive, or a half, and I believe he will deliver. Can you imagine if that happens?

full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JANUARY 29: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals and Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs meet on the field after the AFC Championship Game at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on January 29, 2023 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images When it comes to rivalries, the Cincinnati Bengals have some of the NFL’s best. There’s always going to be animosity between division rivals, but the Bengals have two of the league’s most heated rivalries with the Baltimore Ravens and Pittsburgh Steelers. Anytime the Bengals face one of them, emotions run high, as those matchups typically have playoff implications, and these teams frankly hate each other with a passion. And we can’t forget about the battle of Ohio with the Cleveland Browns, even if they have struggled to stay relevant compared to Baltimore and Pittsburgh. But when it comes to the Bengals’ biggest current rival, that may lie outside the division. Ever since Joe Burrow arrived in Cincinnati, the Kansas City Chiefs have arguably been their biggest rival, especially when it comes to competing for championships. The two clubs met in back-to-back AFC Championship Games from 2021-22 that were instant classics as they split the series. They’ve also had several highly-contested regular-season matchups, including two Bengals wins in 2021 and 2022 that helped them win the AFC North. In all, the two teams have faced off six times since the 2021 season, as though they actually are division opponents, and they’ll have another late-season matchup this year that could have massive playoff implications. title: Multiple outlets rank Dexter Lawrence among the NFL’s top 5 defensive tackles
summary: It is no secret the Cincinnati Bengals needed to do something about their defense, and they needed to do it as soon as possible. The front office truly went all in this offseason to fix that side of the ball, and although it isn’t perfect, the defense is much improved for 2026. The biggest name […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - DECEMBER 28: Dexter Lawrence II #97 of the New York Giants walks off the field during halftime of the game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is no secret the Cincinnati Bengals needed to do something about their defense, and they needed to do it as soon as possible. The front office truly went all in this offseason to fix that side of the ball, and although it isn’t perfect, the defense is much improved for 2026. The biggest name the Bengals brought in this offseason is superstar defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence. Lawrence has been at the top of his position with the New York Giants for years and will now hope to fill a massive hole in the Bengals defense this season. Sports Illustrated has Lawrence listed as the fourth-best defensive tackle in the NFL going into the 2026 season. Lawrence is coming off a down season by his standards, recording just half a sack in 2025 as he returned from an injury, but remains a top-10 defensive tackle in the NFL. Lawrence had one of the best seasons of his career in 2024, as he recorded nine sacks and made his third consecutive Pro Bowl. He was previously a two-time second-team All-Pro in 2022 and 2023. This offseason, the Giants traded Lawrence to the Bengals. Lawrence still ranked top-20 in pass-rush win rate in 2025, but will look to rebound in Cincinnati and help the Bengals’ defense rise from the bottom of the rankings and make the playoffs. Elsewhere, The Associated Press has Lawrence slotted at No. 5 among defensive tackles entering the new season. Lawrence has established himself as the rare nose tackle who can generate pass pressure and stop the run. That made him worth the 10th overall pick when Cincinnati traded for him from the New York Giants before the draft in hopes he can help rebuild a struggling defense. He had 21 sacks from 2022-24, when he made the Pro Bowl all three seasons, but had only a half-sack last season when he faced the fifth-highest double-team rate among defensive tackles at 70.35%, according to PFF. The hype and excitement are there, and Lawrence is in for a big season leading this Bengals defense. Dexter Lawrence commands so much attention. He takes on doubles to free up teammates, and when he is not doubled, he is getting push directly into the lap of the quarterback. Tone setter on the defensive line that will make everyone around him better. pic.twitter.com/yp0PnuN6Zz — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 15, 2026

summary: Wherever you place Joe Burrow among the best QBs in the NFL, there’s no denying he’s in the top five. Meanwhile, you can make a strong argument that his backup, Joe Flacco, is the best thrower of footballs coming off the bench. So it’s no surprise that CBS’ Jordan Dajani has the Bengals QB room […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 27: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals warms up as Joe Flacco #16 looks on prior to the game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on November 27, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images Wherever you place Joe Burrow among the best QBs in the NFL, there’s no denying he’s in the top five. Meanwhile, you can make a strong argument that his backup, Joe Flacco, is the best thrower of footballs coming off the bench. So it’s no surprise that CBS’ Jordan Dajani has the Bengals QB room as the second best in the NFL in his ranking of the five best and five worst QB situations . Here’s some of what he wrote about Burrow: When he remained healthy in 2024, the former No. 1 overall pick led the NFL with 4,918 passing yards and 43 touchdowns while throwing just nine interceptions… Burrow is actually the only quarterback in NFL history to register a 100+ passer rating while making zero playoff starts in a three-season span. He’s also been the most-sacked quarterback (242) since entering the league in 2020, if we include sacks taken in the playoffs. Dajani then explained the value of Flacco, writing: The Bengals also have a former Super Bowl MVP and Comeback Player of the Year in their quarterback room, Joe Flacco — who made the Pro Bowl as an alternate last year. The 40-year-old was starting to look his age with the Browns at the start of 2025, but was rejuvenated by the trade to Cincinnati in October. In his second start with the Bengals, Flacco threw for 342 yards, three touchdowns, zero interceptions and registered his 30th career game-winning drive in an upset of the rival Pittsburgh Steelers. In Week 9, Flacco became the fifth player in NFL history to throw for 470 yards and four touchdowns while scoring 40 points … in a loss. The San Francisco 49ers won the top spot for QB rooms on account of starter Brock Purdy and backup Mac Jones. Third place went to the Kansas City Chiefs, fourth place to the Los Angeles Rams, and fifth place to the Baltimore Ravens. Meanwhile, Dajani named the Cleveland Browns’ QB room the worst in the NFL on account of the “confusion and chaos” of having the $230 million man (Deshaun Watson) on the same roster as the somehow-Pro Bowler Shedeur Sanders. The New York Jets were second worst, the Arizona Cardinals third worst, the Miami Dolphins fourth worst, and the Atlanta Falcons fifth worst.
author: Dadio Makdook

title: Can intriguing rookie Eric Gentry carve out a role in Cincinnati?
summary: Every year, one or two undrafted free agents emerge from relative obscurity to earn meaningful NFL roles. The Cincinnati Bengals are hoping linebacker Eric Gentry can become the next name on that list. After going undrafted out of USC, Gentry landed in Cincinnati as one of the more fascinating developmental prospects in this year’s rookie […]
full_text: Oct 28, 2023; Berkeley, California, USA; USC Trojans linebacker Eric Gentry (18) gestures during the third quarter against the California Golden Bears at California Memorial Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images Every year, one or two undrafted free agents emerge from relative obscurity to earn meaningful NFL roles. The Cincinnati Bengals are hoping linebacker Eric Gentry can become the next name on that list. After going undrafted out of USC, Gentry landed in Cincinnati as one of the more fascinating developmental prospects in this year’s rookie class. At 6-foot-7 with extraordinary length and athleticism, he looks unlike just about any linebacker currently in the NFL. Now, he’ll attempt to turn those rare physical traits into a roster spot under new defensive coordinator Al Golden. Eric Gentry Height: 6’7” Weight: 221 College: USC Age: 23 Years Pro: Entering Rookie Season Hometown: Philadelphia, PA Career at a glance Gentry’s college journey took a unique path. Originally beginning his career at Arizona State, the Philadelphia native flashed immediately as a true freshman before transferring to USC ahead of the 2022 season. Over four years with the Trojans, Gentry developed into one of the defense’s most recognizable playmakers. He totaled 271 career tackles, 27 tackles for loss, nine sacks, two interceptions, 13 passes defended and nine forced fumbles during his collegiate career. But what consistently stood out wasn’t just the production. It was his frame. Standing nearly 6-foot-7 with a wingspan more commonly associated with NBA forwards than NFL linebackers, Gentry became known for disrupting passing lanes, chasing down ball carriers from the backside and serving as a versatile chess piece capable of playing off-ball linebacker while occasionally rushing off the edge. Those traits intrigued NFL evaluators. Questions about his weight, play strength and positional fit ultimately kept him from hearing his name called during the draft. The Bengals wasted little time changing that. Why Cincinnati signed him It’s easy to understand why Al Golden wanted to get a closer look. Gentry simply possesses traits that can’t be coached. His length allows him to affect passing lanes in ways few linebackers can, while his athleticism gives him legitimate sideline-to-sideline range. He’s also shown flashes as a blitzer and has a knack for forcing turnovers, making him an intriguing developmental piece in a defense looking to become faster and more versatile. Of course, there are reasons he entered the league as an undrafted free agent. At roughly 220 pounds, Gentry remains undersized by NFL linebacker standards. He’ll need to add functional strength, improve his ability to shed blocks and become a more consistent tackler before he’s ready for significant defensive snaps. Fortunately for both player and team, Cincinnati doesn’t need him to contribute immediately. 2026 outlook The Bengals significantly reshaped their defense this offseason, but linebacker remains one of the more intriguing position battles entering training camp. Veterans and draft picks are expected to occupy the top spots on the depth chart, meaning Gentry’s clearest path to making the roster will likely come through special teams and showcasing his versatility throughout the preseason. His unique physical profile also opens the door for creative usage. Could Golden eventually mold him into a hybrid linebacker-edge defender? Could he become a designated passing-down defender who drops into coverage while creating disruption with his length? Those answers won’t come overnight. But they’re part of what makes Gentry one of the more fascinating long-term projects on Cincinnati’s roster. What to expect Making the initial 53-man roster won’t be easy for Gentry. The practice squad appears to be the most realistic outcome entering training camp, allowing Gentry to continue developing physically while learning Golden’s defensive system. That shouldn’t be viewed as a disappointment. Several productive Bengals contributors have begun their careers in similar fashion, and Gentry’s athletic ceiling may be higher than that of many players selected late in the draft. If he adds 15 to 20 pounds without sacrificing his movement skills, his long-term outlook becomes even more intriguing. His combination of length, speed and football instincts simply isn’t something teams encounter very often. Final outlook Eric Gentry is the definition of a developmental lottery ticket. His floor may be a practice squad linebacker who contributes on special teams. His ceiling, however, is considerably more interesting. The Bengals have spent the offseason searching for faster, longer and more versatile defenders capable of fitting Al Golden’s evolving scheme. Few players on the roster check those boxes quite like Gentry. He’ll need time, strength and refinement before becoming a meaningful contributor. But if everything clicks, Cincinnati may have quietly uncovered one of the biggest steals of its entire rookie class.
author: Anthony Cosenza

full_text: ENGLEWOOD, COLORADO - JUNE 4: Denver Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II (2), left, and Denver Broncos cornerback Damarri Mathis (27) talks during organized team activities at Broncos Park Powered by CommonSpirit in Englewood, Colorado on June 4, 2024. (Photo by RJ Sangosti/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images When we looked at the Cleveland Browns depth charts , there is a lot of young talent to be found . Unfortunately, the team also lacks the type of veteran, top-level talent needed to be talked about among NFL playoff contenders . The cornerback room is an interesting one with two quality starters, Denzel Ward and Tyson Campbell , followed by a lot of question marks. Just days ago, our projected first six corners looked like this : Starter – Denzel Ward Starter – Tyson Campbell CB3 – Myles Bryant CB4 – Myles Harden CB5 – Dom Jones CB6 – Michael Coats Jr. Cleveland also had the following listed on their 90-man roster at the cornerback position: Trey Avery Nate Evans Tyron Herring D’Angelo Ross Tuesday afternoon, just days before training camp opens, with rookies reporting on Thursday , the Browns waived Dom Jones with a failed physical designation and replaced him with CB Damarri Mathis . Mathis was drafted by the Denver Broncos in the fourth round of the 2022 NFL draft. The 5’11” Mathis spent his first three seasons with the Broncos, starting 18 of the 43 games he played in as well as contributing 300 snaps on special teams. After being waived by Denver during final cuts in 2025, Mathis signed with the Carolina Panthers but tore his ACL in practice and missed all of last season. The 6’2” Jones was an undrafted free agent last year. He played in eight games for the Browns, with 57 snaps on special teams and 49 on defense. The reason for the failed physical has not been announced at the time of this article.

title: Browns free agent signings who overperformed expectations, last 10 years
summary: While the Cleveland Browns have certainly missed on several signings over the last decade, and really missed on at least one trade, several moves greatly surpassed the team’s expectations. Sometimes talent can be found in the most uncertain circumstances. Joe Flacco The Browns were in a desperate position in late November during the 2023 season. Following Deshaun Watson’s injury, […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - DECEMBER 29, 2019: Running back Kareem Hunt #27 of the Cleveland Browns on the field prior to a game against the Cincinnati Bengals on December 29, 2019 at Paul Brown Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio. Cincinnati won 33-23. (Photo by: 2019 Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images While the Cleveland Browns have certainly missed on several signings over the last decade , and really missed on at least one trade , several moves greatly surpassed the team’s expectations. Sometimes talent can be found in the most uncertain circumstances. Joe Flacco The Browns were in a desperate position in late November during the 2023 season. Following Deshaun Watson’s injury, the team needed someone to step in and fill in at quarterback. I don’t think anyone expected 38-year-old Flacco to come in and have the type of impact that he did. He led Cleveland to a 4–1 record and helped the team clinch a playoff berth. He won Comeback Player of the Year for that season and really helped the team to find success in such a turbulent year. Ethan Pocic Pocic joined the Browns on a very cheap one-year deal in 2022 to help with depth on the offensive line. Expectations were low; however, he was put into the starting lineup after center Nick Harris suffered an injury before the season even started. Pocic rose to the challenge, emerging as a consistent and dependable anchor on Cleveland’s offensive line. His play even earned him a three- year extension with the team. Kareem Hunt The Browns signed Hunt during the offseason despite uncertainty over a possible suspension related to off-the-field conduct. It was a risky decision to bring Hunt into the organization when you already had a stable situation with Nick Chubb at running back. Hunt ended up being the perfect complement to Chubb, and the two had many years of success in the backfield together. title: 3 massive Browns questions heading into 2026 training camp
summary: As we get closer and closer to training camp, three Cleveland Browns questions continue to linger on both offense and defense. It’s about time we outline them and discuss how they could sort themselves out during camp. What’s the plan at linebacker for 2026? This has been one of the more overlooked storylines of the […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - MAY 08: Denzel Boston #12 and KC Concepcion #17 of the Cleveland Browns listen to a play call from Taylen Green #15 during a rookie minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on May 08, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images As we get closer and closer to training camp, three Cleveland Browns questions continue to linger on both offense and defense. It’s about time we outline them and discuss how they could sort themselves out during camp. What’s the plan at linebacker for 2026? This has been one of the more overlooked storylines of the offseason, but it’s also one of the biggest mysteries right now. What is Cleveland planning to do if one of Carson Schwesinger or Quincy Williams gets hurt? Who is going to be the third linebacker when the team isn’t in a nickel defense? How does new DC Mike Rutenberg feel about rookie Justin Jefferson ? Countless questions surround the team’s current linebacker room, and they’ll absolutely have to be addressed in training camp and throughout the preseason. Schwesinger and Williams form a top-notch duo, but behind them are guys like Winston Reid , Easton Mascarenas-Arnold , Nathaniel Watson , and rookie 5th-rounder Justin Jefferson. It’s pretty safe to say that those names aren’t very exciting, and it feels like one more legitimate veteran should’ve been added this offseason. How will the starting offensive line shake out ? Heading into training camp season, all Cleveland fans know is that the team added Zion Johnson , Elgton Jenkins , and Tytus Howard in free agency, re-signed Teven Jenkins , and drafted Spencer Fano , Austin Barber , and Parker Brailsford . What everyone doesn’t know is where they’ll end up playing in 2026 and beyond. As of right now, it’s logical to think that the starting five would be: LT – Spencer Fano LG – Teven Jenkins C – Elgton Jenkins RG – Zion Johnson RT – Tytus Howard This is at least what the perception was when everyone was first signed, but it’s been sounding like Todd Monken and the rest of the offensive staff could want it to look like this: LT – Spencer Fano LG – Elgton Jenkins C – Parker Brailsford RG – Zion Johnson RT – Tytus Howard Honestly, this feels like a much better lineup, with Elgton Jenkins being used in his natural position. Whatever the case, it’s going to be extremely interesting to see how the offensive line evolves throughout training camp. What will the wide receiver rotation look like? This is probably the biggest question mark heading into camp, as it’s been one of the team’s biggest problems over the past couple of seasons. Andrew Berry and Co. did a great job this offseason of attacking the wide receiver position in the NFL draft with K.C. Concepcion and Denzel Boston being taken in rounds one and two, and adding an underrated talent in Tylan Wallace via free agency. On paper, things look a lot better than they did in 2025, with the depth chart probably looking like this: X – Denzel Boston, Cedric Tillman Z – Jerry Jeudy , Tylan Wallace SLOT – K.C. Concepcion, Isaiah Bond Though the team will likely only keep six receivers heading into week one, it wouldn’t be surprising to see someone like Malachi Corley make his way onto the roster. He looked really good over the last 4-5 games of the 2025 season, and he ended up being the Browns’ go-to option on their quick-hitting inside sweep play. What other questions do you have entering training camp? Join fellow Browns fans in the comment section below.

title: Browns offseason look back: 5 decisions that concern me
summary: As a generally optimistic person, fan, and media member, I can almost always figure out a way to understand why a team made a move that they did. For me, it is a much more enjoyable way to go about sports, instead of spending a ton of energy on how things could go wrong. That […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 03: Jared Verse #8 of the Cleveland Browns answers questions from the media during a press conference after the Cleveland Browns OTA Offseason Workouts at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 03, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images As a generally optimistic person, fan, and media member, I can almost always figure out a way to understand why a team made a move that they did. For me, it is a much more enjoyable way to go about sports, instead of spending a ton of energy on how things could go wrong. That being said, the Cleveland Browns have also spent most of my adult lifetime making decisions that blew up in their face , often predictably bad. Many of us Browns fans haven’t had to imagine ways things would fail; we just had to wait for them to fail. On Monday, I shared the five moves from Cleveland’s recent offseason that I loved . Even those moves required some level of optimistic thinking. Today, we flip the coin to the other side and look at the things that are concerning. Full disclosure: I hope the Browns prove me wrong in every single one of these concerns. I want nothing but great things for the team and, more importantly, the fanbase. That being said, I have to be honest about decisions that at least had me pause my giddy optimism: Hiring Todd Monken I have no clue if Monken will be a good head coach, but I do know that no one else in the NFL has hired him for the position and rarely has he even made it to the final stage with any other team. That alone causes pause. Cleveland has long done things no other team has done, and it has never (rarely?) worked out. Monken is just the next choice that fits that bill. To be frank, none of the other options were certain home runs either. As shared on Monday, an offensive-minded coach was a positive thing, but I would have much preferred a younger guy who could grow with the group. My entire goal is that the Browns win a Super Bowl, so I’m more willing to take upside, risky swings. Handling of Jim Schwartz Since the hiring of Monken and Schwartz’s departure, it seems like the team clearly wanted to hire an offensive-minded guy as head coach. If so, the Browns should not have strung Schwartz along, should not have made him a finalist for the job, and should have been far more upfront with him. It might work out in the end, with new DC Mike Rutenberg bringing a more varied, flexible system for Cleveland’s defense, but even that will be hard to tell given the departure of Myles Garrett via trade. Mid-level solutions to most of the OLine Drafting Spencer Fano fell on the “loved” list, but the rest of the offensive line revamp at least gives reason for pause. It is very rare that a quality offensive lineman is available in the NFL. That the Houston Texans were willing to trade away Tytus Howard, and the Los Angeles Chargers and Green Bay Packers were willing to let Zion Johnson and Elgton Jenkins walk away in free agency gives me reason for pause. That doesn’t mean a new setting and system won’t fix things for these players, but there was a reason Howard, Johnson, and Jenkins were available, and now Cleveland’s offense is depending on all three of them to fix a huge issue. I have some concerns about that being possible. Jared Verse being the key to the Myles Garrett trade Verse is really good. Verse is really vocal. Verse is really young and has already hit on some big accolades. The only concern on the field with Verse is whether he can be the 1A pass rusher in a 4-3 system. We will find out this season. The concern is that GM Andrew Berry required a player of a certain level, with a certain contract, to deal away Garrett. From a value perspective, it is possible that the Browns could have gotten more for Garrett if they were open to a draft-pick-only deal. Would the Philadelphia Eagles have traded a first in 2027, two firsts in 2028, and more for Garrett? Would another team make a similar offer if a Verse-level player wasn’t required? My concern doesn’t mean the deal wasn’t a good one, but it puts a lot of pressure on Verse to be something he hasn’t proven he can be and could have led to a smaller overall package in return for Garrett. Not being more aggressive trying to sign Tyler Linderbaum Is a three-year deal worth $81 million a huge overpay for a center? Yes. Did the Las Vegas Raiders think it was worth it because of the young quarterback they would be drafting first overall later in the offseason? Also, yes. Signing Linderbaum, given everything else Cleveland did this offseason, would have helped solidify the offensive line, brought over someone Monken knows well, given Shedeur Sanders and Deshaun Watson the best chance to succeed, and provided high-level stability if the Browns draft a quarterback high in the 2027 NFL draft. Most of the reporting was that Cleveland was interested in Linderbaum but was not aggressive with their offers, compared to the Raiders. The Browns have over $16 million in cap space right now (can add significantly more by restructuring Denzel Ward’s deal) and gave the 31-year-old Jenkins a two-year contract worth $24 million. Spending that kind of money on the 26-year-old Linderbaum would have made a ton of sense for where Cleveland’s roster is and will be moving forward.
