title: Cowboys 2026 roster rundown: K Brandon Aubrey
summary: Just three months ago, the Cowboys made Brandon Aubrey the highest-paid kicker in NFL history. Naturally, any discussion about his place on this year’s roster is pretty anti-climactic now. But like so many meals, this series just won’t feel complete without Butter. Background Years in NFL: 3Acquired by: Free agent (2023) Until he was 24 years old, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 23: Brandon Aubrey #17 of the Dallas Cowboys looks on from the sideline during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just three months ago, the Cowboys made Brandon Aubrey the highest-paid kicker in NFL history. Naturally, any discussion about his place on this year’s roster is pretty anti-climactic now. But like so many meals, this series just won’t feel complete without Butter. Background Years in NFL: 3 Acquired by: Free agent (2023) Until he was 24 years old, Aubrey’s athletic aspirations were focused on soccer. He played collegiately for Notre Dame and then had two years in professional leagues, but was was released by a minor league club in 2018. He moved into software engineering, but started considering American football in 2019. He began training as a placekicker, eventually joining the USFL in 2022. In two years with the Birmingham Stallions, Aubrey was an immediate standout. He helped the Stallions win back-to-back USFL Championships, and was the USFL scoring leader in 2022. Aubrey’s spring league performances got him on the NFL’s radar, and he signed with the Cowboys shortly before the start of their 2023 training camp. Aubrey quickly beat out Tristan Vizcaino for the job, helping Dallas find stability after losing Brett Maher in free agency. It didn’t take long for the world to realize that Aubrey was more than just another band-aid kicker. Between his comfort level with 60-yard field goals and 94.7% accuracy overall, Aubrey quickly became a star at his position. He led the NFL in scoring in 2023, and began a streak of All-Pro and Pro Bowl selections that’s still ongoing. Aubrey’s list of NFL records keeps growing, particularly for his long-distance heroics. This offseason, Aubrey’s original deal ended and left him as a restricted free agent with only three years of NFL service. Dallas all but secured his spot on the 2026 roster with a second-round RFA tender back in March, but decided not to leave his long-term future in question for long. In late April, Aubrey and the Cowboys agreed to a five-year deal that made him the NFL’s most expensive kicker. Contract Status Years Left: 5 2026 Cap Hit: $3.4 million In case you missed it, Aubrey’s distinction as the highest-paid kicker is now shared with Pittsburgh’s Chris Boswell. Just a few weeks after Aubrey got his deal, the Steelers and Boswell also came to terms on a similar deal for an equal $7 million average. Aubrey, who is about four years younger, did get more guaranteed money in his contract. 2026 Projections Role: Kicker Roster Chance: 100% So yeah, not much to discuss here. There isn’t even another kicker on the roster, and if there were he’d only be a camp guy. Aubrey is the big leg on campus, and will remain such for at the least the next few years. You may be wondering what Dallas’ options are if Aubrey, who is 31, were to have a sudden dropoff in performance. It’s a fair question at that age, or at any age should a player suffer a major injury. With the guaranteed money in Aubrey’s deal, the Cowboys would suffer a significant dead money hit now through 2027. They could make him a June-1st cut next year and carry some of the cap penalty into 2028, making it more manageable. 2028 is when it becomes much cleaner. There would only be about $5 million in dead money left on the deal, which is less than the scheduled $6.92 million cap hit. It will be interesting to see if Dallas avoids restructuring Aubrey’s deal for cap relief in the coming years, preserving their flexibility as he goes deeper into his 30s. Of course, the hope is that we never have to worry about such things. If Aubrey keeps being a game-changing weapon with his distance, icy-veined in the clutch, and reliable overall as a kicker, few will balk at his compensation. At his age, Aubrey probably won’t have the longevity of the all-time greats. But in terms of peaks, he’s had few rivals in NFL history. title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 54
summary: It is Day 54 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: Oct 19, 1980; Philadelphia, PA, USA; FILE PHOTO; Dallas Cowboys quarterback Danny White (11) in action against the Philadelphia Eagles. Mandatory Credit: Photo By Manny Rubio-Imagn Images It is Day 54 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Welcome back and to Day 54 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit a rivalry game with massive NFC East leverage and a strange historical twist. This regular-season finale was more interesting than others because the Cowboys needed to win by 25 points or more to take the division tiebreaker. What came was all out war between the two rivals. Sunday, December 21, 1980 — 4:00 p.m. ET Texas Stadium, Irving, Texas Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 35, Philadelphia Eagles 27 The setup for this game in 1980 was enormous. Philadelphia entered the final week at 12-3, Dallas was 11-4, and both teams had already clinched playoff spots. The Eagles only needed to avoid losing by 25 or more to win the division. That sounded comfortable because Philadelphia had not allowed more than 24 points in any game all season. But Tom Landry’s team had other ideas, and the Cowboys came out with an aggressive plan designed to make the Eagles feel every bit of that tiebreaker pressure. Dallas started fast. Danny White scored on a one-yard run in the first quarter, then hit Tony Hill for a 36-yard touchdown in the second. White added a nine-yard touchdown pass to Preston Pearson, and suddenly the Cowboys were up 21-0 at halftime, the dream was coming true. In a game where margin mattered almost as much as the result, Dallas had turned the afternoon into a real division-title chase. Philadelphia finally answered in the third quarter on a one-yard Louie Giammona touchdown run, but Dallas kept applying pressure. White found Drew Pearson for an 11-yard touchdown, and after a Tony Franklin field goal made it 28-10, White struck again in the fourth quarter with a 15-yard touchdown to Billy Joe DuPree. The Cowboys led 35-10, exactly the 25-point margin they needed to steal the division and Texas Stadium was louder than ever. The Eagles were losing the game, but they were still fighting the standings math, just a few points would help keep their top spot. Ron Jaworski hit Rodney Parker for a 30-yard touchdown, Franklin added a 19-yard field goal, and Wilbert Montgomery scored from six yards out. Dallas still won 35-27, but Philadelphia had trimmed the margin to eight and preserved the NFC East crown. The numbers for the game were wild. Philadelphia actually outgained Dallas 407 total yards to 340, with 323 net passing yards, while Dallas controlled the scoreboard through efficiency. White threw four touchdown passes and ran for another score. Hill caught four passes for 110 yards and a touchdown, Drew Pearson had six catches for 65 yards and a score, and the Cowboys ran for 168 yards as a team. This game belongs on the countdown because it was a win with a catch. The Cowboys beat their biggest division challenger, finished 12-4, stayed perfect at home, and proved they could score on Philadelphia’s elite defense. But because the Eagles survived the margin, Dallas had to go the wildcard route. This regular-season finale was one of the strangest rivalry wins in Cowboys history. It was satisfying on the scoreboard, frustrating in the standings, and loaded with playoff consequences. #Cowboys vs #Eagles 1980 Week 16 Dallas needed to win by 25 points. What came was all out war. Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 35, Philadelphia Eagles 27 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/VnEiFtYgsm — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) July 20, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game The win closed out a perfect home regular season for Dallas. The Cowboys went 8-0 at Texas Stadium in 1980, and even won the wildcard game at home against the Los Angles Rams. title: Same old Cowboys offseason with one giant exception
summary: When you look at the offseason the Dallas Cowboys have had, it may have made you feel pretty good about the coming year and sense that maybe, just maybe, this team is finally doing things correctly. Many are convinced that they’ve learned their lesson and are finally doing things like a normal front office should. […]
full_text: When you look at the offseason the Dallas Cowboys have had, it may have made you feel pretty good about the coming year and sense that maybe, just maybe, this team is finally doing things correctly. Many are convinced that they’ve learned their lesson and are finally doing things like a normal front office should. While that is a nice thing to think about, this notion that the front office has magically changed its approach might be a bit of an illusion. The reason things feel less dramatic is that there is no looming holdout and fans feel rather satisfied with the number of new additions they’ve acquired this offseason. When you look at things closely, not a lot has changed. Jerry and Stephen Jones are running nearly the exact same playbook they run every single year, with one caveat, which we will get to later. But before we get to that, let’s look at things we think are different but really aren’t. The biggest source of calmness comes from a total lack of contract holdouts. The front office is still up to its old foot-dragging tricks, as wide receiver George Pickens did not get a long-term extension this offseason. Instead, he is stuck playing on the franchise tag. But there is no drama. And it is not because the front office carefully finessed its intentions or made empty promises to appease him. They have been transparent about their plan, and Pickens just happens to not be making a stink about it. At the same time, there started to be some drama with the Brandon Aubrey ordeal when some incorrect claims were being tossed around the media, but then things fizzled, and he eventually got a new deal. A new deal means everyone is happy, but this is pretty much par for the course in how the Cowboys handle contracts. Down to the wire. Last minute. Keep who they want. Rinse and repeat. But it goes beyond the contract stuff. The feeling is that the Joneses actually seem to care about the roster this year because they are actually doing stuff, starting with the signing of free agent safety Jalen Thompson. His three-year, $33 million contract is the most they have paid an outside free agent in over a decade. Finally, they are coming to their senses, right? Well, not really. The Cowboys may have gotten themselves one pricier player, but they have still only invested $59 million in free agency this offseason, ranking them in the bottom 10 for league spending. Only $33 million of that is guaranteed, which is the fifth-lowest of any team this offseason. Don’t be fooled. The front office is still sticking to its guns of sparingly using cap resources on outside free agents. New players are one thing, but what about the new teachers? The Cowboys hired a new coaching staff this offseason to fix a terrible defense. It is perfectly okay to be excited about this change, but we should remind ourselves that at this exact time last year, the Cowboys had a new defensive coordinator who was also supposed to fix a very bad defense. He failed miserably. So, why will this be different? It will be different because defensive coordinator Christian Parker is a young, sharp mind with intriguing upside. He’s unproven. He’s unfamiliar. He’s not the typical type of coach the Joneses hire, as they prefer someone with experience at the position. This would be turning over a new leaf if the Cowboys hadn’t done this exact same type of move last year with the hiring of new offensive coordinator Klayton Adams. The excitement for Parker is great, but we should at least consider that this has a chance to blow up in their faces. Any cynicism seems to be buried under relentless optimism. But whatever you feel, is it any different from what was going on this time last year? Last year admittedly brought some additional worry because both coordinators were new, as was first-year head coach Brian Schottenheimer. Total shakeup, compared to just defense this year. Maybe there was more dread due to fans being skeptical about the new head coach. It certainly did not help that the Cowboys themselves seemed confused about what they wanted, looking like they were trying to awkwardly hang on to Mike McCarthy. But now, are people suddenly feeling better about the decision? What’s changed with that? Sure, there is talk about influence and culture, yada yada yada, but has Schotty actually done anything to warrant excitement? The Cowboys finished with a losing record last season for the second straight year. That is the first time that has happened in over 20 years, dating back to when Dave Campo was the head coach. Even worse, it is the first time it has ever happened when their quarterback started every game during the season. Ever. Across 66 seasons! That is not to suggest we should be in a total panic about Schotty, but based on first-year results, it wouldn’t be unreasonable to continue to label his coaching ability as TBD. Even the players we feel good about this year consist of several young defensive guys, some of whom we are holding our breath for as they return from injury. Remember, this was also the case last year, and things did not go well. This offseason is different because the Cowboys have "finally learned their lesson." Finally spending in free agency Finally making coaching adjustments Finally dealing with contracts correctly False. False. False. But they have done something different. Do you know what it is? — Dan Rogers (@DannyPhantom24) July 19, 2026 This would be a good time for a cliffhanger, as we want to give you a moment to think about this. Do you know where this is going, what thing they have done differently? Let us know what you think the answer is and we’ll revisit this question tomorrow with our reveal.

title: 5 free agents Cowboys could consider bringing to training camp
summary: From the coaching staff to the new roster additions, the Dallas Cowboys have made quite a few changes over the course of the offseason and may not be done. They can still add talent via trade, roster cuts, or even sign a free agent still available on the open market. It wouldn’t be all that […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - DECEMBER 7: Von Miller #24 of the Washington Commanders looks on during an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images From the coaching staff to the new roster additions, the Dallas Cowboys have made quite a few changes over the course of the offseason and may not be done. They can still add talent via trade, roster cuts, or even sign a free agent still available on the open market. It wouldn’t be all that surprising that they used one or all three of these avenues to continue to upgrade the roster. Today, we look at which veteran players are still available on the open market who could potentially be of interest to the Cowboys based on their current roster “needs”. Any one of these veterans could join the Cowboys in Oxnard, California training camp, which kicks off in about a week’s time. OLB Von Miller Seeing Von Miller on this list should come as no surprise. He just recently stated he’d like to play for the Cowboys and the interest could be mutual. His days as an every down starter are probably behind him at his age, but he can still make a big difference as a mentor and in a backup role as well. Just last season with the Commanders he managed to log nine QB sacks, six tackles for loss, and 19 pressures playing just 37% of the defensive snaps, proving he has enough gas left in the tank to provide a boost as a part-time player. LB Bobby Wagner Bobby Wagner is another familiar name to make the list. The 36-year-old just finished his 14 th season with 100+ tackles, starting all 17 games in 2025. He accumulated 162 tackles, 4.5 QB sacks, eight tackles for loss, and two interceptions last season with the Commanders. Wagner may not be the player he once was, but he’s still highly consistent/productive, both traits that would help upgrade Dallas’ current LB position. With concerns about DeMarvion Overshown’s health and the questionable depth, Wagner would stabilize/upgrade the position. RB Joe Mixon After back-to-back 1,000-yard rushing seasons with the Cincinnati Bengals and Houston Texans, Joe Mixon missed the entire 2025 season with the mysterious foot injury. The soon to be 30-year-old (July 24) two-time Pro Bowl RB is one of the better do-it-all backs in the league when healthy. His addition would give the Cowboys another starting-caliber RB to pair with Javonte Williams, something they currently don’t have on the roster. Throw second-year RB Jaydon Blue in the mix and Dallas would have an impressive trio to rotate this year. LT Taylor Decker Taylor Decker was granted his release from the Detroit Lions after refusing to take a pay cut and is still available on the open market. The 33-year-old graded out as the 41 st overall offensive tackle last year by Pro Football Focus , allowing 33 total QB pressures and two sacks. Decker may be just an average to slightly above average LT in the league, but with consistency/injury concerns to both Tyler Guyton and Nate Thomas, he could challenge to be a starter. DT Christian Wilkins Christian Wilkins hasn’t played a single snap in the NFL since 2024 when he was limited to just five games after sustaining a foot injury. There’s also some locker room controversy that ultimately led to his release from the Raiders that could be a red flag as well. That could mean he doesn’t quite fit the culture Brian Schottenheimer is trying to establish in Dallas. But, as a risk/reward player he could be worth the gamble. The 6’4”, 310-pound 30-year-old could be an upgrade at the 4i position in Dallas’ new 3-4 scheme if/when he’s finally healthy. Who would you add out of these five choices? Do you have a different free agent the Cowboys should consider? Hit the comments and let us know.

title: The 3 biggest questions the Cowboys will need to answer in training camp
summary: The Dallas Cowboys 2026 training camp is just around the corner, and that means football is almost officially back. Though we still have about two months before regular season games, training camp gives fans their first feeling of football since the NFL draft. With plenty of new players, coaches, and ideas, this training camp is […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys 2026 training camp is just around the corner, and that means football is almost officially back. Though we still have about two months before regular season games, training camp gives fans their first feeling of football since the NFL draft. With plenty of new players, coaches, and ideas, this training camp is ramping up to be one of the more interesting ones in recent years for the Cowboys. Today we will look at three of the biggest questions that still need to be answered before the Cowboys kick things off against the New York Giants in week one. Do the Cowboys have enough juice off the edge? The Cowboys spent quite a bit of resources addressing their pass rush this offseason. After acquiring Rashan Gary via trade after losing out on the Maxx Crosby sweepstakes, the Cowboys turned to the Green Bay Packers to land Gary for a 2027 4th-round pick. Gary was being rumored to be a possible cut candidate if a trade was unable to be finalized, but the Cowboys were desperate and seemingly got into a bidding war with themselves for Gary. Though his last few years have been disappointing after signing a big extension in 2023, Gary has still put up decent sack numbers and pressures, despite his inability to put up quick pressures and sacks. The Cowboys did improve their value in this trade by getting Gary to rework his deal, making his contract much more team-friendly over the next two seasons. In addition to Gary, the Cowboys used their second first-round pick on Central Florida pass rusher Malachi Lawrence. Lawrence was one of the top pass rushers in this draft class from a traits perspective. While there is still some development to be had in order to be a three-down starter in year one, Lawrence should find a nice role as a pass rush specialist early on in his career. Outside of the additions of Gary and Lawrence, the Cowboys are banking on a big second-year leap from Donovan Ezeiruaku. Ezeiruaku had a decent rookie season, but finishing the year with only two sacks was a bit of a disappointment for the type of player he was viewed as coming out of the draft. Behind those three, the Cowboys have more uncertainty than answers. James Houston was quiet the surprise last year, but similar to Lawrence, he plays more of a pass rush specialist role than an every down pass rusher. The Cowboys are certainly not hurting on bodies, but they are hurting for a top dog to take control of the pass rush room at the defensive end position. Do the Cowboys have a starting left tackle on their roster? Another one of the biggest questions coming into training camp is who will win the starting left tackle job (the answer is Tyler Guyton)? While the safest bet here is Tyler Guyton will be the Cowboys starting left tackle when the Cowboys kick things off against the Giants, the bigger question is will he maintain control of the job for the entire season? Guyton did show some signs of development last season, before missing time due to injury, but injuries are something Guyton has dealt with in his first two years in the NFL. If Guyton is able to stay healthy, he will be serviceable at left tackle for the entire season, but the major question here is can he play most of the season? Nathan Thomas and rookie fifth-round pick Drew Shelton are the other names to watch during training camp. While Thomas will likely get the first crack at the first-team competition, don’t count out Shelton as an option later on in training camp if neither Guyton or Thomas are taking advantage of their opportunities. Is the Cowboys RB2 currently on the roster? This question can be viewed in two different ways. If you tell me Javonte Williams is healthy for most of the 2026 season, then the Cowboys RB2 is absolutely on the roster, whether that be Jaydon Blue, Phil Mafah, or Malik Davis is still to be determined. The bigger question is if Javonte Williams has to miss time, who do the Cowboys feel confident in to take over as the teams number one rusher, pass protector, and pass catcher out of the backfield? Jaydon Blue is the ideal candidate for the RB2 job behind Javonte Williams. Blue’s change of pace and pass-catching ability is something everyone should be very excited to watch in year two. The concerns come when talking about pass protection, which is a very important and often ignored responsibility of down the depth chart running back options. Williams had a tremendous season for the Cowboys in 2025, earning him a nice little payday over the offseason. One of his more underrated traits last season for the Cowboys was just how good he was as a pass protector out of the backfield. That reason in itself is one of the main reasons we could see the Cowboys go out and add a veteran during or after training camp to be an insurance policy for Williams if he is to miss time throughout the course of the season.
author: Connor Livesay

title: Cowboys players with the highest floor for this season
summary: Every year we get excited about the upcoming Dallas Cowboys season because things feel limitless. That is classic fan behavior, and despite our better judgment, we tend to drink from that well on an annual basis. Dreaming about the ceiling is more fun than anything else because just imagine if it all happens! In reality, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 12: CeeDee Lamb #88 of the Dallas Cowboys and Dak Prescott #4 of the Dallas Cowboys are interviewed by Erin Andrews after the game against the New York Giants at AT&T Stadium on November 12, 2023 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images) | Getty Images Every year we get excited about the upcoming Dallas Cowboys season because things feel limitless. That is classic fan behavior, and despite our better judgment, we tend to drink from that well on an annual basis. Dreaming about the ceiling is more fun than anything else because just imagine if it all happens! In reality, the more important aspect of a given team is their floor. The higher the floor, the higher the average landing spot for the team. If the floor is high then the pressure to reach the ceiling is lower, ironically. So with all of that being said, here are the three players on the Cowboys with the highest floor for this season. Dak Prescott You would hope that your quarterback is on this list. Thankfully for the Cowboys, Dak Prescott is. We have come to be able to set our watches by Dak Prescott’s play. His decade of lining up for the team has proven that the floor is indeed always high with him. Outside of the years where the Cowboys saw him deal with significant injuries, they have never bottomed out with him. Prescott is often the subject of all sorts of criticism, but he is more than capable of putting the team in the proper position. He needs to do his part when they get there, but he is one of the primary engines driving the proverbial ship. CeeDee Lamb It is hard to be as consistent and dependable as CeeDee Lamb. Consider that last year Lamb, in 13 games, went for over a thousand yards. He only had three touchdowns on the year, but he had the highest yards/reception of his career at 14.4 in what is considered a down year for his standards. CeeDee Lamb is going to provide elite production from your WR1 which is the literal definition of a high floor commodity. It is a wonderful thing to have him on this team. Quinnen Williams You could go with Tyler Smith here, and he has one of the highest floors, but it just felt right to include Quinnen Williams. He feels so overlooked amid all of the changes this team has undergone. For the first time, um, in this century maybe… the Cowboys have one of their most reliable and dependable players lining up at defensive tackle. Think about how cool this is! Williams has all of the pedigree in the world and the team paid dearly to have it be a part of their operation. It feels fair to expect that to really show itself over his first full season with Dallas. Is there someone else who should be here? Obviously Tyler Smith makes sense, but outside of him? Let us know in the comments below.

title: The last 9 spots: Why Cowboys roster projections go wrong
summary: Every year at around this time, the first 53-man roster projections pop up. And (almost) every year we dutifully chronicle those first roster projections here on BTB. I usually preface these summaries with an introduction like this: “Not to be a killjoy here, but if the past 15 years or so that I’ve been intensely […]
full_text: Dallas Cowboys players gather following a morning walk-through practice during Dallas Cowboys Summer Training Camp in Oxnard, Calif. (Ron Jenkins/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Every year at around this time, the first 53-man roster projections pop up. And (almost) every year we dutifully chronicle those first roster projections here on BTB . I usually preface these summaries with an introduction like this: “Not to be a killjoy here, but if the past 15 years or so that I’ve been intensely following the Dallas Cowboys training camp have taught me anything, it’s that rosters are largely set before the offseason program even begins, and most of the extra players brought in are little more than sparring and training partners for the roster locks. That is the stark reality of NFL life. Injuries and standout performances in camp provide the opportunity for maybe a handful of players each year to work their way onto the roster, but that’s pretty much it.” That sure sounds nice and may even appear insightful, but is that actually true? To find out, I took a look at the pre-camp roster projections from 2023-2025 across a number of sources. To my surprise, the panelists averaged just over 44 correct players – meaning nearly one in every five roster spots changed between late July and Week 1. body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 4px 6px !important; } Year ESPN Athletic BtB DMN Foxports Total Archer Machota Rogers (23), Haynie(24-25) Hoyt Helman 2023 44 44 44 — 45 44.3 2024 45 44 44 — — 44.3 2025 44 44 43 43 — 43.5 Interestingly, every one of the 11 projections I looked had at least 21 starters right, five got every single one of 22 starters right – and that would have been nine if Juanyeh Thomas hadn’t rocketed from an afterthought entering camp in 2023 to a Week 1 starter. The first lesson is straightforward: Projecting the top guys on the roster really isn’t such a hard thing to do. Barring injuries, suspensions, trades, retirements and other things of that nature, a preseason roster projection should have the eventual starters on the roster. The uncertainty isn’t at the top of the roster. It’s at the margins. And that’s where these projections get interesting – the players the projections collectively missed on. Below is a summary chart over the last three years of players that made the season-opening 53-man roster but didn’t show up in any of the projections (or only on one). body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 0px 6px !important; } Source How acquired 2023 2024 2025 Unpredictable Transaction Trade Noah Igbinoghene Jordan Phillips Kenny Clark Trey Lance Andrew Booth – – Free agent – – Linval Joseph James Houston – – Nick Vigil Hakeem Adeniji PS signing – – Buddy Johnson – – Waiver claim – – – – Trikweze Bridges – – – – Reddy Steward – – – – Trevor Keegan Injuries / PUP / suspensions activated from PUP – – – – Trevon Diggs Unexpected camp winners Draft Pick Jalen Brooks (7th, rookie) Israel Mukuamu (6th) – – – – Matt Waletzko (5th) – – Veteran Cooper Rush Perrion Winfrey UDFA Juanyeh Thomas Tyrus Wheat – – Rico Dowdle – – – – Hunter Luepke (Rookie) – – – – T.J. Bass (Rookie) – – – – Brock Hoffmann – – – – Markquese Bell – – – – The chart highlights (in blue and red) that some of the moves the team makes after the start of training camp are simply unpredictable. Trades, players signings, and activations off of various injury and non-injury lists will naturally pull down the “hit rate” on any projection. And then there’s the part marked in yellow where some down-roster guys make the team against all (public) expectations. The table only shows players added to the team; it doesn’t include players that didn’t make the initial 53 because they were suspended, put on PUP/IR, retired, or were traded away. Projecting these roster moves before camp is impossible, and they will naturally make any projection look weak in hindsight. But there’s more to watch out for than just these player transactions. As we’ve tracked these early projections over the last few years, a handful of roster projection pitfalls have emerged which can be broadly classified in the following four categories: The Progress Stopper “Progress stopper” is a term Bill Parcells introduced to Cowboys Nation. The term is mostly used for veteran players with little upside who fans and media alike are convinced should leave to make room for an exciting young talent. But coaches don’t always think in terms of potential. Instead, they see reliability versus lack of experience, and will often take the former over the latter. It’s not sexy and it’s not what fans and the media are clamoring for, but it’s what coaches do. As you look at roster projections, look closely at where there’s a tradeoff between a middle-of-the-pack veteran and a young (and unproven) player. The veteran may have the edge more often than you think. The Pet Cat Everybody has a pet cat. And whether we do it knowingly or not, we all construct our projections to some way, some how fit in that one player we’ve taken a linking to. Similarly, we often try to construct a roster in the hopes of getting rid of that one player we don’t like for some reason. The System Guy In 2023, none of the projections had a fullback making the roster. Turns out, the Cowboys thought a fullback would be an essential element in their ground game. Who’s going to be this year’s system guy, a nickelback, a red-zone specialist, a receiver who can stretch the field vertically? The coaches probably already have a pretty good idea, we don’t. The You-Can-Never-Have-Enough-Players-At-His-Position Guy Last year, some projections had the Cowboys going ‘long’ with five safeties or 10 offensive linemen. The Cowboys ended up going short at both positions, keeping only four safeties and nine linemen. Building the roster is not a color-by-numbers exercise. Fans often think in positional quotas. Coaches think in roles. The lesson here isn’t that preseason roster projections are bad. Quite the opposite. Identifying 44 of the eventual 53 players before training camp even begins is actually remarkably impressive. The mistake is assuming the remaining nine roster spots are simply waiting to be filled by the next nine names on the depth chart. History suggests they rarely are. And the approach to filling those spots changes every year. Here’s how the remaining roster spots (versus the projections) were filled the last three years: body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 4px 6px !important; } Source of surprise 2023 2024 2025 Unpredictable Transaction 2 5 6 Injuries / PUP / suspensions – – – – 1 Unexpected camp winners 7 4 1 Some will be veterans coaches trust more than fans do. Some will be players whose value only becomes apparent once the coaching staff starts installing its schemes. Some won’t even be on the roster when training camp opens. That’s what makes July roster projections so much fun. They’re less a prediction of the final 53 than a snapshot of where the roster stands before reality inevitably gets in the way. So when the next projection leaves off your favorite rookie, or keeps a veteran you’ve already given up on, don’t panic. If recent Cowboys history tells us anything, it’s that the final roster is still being written.

title: Cowboys news: Jaishawn Barham is an intriguing player as a rookie
summary: Jaishawn Barham: A Dark Horse 26′ Defensive Rookie of the Year Candidate – Cody Warren, Inside The Star The Cowboys will need a pass rush by committee approach this season, and rookie Jaishawn Barham could fit into that very well. Christian Parker has a defender, much like Downs, who he can move around the defensive […]
full_text: Jaishawn Barham: A Dark Horse 26′ Defensive Rookie of the Year Candidate – Cody Warren, Inside The Star The Cowboys will need a pass rush by committee approach this season, and rookie Jaishawn Barham could fit into that very well. Christian Parker has a defender, much like Downs, who he can move around the defensive front seven. Barham can play just about every position from linebacker to the defensive line. We don’t have to watch Dallas force this guy into a job. If Christian Parker is as advertised , he will find a way to put this young man in a position to succeed. Or find the position that Barham can cause the most havoc and keep using him there. Jaishawn Barham Gives Dallas Options I would hate to see the Cowboys line Jaishawn Barham up at inside linebacker every snap and just call it good. He can do much more than that . At Michigan, Jaishawn Barham handled linebacker duties while also succeeding near the line. He has the size to fight through traffic and enough burst to make a quarterback nervous. I would keep him inside against a running team and let him get downhill. He could even spy a mobile quarterback, and on passing downs, walk him up to the line and make the offense decide if he’s coming or not. I want to see that kind of uncertainty from this defense. Cowboys 2026 roster rundown: DT LT Overton – Jess Haynie, Blogging The Boys LT Overton was a great pick to help the Cowboys continue adding size to the defensive line. Background Years in NFL: 0 Acquired by: 2026 4th-round pick Overton is no stranger to change. He spent 2022-2023 at Texas A&M before transferring to Alabama, where he’s started the last two years at edge. He posted career highs as a senior with 26 solo tackles, six tackles for loss, and four sacks. Overton just missed playing college ball with fellow Cowboys rookie Caleb Downs, who left the Crimson Tide for Ohio State in the same offseason that Overton left the Aggies. Despite the extra recognition from playing at Alabama, Overton only had middling appeal in the 2026 draft class. He was too big and not athletic enough for the modern NFL pass rusher, looking more like a run stopper. There was pre-draft talk that he might fare best by bulking up and moving inside, and that’s exactly what the Cowboys saw in Overton when they use a late fourth-round pick to select him. 2026 Projections Role: Backup DT Roster Chance: 95% That said, we expect Overton to at least get a season. The Cowboys took him with a clear plan to move him inside. While he may not be a traditional 3-4 defensive end, Overton does fit the modern build of athletic 3-tech tackles. He will likely see work in nickel and other formations where size isn’t as important up front, rotating with veteran Jonathan Bullard as similar players. The transition may keep Overton on the sideline most of the year, or at least the early portion. He will need to learn technique while also developing physically for the role. We’ll probably see more of Bullard and Otito Ogbonnia in the rotation with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark. There are some excellent mentors for Overton in that group, hopefully helping him to develop quickly. If the Cowboys are going to carry him on the 53-man roster this year, he may end up having to play more once any of the veterans gets injured. Role Call: Jalen Thompson has the IQ, versatility to lead Cowboys – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com Even before drafting Caleb Downs, the Cowboys made a splash on the backend of the defense by signing Jalen Thompson. How He Got Here: Jalen Thompson began his journey to the NFL in Compton, where he began to make a name for himself at La Serna High School before transferring to Downey High School, ultimately finding his way as a three-star recruit to Washington State. He went on to earn Second-team All-Pac 12 honors (2017), catching the eye of NFL scouts in the process, and ultimately got the call from the Arizona Cardinals in the fifth round of the 2019 NFL Draft — where he spent seven seasons before signing with the Cowboys in 2026, reuniting with secondary coach Ryan Smith in the process. Plenty — Thompson’s exceedingly high football IQ and versatility makes him a ready-made fit for what defensive coordinator Christian Parker wants in a defensive back. The 27-year-old was signed to multi-year deal in free agency for a reason, and that’s because he’s part of a bigger long-term solution in the Cowboys’ defensive backfield. Expect to see him move around between free safety, strong safety and nickel corner, with a rep or two at off-ball linebacker mixed in as well, at times. Thompson is a field general of the highest order (which is why he’s a green dot candidate) and is expected to combine with rookie first-round pick Caleb Downs to help turn Dallas’ secondary into something … different. Did You Know : Caleb Downs enters as the headline defensive acquisition by the Cowboys this offseason, but Thompson is one of the most important additions in free agency ahead of the NFL Draft that sent Downs to Dallas. Thompson provides a veteran presence but at the age of 27, an exceptional mix of youth and experience. NFL coach hits the nail on the head with Cowboys’ George Pickens conundrum – Levi Dombro, The Landry Hat The Cowboys want to see a repeat performance from George Pickens alongside CeeDee Lamb in 2026. NFL coach perfectly encapsulates George Pickens issue Dallas Cowboys are grappling with Hidden in the top 10 NFL wide receiver rankings that ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler compiled by polling executives, coaches and scouts around the league was a quote from an anonymous NFL offensive coach about Pickens, who came in at No. 7 on this list, just one spot behind CeeDee Lamb: “One of the best I’ve ever seen at the contested catch,” a veteran NFL offensive coach said. “There’s such untapped ability there. It’s just a consistency issue and where his head’s at week to week.” That is the perfect encapsulation of the Cowboys’ Pickens conundrum. On the one hand, Pickens does things on a football field that even some of the best NFL wide receivers can’t dream of. When Pickens is on, he’s on , and there is no stopping him. Scarier for other teams is the fact that he may not have even reached the peak of his powers yet in his young career. And yet consistency is an issue for Pickens, who had almost as many games with fewer than 40 receiving yards (4) as games with over 130 (5). That is a wide range of outcomes for a team to expect from a player in a game, especially one who may be getting paid in the ballpark of $40 million annually. Dak Prescott’s Super Bowl comments spark the wrong question about the Dallas Cowboys’ 2026 season – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports The Cowboys are looking for their first playoff berth in three seasons, and first under Brian Schottenheimer. “Each year you think that, but when you have the last year that we did, the offense that we did, you’ve been making changes and you’ve got a great defensive coordinator and you’ve got young guys, old guys, a great mix of veterans with talent, and us understanding what needs to be done,” Prescott said. He added that if a teammate doesn’t share that mentality, “honestly, I don’t want you on my team.” That’s what you want to hear from your quarterback. You never want to hear Prescott say the team would settle for a playoff appearance. And he’s not alone. Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer recently said in an interview that his plan is to be playing in the Super Bowl on Feb. 14. Whether it comes off as wildly optimistic, realistic, or straight out of a fantasy is not for us to say. But clearly, the organization is leaning into the conversation rather than dodging it. But are they that good? Here’s the thing about that label, though. It typically applies to teams so loaded that anything short of a championship feels like a failure. Take the Los Angeles Rams. They traded for Myles Garrett, acquired cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson, retained Matthew Stafford,…

title: How much of an impact will Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones make in 2026?
summary: Lost in all the dangerous components of the Broncos’ elite defense are a pair of playmakers in their prime. I’m not talking about Nik Bonitto and Jonathan Cooper. I’m not talking about Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss. I’m talking about Brandon Jones and Talanoa Hufanga. When healthy, this is one of the strongest safety […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 7: Ja'Quan McMillian (29), Talanoa Hufanga (9) and Brandon Jones (22) of the Denver Broncos prepare for Cam Ward (1) and the Tennessee Titans during the fourth quarter of the Broncos' 20-12 win at Empower Field at Mile High on Sunday, September 7, 2025. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) Lost in all the dangerous components of the Broncos’ elite defense are a pair of playmakers in their prime. I’m not talking about Nik Bonitto and Jonathan Cooper. I’m not talking about Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss. I’m talking about Brandon Jones and Talanoa Hufanga. When healthy, this is one of the strongest safety tandems in the NFL: Hufanga in 2025 chipped in 11 PD, 1 FF, 2 sacks, 106 tackles, and 6 TFLs. Jones in 14 games in 2025 had 1 INT, 7 PD, 1/2 sack, and 78 tackles. But it is how the defense hums when both of them are on the field that I’m excited about for this season. With Jones out, Hufanga had a bit more of the load to handle on the back end at times. With Jones healthy, either of them can play more aggressive positions knowing they have an excellent veteran on the other side of the field to hold it down. Jones ’ run support has always been a staple. He’s able to help our sub packages be more effective vs the run against more pass-happy personnel groups. I think we all know to expect great things from these two pros. Does the community think we’ll see much of our two new rookie safeties this season? Do you look forward to seeing the Broncos extend Jones, or should the Broncos look to the young guns to develop? Hit us up in the comments and let us know what you think. title: 8 players who could breakout during Broncos training camp in 2026
summary: Every summer, we see a handful of players have breakout performances during training camp and the preseason and turn that into having a breakout performance during the season. Well, this year is no different, as the Broncos have several players who could have breakout performances during training camp that could elevate them up the depth […]
full_text: Oct 26, 2025; Denver, Colorado, USA; Denver Broncos wide receiver Pat Bryant (13) celebrates scoring a touchdown in the second quarter against the Dallas Cowboys at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images | Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images Every summer, we see a handful of players have breakout performances during training camp and the preseason and turn that into having a breakout performance during the season. Well, this year is no different, as the Broncos have several players who could have breakout performances during training camp that could elevate them up the depth chart and potentially have a larger role on the team during the season. I have identified a total of eight players who I believe have the best chances of having a breakout performance during training camp. The list is heavy on young players, but training camp is where these young players build confidence, show their development, and take that next step and become future stars of the team. So, with all that said, here are the eight Broncos players who I believe have the best chances of having a breakout performance during training camp and the preseason. CB Jahdae Barron The Broncos’ 2025 first-round pick took a back seat in his rookie year as Riley Moss and Ja’Quan McMillian played well and held down their starting roles. However, in year two, Barron has an opportunity to push Moss or McMillian (likely Moss more than J-Mac) for their starting job this summer. As we know, both players are in the final years of their contract, so this is a big summer for all three players. JAHDAE BARRON WITH HIS 1ST CAREER INT First of many for the talented rookie pic.twitter.com/cymL7iV5sD — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 26, 2025 Earlier this offseason, Head Coach Sean Payton was asked about the vision for Barron entering year two, and he mentioned that he has inside/out positional flex and that Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph will have packages to get him on the field. He added that Barron is out there competing and doing well. “I think there will be two things. ‘A’, he has position flex inside-out. Then there will be packages I’m sure where in throwing situations, [Defensive Coordinator] Vance [Joseph] and those guys will look at what we’re wanting to do with our people, but he’s out here competing and doing good.” Barron had flashes during his rookie year, but will need to take a big step if he wants to push Moss or McMillian for their jobs. If he does, the Broncos will have to decide if they want to trade from their depth (likely the player they don’t plan on re-signing) or move forward with a deep cornerback room. Barron’s development and who gets that contract will be one of the larger talking points throughout camp, the preseason, and potentially into the regular season and offseason. RB Jonah Coleman The Broncos selected Jonah Coleman in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and he has a chance to be a high-impact player for the team during his rookie season. With veteran running back JK Dobbins being re-signed, he is expected to be the team’s lead ball carrier. However, his injury history tells you that he is likely going to miss some time, so the addition of Coleman adds some much-needed depth and talent to that running back room. A strong performance during camp and the preseason could force the coaches to give Coleman some carries early on in the season to keep Dobbins fresh for the long haul. They also have second-year running back RJ Harvey in the mix as well. So, the Broncos could feature a three-headed monster at the running back position. As for Coleman, he is a patient but powerful runner who can be a three-down back. His pass blocking is a strength and is something that could get him on the field right away in his rookie season. I am a big fan of Coleman and think he will be a solid contributor for this team this season and someone we are talking about throughout camp and the preseason. WR Pat Bryant The battle for the Broncos WR3 job is expected to be the story of camp, and I believe Pat Bryant will be the guy creating the headlines. Bryant looked like the Broncos’ best and most consistent receiver at times during his rookie season and saw his role grow as the season progressed. Unfortunately, injuries derailed all that late in the season, but I think he will carry that momentum into year two and continue to grow and develop as a player. Bryant has good hands, runs good routes, gets open, blocks in the run game, and started to show real chemistry with quarterback Bo Nix. I think we’ll see him have a big second-year jump and solidify himself as the Broncos WR3 behind Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton. Pat Bryant hitting the Mile High Salute 🫡 right after scoring his first career touchdown pic.twitter.com/uGcmkikY60 — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 28, 2025 With that said, keep an eye on Troy Franklin and Marvin Mims. Franklin was the story of camp last year and had a breakout year for the team last season. As for Mims, he is playing for a contract, and we have seen contract-year breakout performances before, so I wouldn’t rule out Mims having a breakout summer as a receiver as well. It’s a talented and deep wide receiver room, so the competition figures to be fun to watch throughout camp and the preseason. EDGE’s Que Robinson/Jonah Elliss I lumped these two together due to the uncertainty surrounding veteran Jonathon Cooper and his off-the-field legal drama. His future with the team is up in the air as of this writing, and he is likely facing some sort of suspension from the league as well. So, with Cooper likely being away from the team for at least a bit, the Broncos’ young depth at edge rusher will have an opportunity to step up. Jonah Elliss is entering his third season with the Broncos and will likely be getting first-team reps opposite Nik Bonitto once camp opens. He has been a talented reserve who came off the bench when the starters needed some rest, but will have an opportunity to nail down a starting job in Vance Joseph’s defense. Has been unblockable during the Broncos’ spring practices and is known for his deadly spin move, so we could see more of that from Elliss once camp opens. QUE ROBINSON SACK pic.twitter.com/oekXyQTdVl — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) January 25, 2026 As for Que Robinson, I am a big fan. I loved what we saw from him in limited action during his rookie year, and I believe he is primed for a big second season with the Broncos. He has the size, length, athleticism, speed, and bend you are looking for in an edge rusher, and I believe he has 10+ sack potential in this league. Robinson also impressed the Broncos coaches last year. Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph told reporters he believed Robinson looked like a future starter when he played last season. Well, he now has an opportunity to become a starter for the Broncos. The Broncos’ pass rush will be very important to their success this season, so the growth and development of Elliss and Robinson will be something to keep an eye on throughout camp and the preseason. IDL’s Sai’vion Jones/Tyler Onyedim With John Franklin-Myers signing with the Titans during free agency, the Broncos will need someone to step up and replace those pass-rush reps. Before the draft, it seemed like second-year Sai’vion Jones would be that guy, but with their first selection in the 2026 NFL Draft, they selected defensive lineman Tyler Onyedim. Now, these two are expected to be competing for those interior pass rush snaps left behind by JFM. After the Broncos selected Onyedim, Head Coach Sean Payton was asked if they believe Onyedim could replace JFM in the Broncos’ defense. Payton told reporters, “Yes, absolutely,” and mentioned that their year one vision for him was positive. “Definitely when we’re taking a player in that spot, we discuss vision all the time. Yes, absolutely. They’re going to come in [and] earn their place. We go through this all the time. After the…

title: Denver Broncos roster review: Guard Quinn Meinerz
summary: Quinn Meinerz is one of the best guards in the NFL. The fact that he’s so complete and dominant is one of the main reasons the Denver Broncos have one of the best offensive lines in the league. Player Profile Age: 27 | Experience: Sixth Year | College: Wisconsin-Whitewater | Height: 6’3” | Weight: 320 pounds The fifth-year guard is coming off back-to-back […]
full_text: CENTENNIAL , CO - JUNE 4: Quinn Meinerz (77) of the Denver Broncos works out with fellow offensive linemen during OTAs at the Broncos Park in Centennial, Colorado on Thursday, June 4, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images Quinn Meinerz is one of the best guards in the NFL. The fact that he’s so complete and dominant is one of the main reasons the Denver Broncos have one of the best offensive lines in the league. Player Profile Age: 27 | Experience: Sixth Year | College: Wisconsin-Whitewater | Height: 6’3” | Weight: 320 pounds The fifth-year guard is coming off back-to-back First-Team All-Pro years. Now the offensive lineman and team captain is looking to add to his resume, for himself and the team. Quinn Meinerz’s 2026 outlook with the Broncos When you’re one of the best at what you do, there isn’t much room for growth. But that’s the plight for Meinerz. And if anyone is up for the task, it’s Denver’s right guard. His approach and mindset are what you need from an offensive lineman. Meinerz wants to destroy his opponents. He wants to be the best. And he will do whatever it takes to make it happen. That’s why he’s coming off consecutive First-Team All-Pro seasons. Meinerz was also named to the Pro Bowl for the first time in 2025. To give you an idea of how valued and respected he is, Meinerz has also been a team captain over the last two seasons. Based on all of that, Meinerz is looking to complete the First-Team All-Pro hat trick. He’ll also likely be a captain for the third season. If anyone has the commitment to pull it off, it’s Meinerz. He’s simply dominant in all facets as a guard, as a run blocker, and as a pass protector. He makes the guys around him better. He makes the offense better. When you come from Division III Wisconsin-Whitewater, you don’t take it for granted. Final thoughts As the Broncos look to take the next step as a team after finishing one game short of the Super Bowl, Meinerz will play a massive role in meeting that expectation in 2026. His work ethic and leadership, his play, and the quality of his play demand the best from himself and his teammates. For the offense to carry the load, one of the best guards on one of the best offensive lines in the NFL sets the foundation for Bo Nix and the rest of the offense to reach higher. It’s a treat to watch Meinerz play the game, and that remains the case heading into 2026.

title: Horse Tracks: Three players who could make a big leap in Year 2
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! Training Camp is just 10 days away, and all the excitement for the 2026 season will finally move from speculation on paper to speculation on the field. And while all eyes will be on how Bo Nix’s ankle is doing, how Jaylen Waddle is fitting into the offense, how the rookies […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - NOVEMBER 16: Jahdae Barron #23 of the Denver Broncos celebrates during an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Empower Field at Mile High on November 16, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! Training Camp is just 10 days away, and all the excitement for the 2026 season will finally move from speculation on paper to speculation on the field. And while all eyes will be on how Bo Nix’s ankle is doing, how Jaylen Waddle is fitting into the offense, how the rookies are adjusting and which stars look solid again, there are several second-year players who could go under the radar if we are not paying attention but have the potential for strong sophomore campaigns. Here are three second-year players I’m most curious about as our July 31 start date inches closer. WR Pat Bryant Bryant quietly became a trusted target for Bo Nix during the second half of his rookie season. He isn’t the fastest receiver on the roster, but he was a reliable target. With strong hands and good route discipline, he could quietly become a secret weapon while defenses focus attention on Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton. If he develops into a consistent red-zone threat, Bryant could easily double last year’s touchdown production. “He’s a quick study. He gets it real fast,” said head coach Sean Payton earlier this summer. “I think one of his great skill sets is his run after the catch because his feet stay on the ground when he catches it. He’s got strong hands in traffic. He’s having a good stretch here.” Payton added that there’s a maturity to Bryant already this season, which is exactly what you hope for with the second-year players. They know the ropes, the system and the playbook. “He’s healthy…he knows exactly what to do and, and there’s a confidence about him, a maturity,” Payton added. “You wouldn’t feel like he was a second-year player if you didn’t know it.” Bo Nix throws it up to Pat Bryant II for the TD! The first career TD for the rookie WR 🙌 DALvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ https://t.co/HkKw7uXVnt pic.twitter.com/C3z7yWt6ft — NFL (@NFL) October 26, 2025 CB Jahdae Barron The Broncos first-round draft pick in 2025 was basically a non-entity for the defense last season, but the second-year cornerback seems ready to step up for a big Year Two. Payton noted that Barron’s early offseason work was looking good and Barron’s film room study was paying off. “You can tell that he is progressively getting better,” Payton said during OTAs. “His IQ and his fundamentals of the game, it seems like he is wise beyond his years going into his second year. I’m excited for him.” As a rookie Barron played just a little over 300 defensive snaps. He and his coach hope for a bigger impact from the former Texas cornerback this season. “I think he’s an instinctual player,” the coach said, “so I think for him it’s just getting the reps and the practice work.” Barron’s progress in the offseason was noted by All Pro cornerback Patrick Surtain, so that’s always a good sign. “He’s been studying in the film room. You can tell he’s progressively getting better,” Surtain said last month. “His I.Q. and his fundamentals of the game, it seems like he’s wise beyond his years going into his second year, so, I’m excited for him.” I think we all forget Jahdae Barron was robbed of a pick-six on Mahomes last season pic.twitter.com/W1Mxj9rBsT — 𝙀𝙙𝙜𝙚 💥 (@BroncosEdge_) May 25, 2026 RB RJ Harvey There’s been a lot of talk already about the running back room this season with the addition of an intriguing rookie in Jonah Coleman and the return of veteran JK Dobbins. How Harvey plays in year two could have a lot to do with how the Broncos’ rushing attack goes in 2026. From everything Payton has said, and everything we began to see the second half of his rookie season, suggests Harvey has the skill set to thrive in year two. Not only can he run, he can catch in the backfield, create explosive plays and pass protect. But perhaps the best indicator of Harvey’s second year potential is how he has spent his offseason — studying fellow running back stars like Christian McCaffrey, Jahmyr Gibbs and Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker. “Just watching more film, watching other guys around the league, watching their film … just trying to see things on film that they do, trying to help better my game,” Harvey said. “In Year Two in the system, I feel way more comfortable and it’s only going to get better from where I left off.” Even with Dobbins considered the main attraction, the Broncos will want to be careful with the veteran’s load, and the guy poised to take on more of it will be Harvey. With more consistency than his rookie year, Harvey could easily become Denver’s most dynamic offensive weapon out of the backfield. title: Survey: How many receiving yards will Sam LaPorta have in 2026?
summary: Throughout the offseason, SB Nation will host surveys for NFL fans, sponsored by the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook. For Pride of Detroit, we are tasked with fielding questions from Detroit Lions fans, and this week’s question centers around an important player returning from injury: Sam LaPorta. LaPorta burst onto the scene as a rookie, setting […]
full_text: Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta (87) makes a catch against Minnesota Vikings during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, November 2, 2025. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Throughout the offseason, SB Nation will host surveys for NFL fans, sponsored by the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook . For Pride of Detroit, we are tasked with fielding questions from Detroit Lions fans, and this week’s question centers around an important player returning from injury: Sam LaPorta. LaPorta burst onto the scene as a rookie, setting multiple records for tight ends in franchise history, including registering 889 receiving yards for the season. In year two, LaPorta’s production was scaled back (726 receiving yards) as he focused on rounding out his overall game, which included stark improvements as a blocker. Last year, a significant back injury limited him to just nine games and 489 receiving yards before he was placed on injured reserve. LaPorta required surgery on his back, and questions surrounding his ability to fully recover swirled. In the spring, the Lions remained positive, and coach Dan Campbell told the media that the Pro Bowl tight end was “trending the right way” toward playing training camp. On Tuesday, ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler confirmed expectations and reported that LaPorta had been “fully cleared (from injury) earlier this month” and that he was indeed on track to participate in training camp. Returning for 2026 healthy is terrific news for LaPorta, but the good news doesn’t end there for the fourth-year tight end. Waiting for LaPorta in Allen Park is new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, a coach with a lengthy history of featuring and elevating tight ends. Petzing spent the last three seasons in Arizona and quickly elevated the play of tight end Trey McBride. After a 2022 rookie season that saw McBride secure 265 receiving yards over 16 games (13 starts), Petzing helped raise his production to 825 receiving yards in 2023, 1146 receiving yards in 2024, and 1239 receiving yards in 2025. McBride was selected to the Pro Bowl each of the last two seasons and was a first-team All-Pro in 2025. With Petzing now in Detroit, expectations are sky high for LaPorta in 2026, including some publications suggesting a career year is on the horizon . Even McBride reached out to LaPorta to tell him how excited he should be to have Petzing in Detroit : “I was like, ‘Man, you’re going to love it. You’re going to eat, you’re going to have a great career,’ I’m excited for him.” While the hype train is certainly picking up some heavy steam this offseason for LaPorta, it’s important to keep in mind that McBride was the top target in the Cardinals offense, while LaPorta has to share the ball with several other terrific players in the Lions’ offense, including All-Pro wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown. Ball distribution, along with maybe some lingering injury concerns, could be why FanDuel Sportsbook is listing LaPorta’s projected receiving yards at a moderate 650.5 (-114). And with that, it’s time to vote. Make sure to vote in the survey below, share your feedback in the comment section of this article or THE FEED post connected to the poll , and check back with Pride of Detroit later in the week for the results. If you want to get these surveys emailed to you weekly, you can sign up here , and don’t forget to check out FanDuel , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation.

title: Report: Sam LaPorta fully cleared from injury for Lions training camp
summary: According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta has been fully medically cleared and is expected to enter next week’s training camp as a full participant. LaPorta suffered a herniated disc in his back last year, forcing him to have surgery and miss the final eight games of the season. But when […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MI - AUGUST 21: Detroit Lions Tight End Sam LaPorta (87) during the joint practice between Houston Texans and Detroit Lions on August 21, 2025 at Detroit Lions Training Facility in Allen Park, MI (Photo by Allan Dranberg/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta has been fully medically cleared and is expected to enter next week’s training camp as a full participant. LaPorta suffered a herniated disc in his back last year, forcing him to have surgery and miss the final eight games of the season. But when the Lions returned to the field for OTAs and minicamp in the spring, LaPorta was back on the field doing walkthroughs—a sign his recovery was still on schedule. “We like where he is going, he is trending the right way,” coach Dan Campbell said during minicamp in June. We have yet to hear from LaPorta himself this offseason, but on locker cleanout day after the 2025 season, he said it was the goal to be a full go by training camp. “Hopefully by OTAs I’m up running around, and then, of course, we’ll be in pads in training camp,” LaPorta said. “So, it’s a lot different than other sports, just to be able to brace for those hits, and the accumulation of a long NFL season, I’ve really got to get this back right before I’m out there running around in pads and taking those hits and such.” Getting LaPorta back will be key to Detroit’s offense in 2026. Last year, he produced 40 catches for 489 yards and three touchdowns in his injury-shortened season. That was actually the most yards per game he’s accumulated in a single season, and there are other signifiers that LaPorta could be in for a career year. That includes the hiring of new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, who helped turn Cardinals tight end Trey McBride into an All-Pro. “I was like, ‘Man, you’re going to love it. You’re going to eat, you’re going to have a great career, ’” McBride reportedly told LaPorta this offseason. “I’m excited for him.” Lions rookies are set to report to training camp on Saturday, July 25, while veterans will report on Tuesday, July 28.

title: Ranking every 2026 Detroit Lions player: 20-11
summary: We’ve finally reached the starters when it comes to our countdown of every player on the 2026 Detroit Lions roster. A good way to see if the Lions improved or got worse is to compare the following 10 players to the players we ranked from 20-11 in our 2025 edition of these rankings. This range […]
full_text: Detroit Lions guards Tate Ratledge (69) and Christian Mahogany (73) walk off the field after the 27-13 loss to the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis., on Sunday, September 7, 2025. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images We’ve finally reached the starters when it comes to our countdown of every player on the 2026 Detroit Lions roster. A good way to see if the Lions improved or got worse is to compare the following 10 players to the players we ranked from 20-11 in our 2025 edition of these rankings. This range of 10 players includes three newcomers, six draft picks, and six linemen. Here are the players we ranked from 20 to 11. Previously: Players ranked 90-81 Players ranked 80-71 Players ranked 70-61 Players ranked 60-51 Players ranked 50-41 Players ranked 40-31 Players ranked 30-21 20. CB Rock Ya-Sin (Highest: 19 Lowest: 22) Last year’s ranking: 51 Ya-Sin has one of the biggest jumps on this year’s list. While some of that is certainly due to him way outperforming expectations last year, I think he likely would’ve been somewhat lower on the list if Terrion Arnold was still on the team. Instead, Ya-Sin is now facing a starting role on the defense, and our staff clearly believes he’s capable of assuming that job. 19. WR Isaac TeSlaa (Highest 17; Lowest: 25) Last year’s ranking: 36 While the Lions have been very careful not to hype up their players too early, second-year receiver Isaac TeSlaa has a fair amount of buzz heading into 2026. “I mean, he is just consistent, and where we expected him to be at this point this time for year two is exactly where we want him, and I would say probably even a little bit more,” Dan Campbell said this spring. “You are impressed. He feels like a veteran right now.” He still needs to prove he can live up to that hype, but it’s safe to say expectations are relatively high for Detroit’s WR3. 18. EDGE DJ Wonnum (Highest: 17; Lowest: 26) Last year’s ranking: N/A Wonnum comes to Detroit with 30.0 career sacks in 86 games—a welcome, productive career to the Lions’ defensive end room. But Wonnum will have to share time with rookie Derrick Moore opposite Aidan Hutchinson, so it’s unclear how much opportunity he’ll have to match a career high 8.0 sacks. 17. iOL Christian Mahogany (Highest: 16; Lowest: 25) Last year’s ranking: 21 Mahogany actually climbs this year’s rankings despite a frustrating 2025 season. Injuries and uneven play plagued his second year, but there is certainly some hope the 2024 draft pick can rebound with a healthier season and a better fit under new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing. 16. C Cade Mays (Highest: 13; Lowest: 19) Last year’s ranking: N/A Detroit’s only true aggressive free agency move came at center, where they handed Cade Mays a three-year, $25 million contract. Mays’ career at center is just 1.5 years deep, and he’s still just 27 years old, so Detroit is hoping Mays is just starting to tap into his potential, and if he does, Detroit will have a budget-friendly pivot for the next few years. 15. OT Blake Miller (Highest: 12; Lowest: 17) Last year’s ranking: N/A The third consecutive projected starting offensive lineman on our rankings, Blake Miller certainly has the highest expectations in the long term. But how much can we expect from the Lions’ first-round pick in his rookie season? It certainly looks like he’ll win the starting right tackle job over Larry Borom, but rookies often take a while to find their footing. 14. DT Tyleik Williams (Highest: 11; Lowest: 19) Last year’s rankings: 25 We go from this year’s first-round pick to last year’s. Tyleik Williams has high, high expectations for 2026 after Detroit opted to move on from DJ Reader and Roy Lopez. Paired with a healthy Alim McNeill, the expectation is for Williams to build on his strong run defending from 2025, but also expand to a bit of a pass-rushing role. 13. G Tate Ratledge (Highest: 9; Lowest: 14) Last year’s rankings: 22 With the way Ratledge finished his rookie season, there’s plenty of warranted optimism that Detroit’s starting right guard can make the jump to a good/great/outstanding player. He won’t have the benefit of Penei Sewell to his right, and he’ll be dealing with a new center, too, but Ratledge showed enough growth last year to be confident he’ll hold his own in 2026. 12. CB D.J. Reed (Highest: 11; Lowest: 15) Last year’s rankings: 12 Reed was last year’s crown of free agency, but a hamstring injury cost him a month, and he didn’t look like the same player when he returned. He now believes he’s fully back with his explosion intact. If true, Detroit may have themselves a legit No. 1 cornerback, but he still needs to go out there and prove it. 11. S Kerby Joseph (Highest: 8; Lowest: 16) Last year’s rankings: 6 I don’t think there’s any doubt that Kerby Joseph is a top-10 player on the Lions when healthy. Unfortunately, the knee injury that cost him most of 2025 is still threatening his football career, and that likely dropped him out of this year’s top-10. Still, if he can somehow navigate the injury this year, here’s an important reminder: no one in the NFL has more interceptions since 2022 than Kerby Joseph (20).
