title: Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview: DT has upgraded starters, questionable depth
summary: In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we shift over to the defensive side of the ball and start by examining the Lions’ interior defensive line, speculating on current and future roles, and discussing how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Roster […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive tackle Tyleik Williams (91) practices during mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we shift over to the defensive side of the ball and start by examining the Lions’ interior defensive line, speculating on current and future roles, and discussing how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Quarterback: Can Luke Altmyer force a QB3 role? Running back: How RB roles could shift in 2026 Wide receiver: WR depth roles up for grabs Tight end: How many TEs will make the roster? Offensive tackle: Can Blake Miller win the starting RT job? Interior OL: How quickly will Cade Mays adapt to scheme? Roster construction Under the Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell regime, the Lions have deployed several different styles of defensive front, but they’ve remained consistent in maintaining the number of players they’ve dedicated to the position. Let’s take a look at what they’ve done on the interior defensive line in the previous five seasons: 2021 : With a two-gapping look with three starting interior defenders, the Lions initially kept and ended the season with seven interior defenders. 2022 : When the front shifted to a 4-3, the Lions reduced their number to five but ended the season with four players active and Levi Onwuzurike on injured reserve. 2023 : The Lions opened and closed with five interior defenders on the roster. 2024 : Rinse and repeat: Open and close with five interior defenders. 2025 : Again, opened and closed with five interior defenders; typically keeping four active on game day. Planned change The Lions’ defensive front has undergone a lot of change under this regime, initially operating out of 2-gapping concepts, then flipping to 1-gapping style, before finally landing on a gap-and-a-half approach. And while the Lions front has been relatively consistent for the last few seasons, it appears they’ll undergo some slight tweaking this season as the team increases its focus on pass rushing. The most noticeable changes among the personnel are that the Lions allowed nose tackles DJ Reader and Roy Lopez to leave in free agency and replaced them with rookies Skyer Gill-Howard and Tyre West, who are more pass rushers than pluggers. The Lions did sign two nose tackles, veteran Jay Tufele and UDFA rookie Aidan Keanaaina, but they appear to be more situational or practice squad players, as opposed to heavy rotational players. This transition wasn’t simply an adjustment to personnel, as we’ve seen at other positions, but something planned well over a year ago when they drafted Tyleik Williams in the first round and planned to pair him with Alim McNeill in the starting lineup. By deploying two players with nose tackle bodies but pass rusher skill sets, the Lions can now present offenses with difficult decisions in the trenches. Much like we see with the Lions’ safeties, the pairing of McNeill and Williams gives the Lions two interchangeable pieces in the middle of their line that can adjust on the fly and disguise intentions pre-snap. If McNeill can return to form now that he’s a year-and-a-half removed from his ACL injury, and Williams takes another step in his development, in theory, the Lions appear to have upgraded their starting talent level and improved their schematic options. The concerns with the interior defensive line reside with their depth. In addition to the young depth mentioned above, Levi Onwuzurike returns after missing last season due to an ACL injury; Tyler Lacy and Mekhi Wingo will hope to expand their limited roles, while Chris Smith and Myles Adams will work to elevate their statuses from the practice squad. The battleground How much time will McNeill and Williams play together? Injuries have been a problem for the Lions’ interior defensive line over the past few seasons, but if we look back at snap counts, we can get some idea of how much the Lions prefer to deploy their interior players. Last year, McNeill didn’t see the field until Week 7, but in his 10 games played, he averaged almost 76% of defensive snaps. The year prior, he averaged around 70% of snaps, but saw over 80% of defensive snaps in half his games. As for Williams, he saw the field roughly 41% of defensive snaps his rookie season, but is expected to see that number significantly increase this year. For reference, if we look at McNeill’s history, we see that he saw 37% of defensive snaps as a rookie, then jumped to roughly 70% of snaps the next two seasons before elevating to 70+% the following two years. Therefore, if McNeill sees roughly 75% of defensive snaps, and Williams is on the field 70% of the time, you can estimate that they’ll likely be paired together for around 50% of defensive snaps, while also pairing up with other players, or in situational fronts the other half of the time. What happens when the starters are not paired together? When McNeill or Williams exit the field, the likely next man up will be Onwuzurike, who pairs with the remaining starter. In the spring, Onwuzurike operated as the Lions DT3, taking the majority of his reps at the 3-technique, but his positional range suggests he could be a weapon the Lions can use up and down the defensive line. While he didn’t play in 2025, in 2024 he was on the field for nearly 60% of defensive snaps, operating at both defensive tackle spots, as well as “Big” end (4i/5T) and traditional defensive end. With the Lions’ investment in edge rushers and Lacy taking on a larger role at the “Big” end, Onwuzurike should be available for more interior snaps this season. What’s the depth plan after Onwuzurike? At this time, there is no clear DT4 on the roster, but instead, a collection of players who are projected to operate in situational-specific roles. As mentioned previously, the Lions only have two traditional nose tackles on the roster, and it’s not clear exactly where they fit in the defensive tackle rotation. The Lions coaching staff tends to prefer veterans, which should benefit Tufele, but Keanaaina received $267,500 in guarantees in his contract —the most this regime has ever handed out to a UDFA rookie—which is worth taking note of. Mekhi Wingo and rookie Gill-Howard look like pass-rushing specialists at this stage of their careers, and while that is a role that certainly aligns with the Lions’ new defensive philosophy, there are no guarantees either will see the field, as was the case with Wingo last season. West, another rookie, could also spend some time on the interior as a pass rusher, but his collegiate history suggests his skill set would be better utilized at the “Big” end, in a similar role to Lacy. Smith and Adams have very balanced skill sets that allow them to be utilized across the Lions’ defensive line, but both spent last season on the practice squad, suggesting they represent reliable depth but are not considered impact players. With the Lions traditionally keeping five interior players (six if you include the “Big” ends), you could surmise that after the trio of McNeill, Williams, and Onwuzurike, the Lions could be looking for one nose tackle (Tufele or Keanaaina) and one pass rusher (Wingo or Gill-Howard) to emerge from the depth battles. That being said, the Lions operate on meritocracy, and it is not clear whether any of the players in positional battles will step up and earn a role. That uncertainty beyond DT3 is a big reason why the interior depth has raised so many concerns.

title: Discussion: Who will be the most improved player at Detroit Lions training camp?
summary: One of the most exciting parts of training camp is seeing which players have taken a step since last year. We often talk about Year 2 or Year 3 jumps, but actually seeing it out there on the field is extremely satisfying. That improvement is never guaranteed, but when it happens, it’s validation that the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback Ennis Rakestraw Jr. (2) walks off the field after practice during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 29, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images One of the most exciting parts of training camp is seeing which players have taken a step since last year. We often talk about Year 2 or Year 3 jumps, but actually seeing it out there on the field is extremely satisfying. That improvement is never guaranteed, but when it happens, it’s validation that the general manager made the right draft pick. But improvement isn’t always just about the young talent. Sometimes, it’s a veteran finding a breakthrough. Sometimes, it’s a player who signed with the team last year but needed a season to adjust to the scheme. Sometimes, it’s someone who has been completely overlooked and came into camp with little expectations. So today’s Question of the Day is: Which Lions player will be the most improved at 2026 training camp? My answer: I’m going to put on my optimistic cap and say, Ennis Rakestraw. Admittedly, this is far less based on actual evidence and more based on actual hope. But it’s still important to remind people that during his rookie season, Rakestraw was set to start a game at nickel before an injury during warm-ups derailed those plans. At one point not too long ago, this team had very high hopes for the 2024 second-round pick. Now, the opportunity is finally his. After losing all of 2025 to an injury, Rakestraw now has a relatively clear path to the starting lineup and all of the motivation to finally get his NFL career off the ground. While I currently have veteran Rock Ya-Sin slated as the starting cornerback opposite D.J. Reed, I do believe that Rakestraw could very well win that job by the end of camp. Detroit has insisted on keeping Rakestraw on the outside, and with Terrion Arnold now out of the picture, everything is set up for Rakestraw to break out this training camp. Which Lions player do you expect to see as the most improved player at training camp? Share your thoughts in the comment section.

title: Packers Discussion: Which rookie are you expecting the most from in 2026?
summary: Here’s an interesting question going into training camp: Which Green Bay Packers rookie do you think will have the biggest impact in 2026? To me, there are probably three potential answers. The first two are fairly similar. If there’s any competition in camp for starting roles, it’s on the defensive line or at cornerback. On […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JUNE 09: Brandon Cisse #2 of the Green Bay Packers participates in drills during the Green Bay Packers mandatory minicamp at Don Hutson Center on June 09, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here’s an interesting question going into training camp: Which Green Bay Packers rookie do you think will have the biggest impact in 2026? To me, there are probably three potential answers. The first two are fairly similar. If there’s any competition in camp for starting roles, it’s on the defensive line or at cornerback. On the defensive line, the assumption is that Devonte Wyatt will be a starting defensive end in the Packers’ new 3-4 defense. Javon Hargrave has played both end and nose tackle in the past, so the question is really which position he will play, rather than if he will start. That third defensive line spot could go to a multitude of candidates, though, including rookie third-round pick Chris McClellan from Missouri. Cornerback is a similar story where it’s assumed that Keisean Nixon will be a starter (and safety Javon Bullard will be the starter in the slot). The other outside cornerback job should go to one of Carrington Valentine, free agent signing Benjamin St-Juste or rookie second-round pick Brandon Cisse. The last player I think will be a popular answer is kicker Trey Smack, who the Packers traded up for in the sixth round. Smack had a little bit of an up-and-down spring, but Green Bay thought enough of him to make him the only drafted kicker in the 2026 class and released Brandon McManus shortly after his selection. title: Green Bay Packers News: Devonte Wyatt’s contract is a worthwhile risk
summary: I have to admit, a Devonte Wyatt extension at this point of the offseason was a bit of a surprise. I figured if anything, Tucker Kraft was next in the pecking order, but the Packers have methodically checked off every possible extension on their to-do list before getting a deal done that could reset the […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 23: Devonte Wyatt #95 of the Green Bay Packers sacks J.J. McCarthy #9 of the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter at Lambeau Field on November 23, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images I have to admit, a Devonte Wyatt extension at this point of the offseason was a bit of a surprise. I figured if anything, Tucker Kraft was next in the pecking order, but the Packers have methodically checked off every possible extension on their to-do list before getting a deal done that could reset the tight end market, so maybe it shouldn’t be that much of a surprise. League-wide, I think the reaction is going to be similar to what we saw from Christian Watson’s extension. People who don’t know what Wyatt can do are going to see the contract numbers and his playing time stats from the past few years and wonder what the Packers are doing. And to be fair, that’s a decent point of contention. Wyatt really hasn’t played much. He has cracked 400 snaps in the regular season just one time in his four years with the Packers, and hasn’t hit that figure since 2023. Sure, he’s been good when healthy, but the “when healthy” portions of his career have come even less frequently than the oft-criticized Christian Watson’s. But when he’s on the field, he’s really good. Just look at how poorly the Packers’ defensive line played without Wyatt on the field last year. It was a night and day difference. Retaining Wyatt at least keeps him as an option for most of the season, assuming whatever injury he inevitably sustains won’t shake the boat too badly. But all moves come with risk, and the Packers are laying out quite a bit of money for a player who’s almost literally never been healthy and who’s already 28. Defensive linemen tend to age a bit better than most, but he’s a far cry from what the Packers had in the eternally young Kenny Clark, who seemed to be permanently 24 years old. Maybe that makes him a bigger risk than the potentially still ascending Christian Watson and Jordan Reed, but if he can be a key contributor this year — preferably a healthy one — it’s probably a risk worth taking. title: Houston Texans Training Camp: Players to Watch
summary: The Houston Texans’ training camp officially kicks off on July 28th, and there are several players worth keeping an eye on as the offseason comes to a close. PLAYER ONE: WR JAYLIN NOEL Although Jaylin Noel didn’t put up eye-popping numbers in 2025, he consistently made plays whenever his number was called on offense and […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - JUNE 02: Jaylin Noel #13 of the Houston Texans and Jayden Higgins #81 arrive during OTA Offseason Workouts at Houston Methodist Training Center on June 02, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans’ training camp officially kicks off on July 28th, and there are several players worth keeping an eye on as the offseason comes to a close. PLAYER ONE: WR JAYLIN NOEL Although Jaylin Noel didn’t put up eye-popping numbers in 2025, he consistently made plays whenever his number was called on offense and special teams. Noel is the fastest player on the Texans’ offense, and he needs to be more involved in 2026. He was very good as Houston’s kick returner, but he’s capable of doing much more, which is exactly why the Texans invested a third-round pick in him. If Noel continues to develop, he has the potential to make a major impact this season. PLAYER TWO: TE MARLIN KLEIN Marlin Klein was selected by Houston in the second round of this year’s draft, and he could quietly become one of the Texans’ biggest weapons heading into the season. Klein dealt with a minor injury earlier this offseason, but he’s expected to be ready for training camp with plenty to prove. He gives C.J. Stroud another big-bodied target and will have the opportunity to learn behind veteran Dalton Schultz. The Texans needed more depth at tight end, and Klein can be brought along at the right pace before eventually competing for the starting job in the future. PLAYER THREE: CB JAYLIN SMITH Jaylin Smith showed plenty of promise early in his rookie season before suffering a season-ending injury in Week 9. Now fully healthy, he’s looking to reclaim his role in the secondary. Smith earned rave reviews from teammates and coaches last offseason and continued to improve as he became more comfortable in DeMeco Ryans’ defense. He’s a player who could contribute immediately. PLAYER FOUR: LB WADE WOODAZ Wade Woodaz has a legitimate opportunity to carve out a significant role in 2026. Azeez Al-Shaair and Henry To’oTo’o will handle the majority of the snaps, but E.J. Speed’s injury opens the door for the rookie. If Woodaz can separate himself during training camp, there’s a real path for him to earn meaningful playing time. CONCLUSION The Texans have most of their starting positions locked in, but there are still opportunities for several young players to separate themselves. Training camp will go a long way in determining who earns a bigger role heading into the 2026 season.

title: Colts Reacts Survey Results: Who Belongs Next in the franchise’s Ring of Honor
summary: Indianapolis Colts fans have spoken, and given the recent news that legendary longtime placekicker Adam Vinatieri will be inducted into the franchise’s illustrious Ring of Honor next season, it begs the question of who should be next among former Colts standout players? While many Pro Football Hall of Famers have made also made the Colts […]
full_text: Bob Sanders of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates a Chicago fumble during Super Bowl XLI against the Indianapolis Colts at Dolphin Stadium in Miami, Florida on February 4, 2007. (Photo by Jim Rogash/Getty Images) Indianapolis Colts fans have spoken, and given the recent news that legendary longtime placekicker Adam Vinatieri will be inducted into the franchise’s illustrious Ring of Honor next season, it begs the question of who should be next among former Colts standout players? While many Pro Football Hall of Famers have made also made the Colts Ring of Honor such as Bill Polian, Tony Dungy, Peyton Manning, Marvin Harrison, Edgerrin James and Dwight Freeney in more recent seasons, the highest honor the Colts franchise can pay to its former players isn’t limited to those also enshrined in Canton. Rather, we’ve seen other Colts greats, who so far have fallen short of earning a gold jacket, such as Jeff Saturday, Robert Mathis, Dallas Clark, and Tarik Glenn make the franchise’s Ring of honor given their high level of production, leadership, and as a result of bringing home the Lombardi Trophy for Indianapolis back in 2006. Colts fans spoke on this topic and 35% of Colts fans believe that Bob ‘The Hitman’ Sanders should be next, who narrowly beat out former franchise wideout great T.Y. ‘The Ghost’ Hilton for the nod here: Both players would be great choices, but Sanders to me should be the ‘Next Man Up’ given how long he’s had to wait and arguably one of the last great members of that Super Bowl winning squad to not earn such an honor. I would make the argument that Sanders’ safety running mate, Antoine Bethea, who was largely underrated throughout his entire 14-year career as a former Super Bowl Champion and 3x NFL Pro Bowler is at least worthy of such consideration as well from that all-time great Colts squad. Nevertheless, Sanders was the catalyst for that 2006 Super Bowl winning defense, that carried the Colts through their magical playoff title run, as his late season return reinvigorated their entire unit—particularly regarding their once much maligned run defense. He was like a big brother showing up to the playground fight. He’s the only player in Indianapolis franchise history to win NFL Defensive Player of the Year honors and was a 2x NFL First-Team All-Pro and NFL Pro Bowler for the Colts—as well as a fellow Super Bowl Champion.

title: Jonathan Taylor hold-in speculation adds another layer to Colts’ offseason
summary: Jonathan Taylor’s contract situation may be worth watching again. According to The Athletic’s James Boyd, Taylor could and should consider a training camp hold-in as he enters another important year with the Colts. The piece does not report that Taylor is planning to hold in, and there is no direct quote from Taylor suggesting that […]
full_text: Jonathan Taylor’s contract situation may be worth watching again. According to The Athletic’s James Boyd , Taylor could and should consider a training camp hold-in as he enters another important year with the Colts. The piece does not report that Taylor is planning to hold in, and there is no direct quote from Taylor suggesting that is where things are headed, so this should be framed carefully. This is more of an analysis from Boyd of Taylor’s leverage than a firm report about his intentions. Still, the topic is important because Taylor’s value to the Colts is obvious. Indianapolis does not have a true replacement for him on the roster. The Colts have talked about wanting to reduce Taylor’s workload and keep him fresher over the course of the season, but that is easier to say than actually do. Taylor remains the centerpiece of the offense and the team’s best skill player. That is where his leverage comes from. Taylor is older than he was during his 2023 contract dispute, but his argument may be stronger now because the Colts are more dependent on him than ever. The quarterback situation is still uncertain, Daniel Jones is trying to re-establish himself, Anthony Richardson’s future with the team is cloudy, and the offense will likely need the run game to carry a major burden again. If Taylor is unhappy, limited, or unavailable, the entire offensive plan changes. Taylor’s workload has been heavy in recent years, and running backs have a shorter prime than most positions. The team has every reason to want to manage his touches, protect his body, and avoid overusing him early in the season. At the same time, Taylor has every reason to understand how important he is. If the Colts need him to carry the offense in big games, and if they do not have another back who can take meaningful pressure off him, then his value is not theoretical. It is built into the entire offense. A hold-in would not be the same as a holdout. Taylor could report to camp, avoid fines, and still limit participation while making his point. That has become a common tactic for players who want contract movement without completely staying away from the team. For now, though, this is still speculation. There is no indication Taylor has made a final decision, and the Colts may not view this as an immediate problem. However, it is another storyline to watch as training camp approaches. The Colts need Taylor healthy, engaged, and central to what they do offensively. Whether that eventually leads to another contract conversation is the part that could make camp a lot more interesting.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Should the Colts already be thinking about Ballard’s successor?
summary: I know. The season hasn’t even started and here I am talking about Chris Ballard’s replacement. We have ten years of data, so I am not sure this is exactly what you’d call putting the cart before the horse, pun intended… I get it though. This isn’t a case of me predicting that the upcoming season […]
full_text: Carlie Irsay-Gordon speaks with media Monday, Jan. 5, 2026, during a press conference held at the Indianapolis Colts practice facility. Irsay-Gordon, the co-owner and CEO of the Colts, addressed questions about the team retaining head coach Shane Steichen and general manager Chris Ballard. | Mykal McEldowney/IndyStar / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images I know. The season hasn’t even started and here I am talking about Chris Ballard’s replacement. We have ten years of data, so I am not sure this is exactly what you’d call putting the cart before the horse, pun intended … I get it though. This isn’t a case of me predicting that the upcoming season for the Indianapolis Colts is going to be a disaster, but if one resides in an area that experiences a lot of disasters, not having a disaster preparedness plan would be foolish. That is why the Colts need to be thinking about Ballard’s replacement now, not later. Getting the GM position right is crucial. In the NFL, there are three things that a franchise must nail to be successful: quarterback, GM, and coach. A good quarterback can mask the other two. I would then give the nod to GM over coach because if the car isn’t built well, it doesn’t matter who is driving. Questions can be raised whether the Colts have the right people in the right seats for any of these roles, but Ballard has more experience to draw from than any of them. The Colts have proven their commitment to Ballard by keeping him around, even with his sordid record. This isn’t a case where riding the fence is a bad thing. This isn’t a time to be “all in” on your guy. This is a time for the Colts to hedge their bets. They aren’t married to the guy. Now is when conversations about potential replacements need to be had. Colts ownership needs to know if there are better options out there before making a move just to make one. If no one available is better than Ballard, they should hold tight; no reason to move laterally. While that doesn’t appear to be the case, it should always be considered. Chris Ballard is getting more than a fair shake with the Colts. For what he has produced, he should be indebted to this organization for the rest of his life. That is the past, though. The Colts need to look to the future, and do it now. There is no time to waste. If this season goes sideways, they need an exit strategy. It’s been a series of disasters for ten years. Build the disaster escape plan, and use it.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Chiefs training camp preview: Who to consider for return specialist job
summary: Rookies report for Kansas City Chiefs training camp this Friday! Veterans report next Tuesday! Wednesday will be the first full-team practice! So you know what that means? It’s time to argue over 2026’s most important position battles. And while there are plenty of questions about the secondary, the defensive line, and who will emerge as […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 08: Emmett Johnson #10 of the Kansas City Chiefs on set during a production shoot at The University of Kansas Health System Training Complex on June 08, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Rookies report for Kansas City Chiefs training camp this Friday! Veterans report next Tuesday! Wednesday will be the first full-team practice! So you know what that means? It’s time to argue over 2026’s most important position battles. And while there are plenty of questions about the secondary, the defensive line, and who will emerge as the fourth wide receiver or third tight end, the return game will sneakily be very interesting to follow. Let’s take a look at the incumbents at return specialist, and we’ll toss a few new challengers in the mix: Nikko Remigio 2025 return statistics Kick returns/yards: 29/741 Punt returns/yards: 25/191 Remigio is the experienced, dependable war horse of the bunch. You can trust him to keep the floor of the return game at a reasonable level. He’s essentially the equivalent of a Domino’s pepperoni pizza. You know what you’re going to get, and it’s fine for a low-key Friday night dinner, or your five-year-old’s birthday party, but it’s not in the same stratosphere as true pie joints like Minsky’s or Waldo Pizza. Remigio is not going to put the ball on the ground. He’s going to get upfield quickly, and isn’t going to try to run laterally and make something out of nothing. And that’s his strength. He always gets you something, and that’s better than nothing. But let’s be real, it doesn’t matter how much extra cheese you put on this pizza; there isn’t a lot of upside to his game. Brashard Smith 2025 return statistics Kick returns/yards: 18/481 Punt returns/yards: 6/68 It was pretty clear from the moves the Chiefs made this offseason, like signing two free agent running backs and drafting another, that Smith is not expected to be relied on in the backfield in 2026. If Smith wants to cement his place on this team, he might need to win the return-man job. Smith’s sample size was small in 2025, but his rate of 11.3 yards per punt return is a respectable mark, one that beats Remigio’s mark of 7.6 yards per punt return. The issue is that just winning the punt return job might not be enough to earn him a spot on this team. He needs to win both return jobs to maximize his value on the roster. Tyquan Thornton 2025 return statistics Kick returns/yards: 18/475 Punt returns/yards: N/A The Chiefs used Thornton as a kick returner in situations where the team was looking for a home-run shot. He averaged 26.4 yards per return, which was only good for 25th best in the league. With a two-year contract signed this offseason, Thornton shouldn’t be in the conversation to be a return man in 2026. I think the Chiefs want to use him primarily as a deep threat to stretch the defense and free up receivers like Rashee Rice and Travis Kelce underneath. I’d be shocked if Thornton is used as the primary return man this year. Cyrus Allen 2023 NCAA return statistics Kick returns/yards: 18/475 Punt returns/yards: N/A Despite not returning kicks since 2023, when he played at Louisiana Tech, I think the Chiefs will take a long, hard look at Allen this training camp in the return game. It’s notoriously difficult for rookie wide receivers to get involved in the Chiefs offense, and that may hold true for Allen. But he has the agility and makeup to be a decent return man in this league while he gets his sea legs under him. Jalen Royals 2024 NCAA return statistics Kick returns/yards: 9/189 Punt returns/yards: N/A Royals did have one kick return for the Chiefs in 2025, and he took it 30 yards down the field. It’s hard to know what to make of Royals after a rookie campaign where he was seen less than the right side of the Phantom of the Opera’s face. Royals was returning from a serious foot injury last season, so who knows if that played into it, but the door is open if Royals wants to fight for the return man job. Emmett Johnson 2024 NCAA return statistics Kick returns/yards: 3/24 Punt returns/yards: N/A Despite not being utilized at all as a kick returner in college, Johnson might be the frontrunner to win the job in 2026. Chiefs special teams coordinator Dave Toub highlighted Johnson as a player to watch in the return game last month, saying that he was excited to see how Johnson fit in with the new kickoff rules in the NFL. When you watch Johnson’s tape, it’s not hard to envision him being an excellent return man in this league. He has great hands, and possibly the best vision of any running back in this class, as well as the ability to navigate traffic and run between and split would-be tacklers. EJ Smith 2024 NCAA return statistics Kick returns/yards: 2/21 Punt returns/yards: N/A Like Johnson, Smith was not used as a return man really in college, despite playing for six seasons between Stanford and Texas A&M at running back and never having more than 220 yards rushing in any of those seasons. But the reason he is on this list is that, like Johnson, Smith was called out specifically as a player to watch in the return game this offseason by Dave Toub. Okay, Uncle Dave, I’m watching. But I still don’t think Smith wins the job or makes the initial 53 for that matter. Who do you think will be the team’s kick/punt returner(s) this season? Let us know in the comments.

title: 55 Days until Chiefs football, we are ‘Frank Clark’ days away
summary: We are 55 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 55 jersey will be worn by second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott this season. He donned it for just five games during his rookie year before suffering a torn ACL in […]
full_text: MIAMI, FLORIDA - FEBRUARY 02: reacts after defeating San Francisco 49ers by 31 - 20 in Super Bowl LIV at Hard Rock Stadium on February 02, 2020 in Miami, Florida. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are 55 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 55 jersey will be worn by second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott this season. He donned it for just five games during his rookie year before suffering a torn ACL in Week 7. The number is tied with a few memorable players in Chiefs lore, some positive, some negative. The 3 most memorable No. 55s in franchise history E.J. Holub (1961 – 1970) Frank Clark (2019 – 2022) Dee Ford (2014 – 2018) Holub was one of the original all-time Chiefs players, winning three AFL Championships and one Super Bowl during his five-time Pro Bowl career. He was named to the first- or second-team All-Pro team four times, the first three as a linebacker. The fourth happened in the 1969 season, his second as the starting center after a mid-career position switch. The all-time No. 55 was a career Chief, but Clark and Ford certainly made their mark on the modern dynasty. In the moments leading up to a fourth-quarter interception of New England Patriots quarterback Tom Brady in the AFC Championship off the 2018 season, a flag sailed into the air at the snap of the ball. Ford aligned offsides, negating the pick and allowing a second life to the inevitable Patriots. The unforgettable error led to two trades: one to send Ford away and another to acquire Frank Clark from the Seattle Seahawks . It ended up as an effective swap for the Chiefs for many reasons, one being Clark’s play in the clutch. Currently, Harvey Martin, Willie McGinest and Bruce Smith are the only players in NFL history with more career playoff sacks than Clark (13.5). 55: The number of passes thrown by Chris Oladokun last season That was more than enough of a sample size in live action for the Chiefs to say goodbye to him this offseason, looking towards the draft for a new reserve quarterback to develop with seventh-round pick Garrett Nussmeier. 55 passes were also 55 too many for fans to stomach seeing from a quarterback besides Patrick Mahomes. It was a dreadful watch during the final three Mahomes-less games, a reminder of how dependent the team’s success is on “15.” When severe enough of an injury to keep him sidelined, there’s a simple mindset to embrace in the words of former Colts offensive coordinator Bob Moore , who coached quarterback Peyton Manning (No. 18) “If ‘18’ goes down, we’re f—d… we don’t practice f—d.’”

Larry Johnson, October 29, 2006 Stats: 155 Rushing Yards, 3 Rushing TDs, 26 Receiving Yards, 1 Receiving TDs Game: KAN vs SEA, 35-28 Win Fantasy points: 42.1 #2. Priest Holmes, November 24, 2002 Stats: 197 Rushing Yards, 2 Rushing TDs, 110 Receiving Yards, 1 Receiving TDs Game: KAN vs SEA, 32-39 Loss Fantasy points: 48.7 #1. Jamaal Charles, December 15, 2013 Stats: 20 Rushing Yards, 1 Rushing TDs, 195 Receiving Yards, 4 Receiving TDs Game: KAN vs OAK, 56-31 Win Fantasy points: 51.5 Chiefs Position Battle I’m Watching Closest in Training Camp (And How It’ll Play Out) | Sports Illustrated None of Sneed, Kohou, Roland-Wallace or Canady made our list of the top 25 Chiefs entering the 2026 season, but all four have a path to become a starter and one of Kansas City’s most vital defenders this year. For now, Canady may have the longest path. That’s not cause for alarm; Canady is still the team’s best-case long-term solution, potentially building an excellent young trio with Delane and Williams in 2027 and beyond. But with three more veteran players ahead of him, he’d have to prove quite a lot in camp to take the starting role. Pre-Camp Breakdown: Evaluating the Chiefs Group of Defensive Backs | The Mothership Prior to joining the Chiefs, Knowles was starter at nickelback at Florida State in 2024, tallying 32 tackles, four pass-breakups, two tackles-for-loss and a sack in 12 games. It’s also worth mentioning that the 5-foot-10, 189-pound Knowles recorded a 41-inch vertical jump at his pro day last year that would have led all cornerbacks at the NFL Scouting Combine. His continued development as a potential slot corner and ace special teamer will be something to watch in camp. Noah Gray has 17 games to escape the Chiefs hot seat | Arrowhead Addict If Gray can return to his career-best form from 2024—437 yards, 40 receptions on 49 targets, five touchdowns, and 25 first downs—then maybe that will prove to the Chiefs that he can be a reliable TE1. Maybe. But even then, those kinds of numbers still might not be enough. And if having the best season of your career isn’t enough to save your job, which very well might be the case for Gray, then I can’t imagine how a seat could get any hotter than that. Hot seat verdict: A steep decline in production and a high price tag mean Gray’s seat is hotter than the surface of Mercury (867° F), the hottest planet in our solar system. 9.5/10. Around the NFL Packers, DT Devonte Wyatt agree to terms on three-year, $57M extension | NFL.com A former 2022 first-round pick out of Georgia, Wyatt’s career in Wisconsin has included glimpses of top-tier potential but has also been hampered by his injury struggles. In Wyatt’s last two campaigns, he’s played in 24 of 34 regular-season games and saw his 2025 season cut short by season-ending fibula and ankle injuries. When healthy, Wyatt rounded into form in his second and third seasons, logging 10.5 sacks and 59 tackles between 2023 and 2024. He posted higher rates of production in 2025, too, tallying another four sacks and 27 tackles in 10 games before spending the remainder of the season on injured reserve. NFL All-Backup Team: Could a roster of bench players contend? | ESPN We’re going to take a flier on Fulton, who was impressive under Jesse Minter with the Chargers in 2024 before earning a two-year, $20 million deal with the Chiefs in free agency. Injuries cost him most of his debut season in Kansas City, though it never seemed that he persuaded defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo to give him more significant playing time. The Chiefs are rebuilding their cornerback room, but I’d expect Mansoor Delane, L’Jarius Sneed and Nohl Williams to be the top three options, opening up the opportunity to add Fulton or former Dolphins starter Kader Kohou to this lineup. More ESPN, NFL Network layoffs are coming Tuesday | Pro Football Talk ESPN’s clunky, on-air termination of NFL analyst Ryan Clark was just the beginning. Via Andrew Marchand of The Athletic , ESPN and NFL Network are expected to have more layoffs on Tuesday. It’s an unavoidable consequence of ESPN absorbing NFL Network. Tasks are necessarily duplicated. Now that the dust has settled on ESPN’s April 1 acquisition of NFL Network and other NFL Media assets (with the NFL securing a 10-percent stake in ESPN), Disney is about to kick up some fresh dust by issuing pink slips In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs training camp preview: How real is competition at right tackle? Reid values continuity and veteran leadership along the offensive line. Having a solid right tackle would significantly bolster an already strong line. He has openly called the right tackle position a competition entering training camp. Is this a serious battle, or just terminology used by Reid to light a fire under Moore to improve training camp and offensive line performance? title: Los Angeles Chargers Roster: Deane Leonard, CB, scheme fit, 2026 outlook
summary: Next up in our 90-in-90 series is veteran cornerback Deane Leonard! From seventh-round pick to entering his fifth season with the Chargers, let’s get to know him and how he came to be here all the way from Canada! The Basics Height: 6’0Weight: 195 poundsCollege: Ole Miss/CalgaryExperience: 4 Deane Leonard was born and raised in […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - JANUARY 11: Cornerback Deane Leonard #33 of the Los Angeles Chargers celebrates after an interception during the first half of an AFC Wild Card game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on January 11, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Next up in our 90-in-90 series is veteran cornerback Deane Leonard! From seventh-round pick to entering his fifth season with the Chargers, let’s get to know him and how he came to be here all the way from Canada! The Basics Height: 6’0 Weight: 195 pounds College: Ole Miss/Calgary Experience: 4 Deane Leonard was born and raised in Calgary, Alberta, Canada where he attended nearby Notre Dame High School. In 2014, he helped his school win the Provincial Title while also lettering in both basketball and track. Also a fun fact: Chargers teammate Amen Ogbongbemiga also played alongside Leonard at Notre Dame. Following his prep career, Leonard played three seasons for the University of Calgary where he helped them win the Vanier Cup in 2019. In 23 games, he recorded six interceptions and was twice named an All-Canadian selection. Prior to the 2020 college football season, Leonard transferred to Ole Miss where he’d finish out his college career. His first year in Oxford saw him earn a pair of starts while seeing action in eight total games. Leonard earned a full-time starting job at cornerback in 2021 and finished with 50 total tackles, one tackle for loss, and seven pass breakups. At Ole Miss’ pro day, Leonard impressed with a 4.39 40 time at 6’0 and 195 pounds. He also had a solid 4.18 in the short shuttle but underwhelmed with a 33-inch vertical. Leonard would eventually be selected by the Chargers in the seventh round of the 2022 NFL draft with the 236th-overall pick. The year prior, Leonard was actually drafted second round of the 2021 CFL draft but decided to go back to Ole Miss for his final year of eligibiity. As a rookie with the Chargers, Leonard played mainly on special teams but finished the year with five total tackles to go with a big-time forced fumble and recovery. During the 2023 season, Leonard earned the first three starts of his career while playing in 11 total games. He ended the year with 28 total tackles, one tackle for loss, three pass breakups, and one forced fumble. Leonard played mainly in a special teams role during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, appearing in 18 games total over that span and recording 13 total tackles with one tackle for loss and three pass breakups. The Good Leonard offers excellent speed and agility which he utilizes as a mainstay on the team’s special teams coverages. The moment he’s likely remember for the most came against the Broncos during Monday Night Football his rokie season that helped the Chargers down Denver in overtime. Leonard’s ability on special teams has cemented him as a core special teams player and that’s what will do most of the heavy lifting when it comes to keeping him on the active roster for the foreseeable future. Deane "clutch" Leonard. 💪🇨🇦 pic.twitter.com/E2ufagJrtG — NFL Canada (@NFLCanada) October 18, 2022 The Bad In four seasons, Leonard unfortunately has not progressed in a manner that has kept him within the two-deeps for the Chargers. His playing time has only gone down over the last two seasons and right now the only thing he offers the Bolts is a consistent and reliable role-player on kick coverages. 2026 Outlook Leonard will likely be one of the last cornerbacks kept on the active roster barring some massive performance by the UDFAs signed by the team this offseason and last. Eric Rogers will return from injury and Niko Reed once solid in very limited snaps as a rookie. Those latter players may see more time on defense but it’s hard to argue that Leonard doesn’t deserve a spot on the roster given how important the third phase of the game has become in the modern NFL. Cam Hart, Tarheeb Still, and Donte Jackson are the team’s top corners entering training camp. I wouldn’t be shocked to see the team add another veteran body to the room, but right now Leonard could be as high as the team’s CB4 or CB5, depending on how high Reed climbs before the season, if at all.

title: The $30M dilemma surrounding Aaron Donald’s return
summary: Aaron Donald’s return to the Los Angeles Rams seems imminent if the star feels he is capable of performing at a high level in 2026. Donald is ramping up his training camp regimen in hopes of joining Myles Garrett and company on the defensive line. But there are major financial implications for the Rams if […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - JANUARY 14: Aaron Donald #99 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on during pregame warmups prior to an NFC Wild Card Playoff football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on January 14, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Ryan Kang/Getty Images) | Getty Images Aaron Donald’s return to the Los Angeles Rams seems imminent if the star feels he is capable of performing at a high level in 2026. Donald is ramping up his training camp regimen in hopes of joining Myles Garrett and company on the defensive line. But there are major financial implications for the Rams if Donald’s unretirement becomes official. Because Donald retired in 2023 prior to the end of his contract, LA would owe the future hall of famer $30M that was dead money against the salary cap. This was made clear by a report from ESPN’s Adam Schefter and subsequent confirmation from Over The Cap: Yes. When he retired his last contract still had $30m remaining. My guess is he would look for more. https://t.co/JdxenaYgnJ — Jason_OTC (@Jason_OTC) July 21, 2026 This is mostly a cash issue for the team. The NFL salary cap is a separate calculation and the Rams have already been charged for money they pushed into later years prior to Donald’s retirement. Even with that in mind, LA has roughly $18-19M in open cap space available for 2026. That ranks right in the middle of their league peers. Still, $30M isn’t nothing. Even for a team in a major market like the Rams. They also have a number of core players in need of new contracts, and forking over unexpected money to Donald could complicate that equation. And the Rams have options. Deals can be reworked and renegotiated, although Over The Cap does suggest that Donald will likely want more than $30M to return to football. While Donald’s return may seem more likely than not, the financials are a notable speedbump and the first sign that a reunion may be more complicated than expected. It’s still not an insurmountable challenge. The Rams and Donald can figure this out if they want to.

title: The traits that could carry CJ Daniels to a key role on Rams
summary: It appears that L.A. Rams’ receivers Jordan Whittington and Konata Mumpfield will have some serious competition for Sean McVay’s number three spot, because rookie C.J. Daniels has traits that make him one of the most intriguing players to watch in training camp this year. Although he was only the 197th pick in the draft, Daniels […]
full_text: Jan 19, 2026; Miami Gardens, FL, USA; Miami Hurricanes wide receiver CJ Daniels (7) runs with the ball against Indiana Hoosiers defensive back Jamari Sharpe (22) during the second half of the College Football Playoff National Championship game at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | Kirby Lee-Imagn Images It appears that L.A. Rams’ receivers Jordan Whittington and Konata Mumpfield will have some serious competition for Sean McVay’s number three spot, because rookie C.J. Daniels has traits that make him one of the most intriguing players to watch in training camp this year. Although he was only the 197th pick in the draft, Daniels shares a couple of traits in common with the Rams’ two biggest stars at the position: Puka Nacua and Davante Adams. Even if Daniels doesn’t become an NFL superstar like those two, Les Snead clearly traded a few late picks to move up for him for a reason, and I think those include a Puka-like toughness and Davante-like route running. As you can see in this highlight from his time at Miami, Daniels is also no stranger to the nifty one-handed catch: With catches like this, it’s still a bit dumbfounding that Daniels fell all the way to the sixth round. There’s no doubt he would have landed somewhere eventually, and while it would be foolish to try to compare any receiver to Nacua and Adams, Daniels displays many of the traits that Snead and McVay look for in their receivers: Willing and capable run blocker, per NFL Draft Buzz Competitive toughness shows up in contested catch situations; converted 11 of 17 contested targets at Miami for a 64.7% rate while also drawing 3 pass interference calls. Fantastic ball-tracking skills , allowing Daniels to make over-the-shoulder catches in stride When you watch CJ Daniels on tape, you notice how easy he makes it all look. During his breakout year at Liberty, albeit against lesser opponents, he forced 31 missed tackles on only 55 receptions and averaged 5.9 yards after contact; that’s yet another trait that seems similar to Puka. The toughness to never go down. They weren’t all weak opponents at Liberty: Daniels had 8 catches for 79 yards in the Fiesta Bowl against No. 6 Oregon. Puka Nacua isn’t the only one who Daniels seems to emulate a little bit. Much like Davante Adams, Daniels has those little, subtle moves, the head fakes and the tempo changes to sell routes and get instant separation in short-yardage situations. And although his 40 time of 4.58 seconds surely dropped him in the draft, it’s not that much different than the 4.56 that Adams ran once upon a time. That’s why Adams learned how to use the twitchy moves and head fakes to create separation on his downfield routes. Now Daniels has Adams as a teammate who he can study up close. A high football IQ One of the traits you see over and over in Les Snead’s and Sean McVay’s draft choices is a high football IQ. With the sophisticated schemes the Rams use on both offense and defense, players must be able to understand the concepts or they will never fit on the team. Per NFL Draft Buzz, Daniels wins with his brain to overcome shortcomings as an athlete: “ Daniels is the type of receiver who probably won’t light up a room during the pre-draft process, but put his tape on and you see a guy who understands how to play the position. His route craft is legitimate . He uses his lower body to deceive defenders, changes pace within his stems, and consistently wins out of breaks with quickness rather than raw speed. The savvy is real, and it shows up week after week regardless of the uniform he’s wearing. He’s not going to run by NFL corners on go routes, but he’ll find ways to get open on the intermediate and short areas of the field where most offenses live anyway. “ Daniels fits best in a McVay type offense that values precision over explosiveness. Concepts built around timing throws, screen packages, and route combinations that create space through design fit him to a T. But now he has to prove himself in the ultimate “T”…an NFL Training camp. Daniels will face off against the likes of Whittington, Mumpfield, Xavier Smith, and others for a wide receiver 3 role that may ultimately not get that many snaps anyway. If McVay insists on running as many 12 and 13 personnel concepts as he did in 2025, the team’s third receiver will get fewer snaps than the team’s third tight end; Whittington had the third-most snaps among LA receivers last season, but fewer than Davis Allen. That’s why the player who is the Rams WR3 may not be the guy to start in 11 personnel, but the guy who reminds McVay the most of his two starters. A backup ready to insert into the lineup, not just a support piece. That’s why Daniels is one to watch moving forward: Not only because of how he complements the other receivers, but also because of how reminiscent he is of them.
author: John Newman

title: Will the 50-touchdown mark finally be surpassed in 2026?
summary: There are officially 50 days until the start of the season, so will the 50-passing-touchdown mark finally get surpassed in 2026? Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford threw the most touchdown passes in the 17-game era last season and still fell short, showing how difficult reaching the 50-touchdown plateau is. Earlier this month, I noted […]
full_text: WOODLAND HILLS, CALIFORNIA - MAY 26: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams drops back to pass during an OTA offseason workout at Rams Village at Warner Center on May 26, 2026 in Woodland Hills, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are officially 50 days until the start of the season, so will the 50-passing-touchdown mark finally get surpassed in 2026? Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford threw the most touchdown passes in the 17-game era last season and still fell short, showing how difficult reaching the 50-touchdown plateau is. Earlier this month , I noted that it’s surprising how the passing touchdown mark hasn’t been seriously challenged in the 17-game era. Peyton Manning currently holds the record with 55, a mark that has stood for 12 seasons and counting. Patrick Mahomes is the only other quarterback within the last decade to challenge Manning’s record, and he fell five short during his 2018 MVP campaign. Two other quarterbacks have thrown 50 touchdowns in a season — Tom Brady (2007) and Mahomes (2018) —showing how difficult an achievement it is. Despite the NFL throwing in an extra game beginning with the 2021 campaign, only six quarterbacks have thrown over 40 touchdown passes. Theoretically, the extra game was supposed to make it more attainable for QBs to throw for 50 touchdowns. Instead, the opposite has happened. Stafford is the only player to have thrown 40+ touchdowns twice in that span. It was reasonable to believe that with the addition of the 17th game, Manning’s passing touchdown mark would be approached sooner rather than later, yet that hasn’t been the case. These are the most touchdowns thrown by a quarterback in the 17-game era: 1.) Matthew Stafford – 46 (2025) 2.) Tom Brady – 43 (2021); Joe Burrow – 43 (2024) 3.) Patrick Mahomes – 41 (2022); Stafford – 41 (2021) ; Lamar Jackson and Baker Mayfield – 41 (2024) As efficient as Stafford was last season, he still fell a few touchdowns shy of the 50-touchdown plateau. More games haven’t translated into higher passing numbers, as expected when the extra game was announced. For example, Dak Prescott led the league with 36 touchdown passes in 2023. It was certainly a rough year for quarterback play that season. Even the number of passing attempts to reach those previously mentioned numbers in the 17-game era hasn’t been as high as you would expect, according to Pro Football Reference . Tom Brady (2021) – 719 passing attempts (No. 3 all-time) Joe Burrow (2024) – 652 passing attempts (No. 20 all-time) Patrick Mahomes (2022) – 648 passing attempts (No. 24 all-time) Matthew Stafford (2021) – 601 passing attempts (No. 81 all-time) Matthew Stafford (2025) – 597 passing attempts (No. 90 all-time) Amazingly, the extra game hasn’t led to a greater volume of passing attempts. Most of the highest touchdown totals of the 17-game era have come without historic passing volume, with Stafford’s under 600 attempts paving the way for his 46-touchdown season a year ago. Seems to be less is more, given that Brady only needed 578 attempts to reach 50 touchdown passes during his historic 2007 season with the Patriots, while Mahomes needed 580 attempts to reach his 50. However, Manning had 659 attempts (14th all-time) en route to his record-breaking campaign. Reaching the 50-passing-touchdown plateau is a challenging milestone for the vast majority of quarterbacks. For now, Stafford has the most passing touchdowns of the 17-game era. Until another QB clears 50 touchdown passes, Manning’s record will remain more secure than expected when the league schedule expanded.

title: The Rams starter under the most pressure to keep his job
summary: Omar Speights is not the first name that fans think of when they think of Rams training camp opening this week. He’s not one of the first 10 names, or probably the first 20. But if camp is for competition, then Speights is the face of one of the most intense battles expected to happen […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - JANUARY 10: Omar Speights #48 of the Los Angeles Rams warms up before the NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on January 10, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Omar Speights is not the first name that fans think of when they think of Rams training camp opening this week. He’s not one of the first 10 names, or probably the first 20. But if camp is for competition, then Speights is the face of one of the most intense battles expected to happen for a starting job on L.A.‘s depth chart in the next two months. Will Speights fend off two linebackers coming for his job? How Speights got here During his rookie season, Speights made his instincts and high football IQ clear after playing a handful of snaps against the Seahawks : “They motioned a little bit before, so I just kind of knew wherever that motion ended up going, that was where the run was gonna go,” Speights said. “So I ended up just being a cut back, so I just checked my gap first and then flew over the top just looking for an open gap to hit and I found it, and (the defensive line) did a great job up front of getting penetration… so it was easy for me to just clean up.” “Playing ball for a long time, you get a feel for certain things,” Speights said. That “playing ball for a long time” included five seasons of college football, including four at Oregon State and one at LSU. Speights racked up 378 tackles and 25 tackles for a loss during his career, but sometimes extra experience in college can be a hindrance to a player’s draft stock, not an aid. Especially after Speights was named as a freshman All-American in 2019, an honor that could have propelled him to leave school early instead of late. Teams expect true NFL players to enter the draft soon after they’re eligible. Not to wait it out as long as possible. So Speights went undrafted in 2024, largely held back for physical and athletic reasons. Lance Zeirlein of NFL.com was perhaps also lower on his instincts than Rams coaches have been in the last two years: “With average size and instincts, Speights appeared to be more comfortable in the comfort of the Oregon State defense than he was at LSU in 2023. He can be hit or miss in reading play design and finding his best positioning to make plays and he tends to sit back and wait a hair too long. He plays with active feet and good lateral slide quickness and rarely drifts into traffic unnecessarily. He sees what he hits in the box but lacks agility as an open-field tackler and can be exploited in coverage. The pre-2023 tape is better, but he might not be enough of a downhill alpha and playmaker to garner draft attention.” But physically, Zierlein may be overselling Speights compared to most NFL linebackers. At 6’, 229, he checks no boxes in that regard. However, that didn’t stop Speights from signing with the Los Angeles Rams after the draft, truly the most ideal team to find himself on given the depth at the time between Christian Rozeboom and Troy Reeder. Speights merely had to beat out Jake Hummel and Elias Neal, and he was good enough for the Rams to trade Ernest Jones to the Titans at the end of training camp too. Only six games into the season, Speights was called on to start, and he hasn’t stopped since then. Sean McVay was impressed with his effort : “I’ve seen a guy that’s consistently put in the work,” head coach Sean McVay said. “He’s got a routine and a rhythm that he has established where he’s doing extra work, taking care of his body, he’s got film, very conscientious, and this guy is a pro.” But now Speights finds himself on the other side of the Troy Reeder coin. Can Speights hold off competition? In two seasons, Speights has amassed 152 tackles, but very little else in terms of raw defensive production. No turnovers, no pass rushing, and merely acceptable in pass coverage, although that is inconsistent. PFF ranked him 25th among all linebackers in coverage in 2026. Now for the second year in a row, Speights finds himself in a competition with Shaun Dolac, another undrafted free agent with a chip on his shoulder. Dolac earned himself some fans last preseason and appeared in every game last season with the Rams, but almost exclusively on special teams. His one extensive defensive appearance came with 35 snaps against the Ravens and he had seven tackles, including one TFL. An elite linebacker in the MAC and an All-American, Dolac also has high expectations of himself and will expect to push for Speights’ job. Dolac does not have a size advantage over Speights, but could be better in other ways, as JB Scott noted last month : This sample size cannot be easily extrapolated, but it at least makes you wonder if the second-year linebacker could take over for Speights. Dolac is a better coverage than Speights, but the team needs strong run defense when its in base personnel. We know Speights does that job effectively. Dolac could bring a little extra to the table. And on free agent special teamer Grant Stuard, McVay told Bussin’ with the Boys that he’ll “probably” find a way to contribute defensively this season too . Stuard was drafted — he was the LAST pick of his draft — but through five seasons has only started five games, all with the Colts in 2024. When a guy gets an opportunity and loses it, rarely does he ever get it back. Stuard is trying to prove that’s not always the case. And Speights is trying to prove that losing it won’t be the case for him. As Rams open training camp this weekend, all eyes will be on the stars. Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, Puka Nacua, and Matthew Stafford. But the real action is on the fringes. That’s where you’ll find Speights, Stuard, and Dolac battling for an important job. That’s where you’ll find the competition to compete.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: L.A. Rams News: Matthew Stafford still had the comeback magic in 2025
summary: Matthew Stafford is still one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL when it comes to putting together go-ahead drives. He’s been pulling off comeback magic basically his whole career. Will Stafford be able to do it again? And here’s another reality, the Los Angeles Rams have lost their last few playoff games by failing […]
full_text: WOODLAND HILLS, CALIFORNIA - MAY 26: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams talks with members of the media after an OTA offseason workout at Rams Village at Warner Center on May 26, 2026 in Woodland Hills, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Matthew Stafford is still one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL when it comes to putting together go-ahead drives. He’s been pulling off comeback magic basically his whole career. Will Stafford be able to do it again? And here’s another reality, the Los Angeles Rams have lost their last few playoff games by failing to take a lead late in the game. That happened against the Detroit Lions, the Philadelphia Eagles and last year against the Seattle Seahawks. Of course, to be fair, the defense and or special teams haven’t quite held up their end in some cases either. Still though, there is an argument to be made that the Rams have been just one more drive away from putting together some even more special seasons the last few years, and they’ve come up short. That’s not exactly on Stafford, but it does show that Stafford needs more than just his own magic to go on another Super Bowl run. He needs the team to back him up too. Please comment on whatever you want and thank you for checking out Turf Show Times! Matthew Stafford was the best QB in NFL when trailing in second half (ramswire) “Matthew Stafford was at his best in 2025 exactly when the Los Angeles Rams needed him most. Stafford led all NFL quarterbacks in expected points added per dropback while trailing in the second half at +0.45, per Warren Sharp of Sharp Football Analysis , ahead of Jordan Love (+0.31), Bo Nix (+0.28), Josh Allen (+0.28) and Caleb Williams (+0.27).“ Aaron Donald told Chris Simms he’s still unsure about a comeback (ramswire) “As training camp approaches for the Los Angeles Rams , all anyone is talking about is Aaron Donald’s future. The former All-Pro defensive tackle is considering a return to football, which would end his two-year retirement in order to chase another Super Bowl ring. There’s no clear timeline for a decision to be made, and it could even spill into the regular season, but the Rams aren’t going to rush or push him. Donald hasn’t spoken publicly about his plans, only telling Pat McAfee and Jordan Schultz last month that he’s considering a comeback.“ Best fantasy performances in Los Angeles Rams history (sfweekly) “Every season in the NFL produces performances that feel less like a single game and more like statistical outliers — explosive outings where quarterbacks pile up passing yards, running backs break off long scoring runs, and receivers turn routine targets into multi-touchdown afternoons. These are the kinds of games that separate good fantasy weeks from historic ones. Stacker compiled a ranking of the best fantasy performances in Los Angeles Rams history using data from Stathead . The list includes the highest single-game fantasy scores by quarterbacks, running backs, and wide receivers/tight ends across the franchise’s history, based on standard fantasy scoring.“

title: Fernando Mendoza versus Wisconsin, Part XI of Las Vegas Raiders’ Mendoza Mania
summary: We’re getting close to the end of the regular season in Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series, diving into new Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza’s Week 12 matchup against Wisconsin. Indiana cruised to a 31-7 victory in this one, thanks to one of the best stat lines the Heisman Trophy winner had during […]
full_text: BLOOMINGTON, IN - NOVEMBER 15: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Indiana Hoosiers throws a pass during a college football game against the Wisconsin Badgers on November 15, 2025 at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Indiana. (Photo by Joe Robbins/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We’re getting close to the end of the regular season in Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series , diving into new Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza’s Week 12 matchup against Wisconsin. Indiana cruised to a 31-7 victory in this one, thanks to one of the best stat lines the Heisman Trophy winner had during the 2025 campaign, completing 22 of 24 passing attempts (91.7%) for 299 yards and four touchdowns with no interceptions . While Mendoza had a handful of impressive throws against the Badgers, including a pair of “big-time throws” according to Pro Football Focus , how he handled working through his reads/progressions was the biggest theme of the afternoon. Something I'd like to see Fernando Mendoza get at little better at is being faster at finding his checkdowns, ends up taking a sack here i/o taking the completion to stay in FG range pic.twitter.com/qHpMGLj1kX — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 14, 2026 This is the case with a lot of young quarterbacks; Mendoza can get caught big-play hunting and needs to learn how to recognize when to just take what the defense is giving him in the NFL. It’s third and seven here, and it looks like Wisconsin is running Cover 7 or some variation of pattern matching, which helps take away all of Indiana’s deep routes. The corner at the bottom of the screen is in off coverage and can run with Charlie Becker (No. 80) on the post route; the nickelback is also giving cushion and staying deep against the out and up from E.J. Williams (No. 7), and Omar Cooper Jr. slips on the deep out. Also, the boundary safety (top of the screen) is in a great spot to take away the backside dig from the tight end. In other words, the defense is taking away any options that are at or past this sticks. So, especially in this area of the field, the quarterback has to be quick to the checkdown and just take what the defense is giving him. To be fair, Mendoza eventually gets to the running back, but it’s too late since the pass-rush is starting to hit home. He does manage to escape the first sack attempt, but instead of getting rid of the ball after avoiding disaster, he scrambles and ends up taking a sack anyway. Yes, it’s third down so an incompletion or a completion short of the sticks leads to fourth down regardless. However, the offense is on the cusp of field goal range where every yard is significant because negative plays are the difference between having an opportunity to put points on the board and having to punt. Again, this is a fine line that just about every young quarterback has to learn how to toe. But understanding when it’s okay and not okay to take a sack is something the No. 1 pick can work on. Throw is nothing to speak of, but good job of working thru the progressions and finding the checkdown by Fernando Mendoza, then let Nowakowski do the dirty work for the TD #Raiders pic.twitter.com/0dUrmUVvui — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 14, 2026 The good news is that Mendoza does have instances where he does a good job of getting to the check down, with the play above serving as a strong example. The coverage is pretty similar here, as the Badgers are running a three-deep, three-under fire zone where one of the linebackers blitzes, and the defenders dropping in coverage are pattern matching. With the tight end chip blocking before releasing as the checkdown option, the defense has a three-on-two advantage on the playside of the offense’s call. This time, Mendoza is a lot faster at recognizing that nothing is open and moving on in the progression. However, the backside routes are also covered since the boundary corner is playing with off coverage to stay on top of the post route from the single receiver, and the safety is already coming downhill to pick up the running back out of the backfield. Instead of looking for the big play and scrambling, this time, Mendoza just finds his checkdown for an easy completion. Since the tight end was blocking initially, he has a delayed release, and that gets the linebacker who dropped in coverage to drift away from the offensive line to cover the middle of the field. That puts the backer out of position to pick up the tight end, leading to some YAC and a broken tackle for the touchdown. So the throw is nothing to speak of, but this is impressive quarterbacking to take what the defense is giving up and let the pass-catcher do the dirty work to get in the end zone. Impressive off-script play from Fernando Mendoza to evade the sack and find E.J. Williams on the scramble drill to pickup the 3rd down conversion #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/RQPZZMwoaH — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 14, 2026 This is a great example of the Raiders’ new quarterback finding the middle ground between the two previous plays. It’s another third and medium situation on the plus side of the 50-yard-line. However, with the line of scrimmage being at the 43-yard-line instead of the 36, as it was in the first clip above, taking a sack is okay here since the offense isn’t in field goal range yet. In fact, a loss of yards isn’t such a bad result because it would give the punter more room to pin the other team deep in their territory. In other words, this is a situation where it makes sense to extend the play as long as possible if nothing is open. That’s exactly what Mendoza does, as Wisconsin has every route past the first down marker covered. Maybe he can hit Becker on the post at the bottom of the screen since the two safeties are in quarters and occupied by the two receivers on the other side of the formation. But the corner has decent coverage on Becker, staying in the wideout’s hip and in a position to make a play on the ball. So, it’s understandable why the quarterback turned that down. Now, both the checkdowns are open with the tight end and running back working the flats. However, the defense has a linebacker to account for each of them, and both backers are in good spots to rally and make the tackle short of the sticks. On top of that, the quarterback is running out of time because both defensive tackles win their matchups and get pressure to collapse the pocket. That means it’s time for Mendoza to make a play. He delivers by evading the sack in the pocket and scrambling, which gets the third linebacker or middle hook defender to come downhill. Meanwhile, Williams (the outside receiver at the top of the screen) recognizes the scramble drill and works back toward the quarterback or where the linebacker was. As a result, Mendoza has an open target to throw to and hits his man to move the chains and keep the drive alive. That’s good situational football and a good play out of structure to create a scoring opportunity. Nice read and throw from Fernando Mendoza Finds the boundary safety to make sure he stays low, throws the skinny post and drops in the bucket to beat the other safety #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/wmlF1fHbLC — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) July 14, 2026 This time, we’ll get a look at one of the “big-time throws” mentioned above, in addition to a good read. Indiana comes out in a three-by-one formation with the ball on the hashmark, and Wisconsin responds by having its field safety (bottom of the screen) cheat to the three receiver side instead of staying in the middle of the field. Meanwhile, the boundary safety (top of the screen) lines up a few yards closer to the line of scrimmage than the field safety to serve as the “rat in the hole” or low hole defender in Cover 1. That’s significant because Mendoza is looking to hit Becker on a skinny post. But he needs to confirm the coverage first. Watch the quarterback’s eyes post-snap. Initially, he checks to see if Becker wins off the line of…
