title: Best- and worst-case scenario for Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 NFL draft class during training camp
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders’ rookies report to training camp on Thursday, meaning the Raiders’ 2026 NFL draft class will have its first chance to make a stamp on the roster soon. With that in mind, let’s dive into the best- and worst-case scenarios for each of Las Vegas’ 10 draft picks during training camp. Fernando […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - MAY 02: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders looks to pass during the team's rookie minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on May 02, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by David Becker/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders’ rookies report to training camp on Thursday, meaning the Raiders’ 2026 NFL draft class will have its first chance to make a stamp on the roster soon. With that in mind, let’s dive into the best- and worst-case scenarios for each of Las Vegas’ 10 draft picks during training camp. Fernando Mendoza Best case: Win starting QB job While it seems like the coaching staff’s plan is for Kirk Cousins to begin the season as the starter, even Cousins has said that the best quarterback needs to be on the field. And let’s be honest, the “competition” is less about Cousins versus Mendoza and more about Mendoza battling himself. If the rookie proves that he’s ready to be thrown into the fire during camp, he should be the Week 1 starter. Worst case: Falling behind Aidan O’Connell It’s completely reasonable for the No. 1 pick to begin the year on the bench and take some time to get adjusted to the NFL before being ready for action. However, if he doesn’t prove capable of at least holding down the backup job, then that could be a bad sign that the franchise is in trouble. Treydan Stukes Best case: Win starting FS job The Raiders’ defense desperately needs someone on the backend who can create turnovers. That’s a big reason why Stukes likely enters training camp as the favorite to take over for Isaiah Pola-Mao at free safety. Ball skills are one of the Arizona product’s biggest strengths, making him exactly what the secondary needs right now. Worst case: Struggle to find a position While the second-rounder is a versatile defender, sometimes those types of prospects can have a hard time finding a home in the NFL because they fall into the “jack of all trades, master of none” category. That has the potential to happen with Stukes, especially since he was primarily a nickelback and had very little experience playing free safety in college. Keyron Crawford Best case: Become third-down rusher As long as Maxx Crosby is on the roster, it’s hard to see Crawford winning a starting job over Crosby and free agent signing Kwity Paye in year one. However, it’s not out of the question for the third-round pick to beat out Malcolm Koonce as the defense’s third-down rusher. Koonce is living off an impressive nine-game run during the second half of the 2023 season, but he hasn’t done much outside of that stretch. That leaves the door open for the rookie to take over the role moving forward. Worst case: Fall into “healthy scratch” category Even if he’s awful in training camp, it’s highly unlikely that the 67th overall pick will get cut. But he is a project who needs development, and it wouldn’t be out of the question for a Top 100 selection to barely see the field as a rookie. Just ask Caleb Rogers and Charles Grant. The depth chart at edge is already crowded with Crosby, Paye and Koonce at the top, while Cian Slone and Brennan Jackson are also looking to make names for themselves to put some pressure on Crawford. Trey Zuhn III Best case: Become a surprise starter Zuhn coming out of camp with a starting job would be a surprise since he isn’t a favorite to win either guard battle or take over at right tackle. But he should be in the mix at both spots, and it isn’t like Spencer Burford, Jackson Powers-Johnson, Rogers, Jordan Meredith, DJ Glaze and Charles Grant are such heavy favorites that the rookie third-round pick doesn’t have a fighter’s chance. Worst case: Fall into “healthy scratch” category On the other side of the coin, there is a world where 2026 is a “redshirt year” for Zuhn, especially since he’s another versatile player who will be finding his true position at the next level. That doesn’t mean the third-round pick will be a bust and never see the field during his tenure in Las Vegas, but it would certainly be underwhelming if he doesn’t get much playing time as a rookie. Jermod McCoy Best case: Win a starting CB job It’s been said multiple times throughout the offseason that McCoy is the most talented corner on the Raiders’ roster, and his ability to become a starter is primarily just a matter of how healthy his surgically repaired knee is. So, it shouldn’t come as a surprise if the first-round talent earns a starting job when he’s back to 100 percent. Worst case: Knee is too fragile While McCoy has been medically cleared to play and the concerns with his knee seem to be more of a long-term issue, training camp will be the first significant stress test the joint faces. Hopefully, that doesn’t prove to be an issue, but it has to be in the back of the coaching staff’s and John Spytek’s minds. That’s part of the risk of drafting someone who has medical concerns. Mike Washington Jr. Best case: Win RB2 job It feels like Washington has the least variable outcome of the entire draft class heading into training camp. Baring an injury, it’d be a massive shock if he beat out Ashton Jeanty for the starting job, and the rest of the running back room is a collection of unproven talent. Dylan Laube and Chris Collier are a pair of veterans who barely have any regular-season experience, while Roman Hemby enters as an undrafted rookie. Worst case: Fall to RB3 Again, there’s a pretty narrow range of outcomes for the Arkansas product. But if he isn’t playing well and Laube, Collier or Hemby are standing out, then it isn’t out of the question for Washington to begin the campaign buried on the depth chart. Dalton Johnson Best case: Earn role as big nickel “Big Nickel” personnel (five defensive backs but an extra safety instead of an extra cornerback) has become more popular in the league (h/t Ryan Paganetti on X ), and expect to see more teams pivot toward the trend since the Seattle Seahawks leaned on it heavily during their Super Bowl run last year. Especially with Klint Kubiak coming from Seattle and Rob Leonard working for Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald in the past, the third safety spot on the Raiders’ depth chart will be important. Pola-Mao is likely the favorite for the role, but Johnson should be in the mix for it, too. Worst case: Special teams contributor only To be clear, this wouldn’t be a terrible situation for a fifth-round pick in year one, and getting production on special teams from a Day 3 rookie is a win. So, it certainly feels like Johnson is entering camp playing with house money. Hezekiah Masses Best case: Become 3rd outside CB There is a scenario where McCoy isn’t healthy, and Masses beats out Darien Porter for a starting spot. However, that includes one variable that is out of the fifth-rounder’s control and another that works in his favor. So, a more realistic “best case scenario” is that one of those two factors goes in his way rather than both, creating an opportunity for the Cal product to carve out a role off the bench. Worst case: Special teams contributor only Again, this isn’t the end of the world for a late-round rookie and would be a completely reasonable start to Masses’ career. In other words, he’s also entering camp with some house money. Malik Benson Best case: Become WR4 Since Benson’s skill set is similar to Tre Tucker’s and Jalen Nailor’s, it seems unlikely that the rookie will earn a starting spot in camp, barring an injury. He likely has to bring something different to the table compared to Tucker and Nailor to beat out Jack Bech or whoever else holds the third receiver spot. But the Oregon product could easily become the first receiver off the bench with a strong showing this summer. Worst case: Cut It’d be a bit of a surprise if Benson doesn’t make the team, but the Raiders cut two sixth-round picks last year: Cam Miller and Tommy Mellott. Granted, that was a different coaching staff. But it’s not out of the question since Shedrick Jackson,…

full_text: FRISCO, TX - DECEMBER 18: Missouri State Bears quarterback Jacob Clark (12) passes the ball in the Xbox Bowl between the Missouri State Bears and the Arkansas State Red Wolves on December 18, 2025 at The Ford Center in Frisco, TX (Photo by John Bunch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders signed quarterback Jacob Clark as an undrafted free agent. He was a Walter Payton Award (which goes to the best small-school player in the country) in 2024 and he was American Bowl MVP in 2025. But that doesn’t mean the Raiders don’t have plans for Clark. He is a big, strong quarterback who has a chance to stick around the program. The best case scenario for Clark in 2026 is for him to be the No. 3 quarterback on the 53-man roster, thus beating out veteran Aidan O’Connell for the job. Still, even if O’Connell is kept in Las Vegas, the Raiders could find room for Clark on the practice squad as they continue to develop him.

title: About Fernando Mendoza not starting all season
summary: A recent report by Ian Rapoport of NFL Media raised some eyebrows about the Las Vegas Raiders’ plan for rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza this season. According to Rapoport, the team’s ideal plan for the No. 1 overall draft pick is to keep him on the shelf for his entire rookie season. Rapoport said the team […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JUNE 09: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders practices drills during mandatory minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on June 09, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Louis Grasse/Getty Images) | Getty Images A recent report by Ian Rapoport of NFL Media raised some eyebrows about the Las Vegas Raiders’ plan for rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza this season. According to Rapoport, the team’s ideal plan for the No. 1 overall draft pick is to keep him on the shelf for his entire rookie season. Rapoport said the team would like to see Cousins, who was signed this offseason and who will turn 38 next month, play for the entire season. The Raiders have yet to publicly say what their plan is other than saying they do, indeed, have a quarterback plan. Both Las Vegas general manager John Spytek and head coach Klint Kubiak have said they would like to see rookie quarterbacks, in general, sit and learn in an ideal world. But an exact timeline for Mendoza hasn’t been announced. So, Rapoport’s report is interesting to suggest that Raiders would rather not insert Mendoza in the lineup att all in 2026. From The Insiders on @NFLNetwork : Looking at the #Raiders QB situation and what the best-case scenario is. pic.twitter.com/fuNujx698A — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) July 17, 2026 However, Rapoport made it clear there are no absolutes in this plan and he left plenty of outs for the plan to change. His point is if Cousins, who played under Kubiak for three successful seasons in Minnesota, plays well and stays healthy, there will be no reason to move away from him. Rapoport also mentioned Mendoza can simply steal the job if he plays well in the training camp and the preseason. So, in reality, this is simply a fluid situation. could Cousins play the entire year? Yes. Could Mendnza win the job by Week 1? Yes. It’s as simple and as complicated, at the same time, as that.

The ligament tear happened on November 22nd in a game against SMU, however since Bell wasn’t in the National Football League at that time, his designation is of the non-football variety. According to Cameron Wolfe of NFL Network, Bell is still working to get back to “football mode” and the team is being cautious with their young investment. Miami’s rookies reported to the facility on Tuesday morning to get a jump on training camp. Dolphins’ veterans will report one week from today — on July 28th. In four seasons with Louisville, Bell played in 47 games, amassing 151 receptions for 2,166 yards and 12 touchdowns. He averaged 14.3 yards per reception in college. His senior season (2025) was his most productive — catching 72 passes for 917 yards and 6 touchdowns in just 11 games played. Prior to his injury, Bell was being discussed as a late first-round pick in some draft circles. We will continue to keep you updated with all things Miami Dolphins as the long, football-less summer nears its conclusion.

title: Dolphins’ ‘three pillars’ signed; who is next?
summary: When Jon-Eric Sullivan was hired as the Miami Dolphins’ newest general manager this offseason, he immediately put his stamp on the organization. Miami’s roster has undergone significant changes, with many players jettisoned by Sullivan in short order. However, when asked who he views as building blocks for the team moving forward, Miami’s GM named three […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 28: Offensive tackle Patrick Paul #52 of the Miami Dolphins stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Green Bay Packers, at Lambeau Field on November 28, 2024 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images When Jon-Eric Sullivan was hired as the Miami Dolphins’ newest general manager this offseason, he immediately put his stamp on the organization. Miami’s roster has undergone significant changes, with many players jettisoned by Sullivan in short order. However, when asked who he views as building blocks for the team moving forward, Miami’s GM named three pillars; running back De’Von Achane, center Aaron Brewer and linebacker Jordyn Brooks. With Brooks signing a three-year, $51.3 million deal with the Dolphins on Tuesday, all three of Sullivan’s pillars have been inked to big-money contract extensions ahead of the 2026 NFL season — leaving no doubt that Miami views Achane, Brewer and Brooks as the team’s core heading into the upcoming year. However, beyond those three, who else is deserving of a new deal? In an article posted to ESPN today , Marcel Louis-Jacques dropped a clue that Miami’s starting left tackle — Patrick Paul — may be the next in line for a contact extension in sunny South Florida. “With the three “pillars” signed, the Dolphins are set to open training camp next week with no unsettled contract negotiations. The next logical choice for an extension is left tackle Patrick Paul, who is entering his third season with the team.” Extending Paul before his price-tag goes through the roof would be a smart strategy for Sullivan, as left tackles earn massive paychecks while protecting a team’s most important player — the starting quarterback. However, after emerging as an impact player for Miami during his first full season as a starter in 2025, Paul could already command a top-10 salary at the position. Currently, Kolton Miller of the Las Vegas Raiders and Jordan Mailata of the Philadelphia Eagles are tied as the 10th highest paid left tackles in the NFL according to Over the Cap — averaging $22 million per year. NFL rules state that players playing on their rookie contract cannot sign an extension until they’ve had at least three years of service at the pro level, so Paul wouldn’t even be eligible for a new deal until after the 2026 season anyway. However, that won’t keep Sullivan from having exploratory conversations with Paul and his agent this year.
author: Marek Brave

title: Dolphins, Jordyn Brooks agree to extension
summary: The Miami Dolphins and linebacker Jordyn Brooks have agreed to a three-year contract extension, keeping the veteran with the team through the 2029 season. Earlier in the offseason, new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan identified core players he envisioned the Dolphins building around as they reset their roster for the future. With the extension of Brooks, […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - DECEMBER 15: Jordyn Brooks #20 of the Miami Dolphins reacts as he leads a huddle prior to an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Pennsylvania on December 15, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins and linebacker Jordyn Brooks have agreed to a three-year contract extension, keeping the veteran with the team through the 2029 season. Earlier in the offseason, new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan identified core players he envisioned the Dolphins building around as they reset their roster for the future. With the extension of Brooks, Miami has now reached contract agreements with three of those players, including running back De’Von Achane and center Aaron Brewer. Brooks’ extension and contract details were first reported by ESPN’s Adam Schefter. Brooks contract details The new extension, which adds the 2027, 2028, and 2029 seasons to Brooks’ contract, is worth $51.3 million. It includes $35 million in guarantees. The new money, when it kicks in, will jump Brooks to $17.1 million in average per year, making him the fifth-highest paid linebacker in the league. Prior to the extension, Brooks was entering the final season of the three-year contact he signed with the Dolphins as a free agent in 2024. He participated in all of the team’s offseason training program, including all voluntary events, while working toward the extension. Brooks’ Dolphins’ tenure Since joining Miami, Brooks has locked down the middle of the team’s defense. The 28-year-old has started all 34 games for the Dolphins, tallying 326 tackles, 6.5 sacks, nine passes defensed, one forced fumble, and three fumble recoveries. Last season, how 183 tackles led the league and he earned his first Pro Bowl selection. He was also a First-Team All-Pro selection for the first time in his career. He originally entered the league as a first-round pick in 2020 by the Seattle Seahawks, spending his first four seasons with the team. Who could be next? The Dolphins have now extended three key members of their roster rebuild, working to add pieces around Achane, Brewer, and Brooks. But, who could be next in line for an extension? Right tackle Austin Jackson signed a three-year contract extension with the team in 2023, making 2026 the final year on that deal. Based on his play, Jackson could be in line for another extension, but questions about his health continue to linger and probably forces the team to wait until he completes this season to consider a new contract. Jackson has only played 14 games the last two years, and Miami needs to see more availability from their 2020 first-round pick before they agree to another extension. Linebacker Tyrel Dodson could also be a consideration for an extension, but the team may have positioned themselves this year to move on from the veteran after the season. During the 2026 NFL Draft, Miami selected Jacob Rodriguez in the second round and Kyle Louis in the fourth round, both of whom could be a projected replacement for Dodson in 2027. Dolphins salary cap space According to OverTheCap.com, the Dolphins have about $11.7 million in salary cap space for this season. The extension for Brooks may add some additional space if any of his salary was converted to a signing bonus or any void years were added to the back end of the deal. Miami could still consider adding a free agent this summer to bolster their roster, or they may hold on to the money to address any injuries during the season. The Dolphins could also roll unused cap space into the 2027 salary cap.

title: Not a Drill: Training Camp is Here!
summary: We’re almost there, folks: training camp. While the NFL offseason is tediously long, I’m usually fine and adequately preoccupied with baseball and the usual summer activities that fill evenings and weekends. The World Cup was also a welcome distraction this year. Nonetheless, when the MLB All-Star Break hits, the itch becomes impossible to scratch, and […]
full_text: We’re almost there, folks: training camp. While the NFL offseason is tediously long, I’m usually fine and adequately preoccupied with baseball and the usual summer activities that fill evenings and weekends. The World Cup was also a welcome distraction this year. Nonetheless, when the MLB All-Star Break hits, the itch becomes impossible to scratch, and football season can’t arrive soon enough. The focus will be on the quarterback competition. Since I last touched on the topic a few weeks ago, the odds have shifted ever so slightly in J.J. McCarthy’s favor (-770, 88.5% implied probability, down from -1000, 90.9%). Regardless, it can still comfortably be filed under “shock” if Kyler Murray isn’t under center in Week 1. How I feel and what I want are utterly irrelevant. The important thing is that the Vikings’ front office has secured the appropriate insurance policy with Murray and (a healthy) Carson Wentz to ensure last year’s quarterback situation is not repeated. Good luck to Kyler and J.J., and whatever happens, happens. There’ll be plenty of time to analyze and discuss all of that soon enough. For the purpose of this article, I’d like to take a look at the Top 5 non-QB competition-related storylines I’ll be focused on when training camp begins in a few days. KOC Scheme Tweaks? Year 5 is always a tricky spot for head coaches, especially those who also call plays. Tendencies are well known, and situational preferences are closely scouted. It’s wise at this point to consider new looks, or at minimum, tweaks to established norms. Stubbornness and a refusal to do so can be counterproductive. Take Mike Zimmer. He was a “the scheme is the scheme” guy. I specifically remember misplaced confidence, in quotes, before the 2020 season. The result? It was fantastic from 2014-2019, but then it literally fell off a cliff. There was no gradual decline; it went from great to horrific in record time. I certainly don’t expect that from KOC, but perhaps slightly less reliance on 11 Personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) and addressing pass-vs.-run balance and short-yardage criticisms wouldn’t hurt. In 2025, 11 Personnel was used for approximately 60-65% of snaps, and 55-70% in prior seasons. This comes as the Vikings were effective in EPA/pass metrics out of 12 Personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR) when it’s been used upwards of 25% of the time. KOC could look no further than his mentor, Sean McVay, and what McVay did with the Rams last year. He embraced 13 personnel (1 RB, 3 TEs, 1 WR) far more than ever before, with tremendous results. I can’t get over this : From 2021-24, Los Angeles used 13 personnel on just six plays total, and against the Jaguars, they ran 13 personnel on nearly 40% of their snaps. The Vikings could definitely benefit from some unpredictability this season. Likewise, given that Murray is among the most mobile QBs in history and many of McCarthy’s best highlights came from him creating plays on the ground, incorporating more read-option and designed runs to maximize this makes a ton of sense. Yes, I’m well aware that KOC isn’t going to show many substantive changes in open practices and preseason games, but that doesn’t mean it’s not happening. And it doesn’t mean you won’t see a hint of something in small doses here and there. Who Will Be WR4? The starting three of Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and Jauan Jennings is set, but it gets interesting after that. While it may not have a dramatic impact this year, the WR4 could see considerable playing time in the future, as Addison has yet to sign an extension and Jennings’ deal is only for this season. My optimism that former third-round pick Tai Felton would be ready to assume the WR3 role this season was premature. Now there appears to be a legitimate competition for WR4. UFA Dillon Bell, out of Georgia, is an interesting prospect with clear dual-threat capabilities similar to Deebo Samuel. His output was not eye-popping by any stretch, but he seemed to be part of many big-time plays in key moments for the Bulldogs over the past few seasons. Myles Price is a likely roster lock due to his proven special-teams ability, so he is unlikely to make much noise in this spot. But hey, you never know. Speaking of you never know, this is the team of Adam Thielen, who attended a rookie tryout and became Adam Thielen – a multi-time Pro Bowl selection who holds the NFL record for most consecutive 100-yard receiving games. The WR position is always interesting for the Vikings, and it wouldn’t surprise me at all if someone unexpectedly makes a name for themselves over the next six weeks. Harrison Smith Watch/Competition at Safety. Lots of moving pieces on the backend of the defense. I still expect Harrison Smith to return for a 15th season. If so, that will make the Jay Ward-Theo Jackson competition for the starting role something to watch. Ward’s defensive snap count share rose considerably in the final three games of the season (78% – 61% – 88%), while Jackson’s dipped from his early-season highs. There were injury issues for Jackson, but that doesn’t fully explain the decline in production and role. A strong training camp is going to be of paramount importance for both, especially Jackson. Third-rounder Jakobe Thomas’ skill set and scheme flexibility are a perfect fit for Flores’ Big Nickel packages, and it wouldn’t surprise me if he doesn’t make a case for starting reps come September. Flores has not hesitated to give rookies valuable playing time if he believes they’re ready. Josh Metellus is the only one given at this point. The rest of the story will be written throughout August in Eagan. Blake Brandel, Starting Center. The center position has always been important, but it’s taken on even greater importance in today’s NFL. Not only do centers need to be the general of the offensive line, reading defensive alignments and guiding protection calls, but they also need to be exceptional pass blockers. With the focus on interior pressure, in addition to the traditional outside pass rush, the modern interior d-lineman is far more athletic and capable of creating havoc on their own than in eras past. The good news? In the 363 snaps he played at center last year for Ryan Kelly, Brandel logged a solid 67.6 PFF pass-blocking grade, good for 14th among eligible centers. An entire offseason of reps should lead to improvement, but how he handles the onslaught of nightmares Brian Flores’ scheme will surely present throughout training camp will go a long way toward instilling confidence (or not) as the calendar turns to September. This issue has been a persistent thorn in the side of the Vikings for far too long. Here’s hoping for the best outcome. Dallas Turner’s Development. So far, no additional veteran pass-rushers have been brought in. If this holds, Turner appears to be in line for the entirety of the snaps Jonathan Greenard received over the past two seasons. I’ve covered this in a previous post , but when you drill down into the 2025 numbers, Greenard’s output wasn’t as bad as the topline numbers suggested, while Turner’s wasn’t quite as good. Unlucky breaks and fortuitous circumstances were at play. As of now, I can’t, in good conscience, say there won’t be a drop-off in production. But just as records are made to be broken, so are narratives. A dominant camp by Turner would ease many concerns in a season where so much is on the line. The defense must match its 2025 late-season dominance to meet fans’ considerable expectations this season, and it’s hard to see that happening if Turner isn’t a major part of the equation. So, there you have it. We made it, folks. The offseason proper will soon be in the rearview mirror – and it couldn’t happen soon enough.

full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 11: J.J. McCarthy #9 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on during training camp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 11, 2025 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the 2026 season approaches, The Real Forno Show hosted a deep-dive episode breaking down the hottest narratives surrounding the Minnesota Vikings. From the quarterback competition between J.J. McCarthy and Kyler Murray to legitimate questions about Kevin O’Connell’s coaching identity, Tyler Forness challenged conventional wisdom with film study and analytics. “I’m just honest with my opinions,” Forness said. “I’m always gonna tell you what I think, and just because that’s what I believe based on the data doesn’t mean that’s how I would like it to go.” On Kyler Murray’s often-misrepresented injury history, Forness offered important context: “We’re not talking about somebody who’s constantly injured — it’s three injuries across seven years.” The offensive line also received a nuanced defense: “Of the 60 sacks, only 26 of them were deemed the fault of the offensive line.” On O’Connell, Forness reframed the narrative: “Kevin O’Connell is a veteran quarterback whisperer — he can take somebody who already has a built-in foundation and maximize everything they can do well.” Key Episode Bullet Points: J.J. McCarthy played FOUR strong games, not five : “It is semantics, I understand, but it was not five, it was four — because he did not play against the Detroit Lions.” Kyler Murray’s injury history is overstated : “He’s suffered three injuries that have cost him time over his career… we’re not talking about a guy who’s constantly injured.” The offensive line was misunderstood : “Only 26 of 60 sacks were deemed the fault of the offensive line.” The unit ranked 14th in both run and pass blocking per PFF. Turnover luck swung 21 plays year-over-year : “The Vikings went from plus-nine in the turnover margin to minus-twelve — that is a 21-turnover swing,” directly correlating to their drop from 14-3 to 9-8. The run defense was average, not a disaster : “The run defense was 15th in the league. When your overall defense is fifth and your pass defense is second, are we maybe focusing on the wrong thing?” O’Connell is a “veteran quarterback whisperer” : “He has maximized Kirk Cousins, maximized Sam Darnold, maximized Josh Dobbs, maximized Nick Mullens… but we won’t know he’s a true quarterback whisperer until he elevates a young player.” Rookie defensive linemen Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange should be eased in : “They weren’t taken to be year-one players. title: Patriots training camp preview 2026: Running backs searching for efficiency
summary: On paper, New England Patriots fielded one of the NFL’s most productive rushing attacks in 2025. Despite finishing sixth in rushing yards and fourth in rushing touchdowns, however, there was more to offer from the team’s designed run game.  Still, the potential upside of a second year of the Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson pairing […]
full_text: Feb 8, 2026; Santa Clara, CA, USA; New England Patriots running back Treveyon Henderson (32) warms up before the game against the Seattle Seahawks in Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images | Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images On paper, New England Patriots fielded one of the NFL’s most productive rushing attacks in 2025. Despite finishing sixth in rushing yards and fourth in rushing touchdowns, however, there was more to offer from the team’s designed run game. Still, the potential upside of a second year of the Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson pairing left New England comfortable making minimal changes to the room this offseason. In the next edition of our Patriots training camp preview series, we’ll take a look at New England’s running back corps in its entirety and discuss the biggest takeaways heading into the summer practices. Veterans will report to the facility on July 24. *Denotes player on the Pats Pulpit 53-man roster projection Depth chart Starters: Rhamondre Stevenson (28)* , TreVeyon Henderson (23)* | Backups: Lan Larison (24)* , Terrell Jennings (25) , Jam Miller (22/R) , Myles Montgomery (23/R) Stevenson is projected to remain the starting back in 2026 after an up-and-down season. The sixth-year back lost three fumbles within the first five weeks; however, Stevenson fought through the hurdle and established himself as a dependable presence. En route to a Super Bowl appearance, Stevenson finished with the 10th-highest yards over expected percentage among running backs at 45% (a measure of the rushing attempts where a rusher gains more yards than are blocked for them). Alongside Stevenson is Henderson, who immediately established himself as one of the most explosive rushers in the league with four touchdown runs of 50 or more yards and 30 missed tackles. The 23-year-old had apparent lapses as a blocker and efficient runner between the tackles, but he’ll look to expand on a positive rookie season. Both Lan Larison and Terrell Jennings saw time as the third running back in the rotation during spring practices and will continue to compete with each other for that role heading into training camp. Jennings has over 36 rushing attempts for the Patriots over the past two seasons and will open camp on the non-football injury list , while Larison is returning from a season-ending broken foot he suffered in 2025 as a rookie. Rounding out the back end of the depth chart are powerful seventh-round rookie Jam Miller from Alabama and dynamic undrafted free agent Myles Montgomery from UCF. The two additions have worked with the third-team offense thus far and will continue to acclimate to the NFL as the offseason workouts progress. Key question: Can the O-line provide enough as a run-blocking unit? While the volume numbers reflect the run-game production near the top of the league, the efficiency metrics suggest otherwise. New England’s running backs performed at a league-average 4.4 yards per attempt. Yet, they only totaled an EPA (expected points added) per rush of -0.03, which ranks No. 17, meaning the offense wasn’t consistently creating favorable situations on the ground. Although that figure stems from a multitude of factors, New England’s offensive line played a noticeable role in that underperformance. The Patriots’ line needed more push and play strength at the point of attack to routinely create running lanes, leading to the signing of Alijah Vera-Tucker at left guard. The former New York Jet slots in between left tackle Will Campbell and newly transitioned center Jared Wilson, who will be entering their second seasons. Padded practices during training camp, when the offense can begin integrating live designed runs, will be a measure of how improved the run blocking will be. X-Factor: TreVeyon Henderson Additionally, though Henderson proved he’s a dynamic playmaker who is a touchdown threat whenever the ball is in his hands, the ball carrier’s vision and pass protection ability held him back. The highly touted pass blocker out of Ohio State couldn’t replicate the same collegiate success during his rookie year. Furthermore, he lacked the proper field vision to improvise behind the line of scrimmage, resulting in stuffed attempts behind the line of scrimmage. In terms of improvement, Henderson identified similar areas of emphasis earlier this offseason. “The biggest thing I want to continue to develop, blocking and just during this time running routes out of the backfield, catching the ball out of the backfield,” Henderson said to reporters at the beginning of June. “This is a time when we can really just continue to enhance those skills. Specifically those two skills, I definitely want to continue to develop.” Much of the running back room’s potential relies on the development of Henderson entering year two. If he can find his stride, Henderson and Stevenson can make New England’s offense a significant two-dimensional threat in 2026.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Patriots to work out free agent tight end as training camp begins
summary: The New England Patriots are set to take another look at a former member of their practice squad. Thomas Odukoya, whose contract with the team expired in February, will be in town for a free agency workout this week. Aaron Wilson of KPRC 2 Houston was first to report the team’s interest in the 29-year-old. […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - OCTOBER 19: Thomas Odukoya #88 arrives to Nissan Stadium prior to the NFL 2025 game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on October 19, 2025 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots are set to take another look at a former member of their practice squad. Thomas Odukoya, whose contract with the team expired in February, will be in town for a free agency workout this week. Aaron Wilson of KPRC 2 Houston was first to report the team’s interest in the 29-year-old. A 6-foot-6, 253-pound tight end, Odukoya originally joined New England’s practice squad last October. He spent the remainder of the season with the team, but was moved to the practice squad injured reserve in December after suffering a broken leg in practice. Now fully healthy again, he will get an opportunity to showcase his readiness. Born in the Netherlands, Odukoya entered the NFL through the International Player Pathway Program in 2022. He spent his first three seasons with the Tennessee Titans, including two under now-Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel, before being let go and reuniting with Vrabel in New England. The Patriots are entering their 2026 training camp with uncertainty at tight end. While Hunter Henry is entrenched into the starting position, the depth behind him is a collective question mark following the season-ending injury suffered by Julian Hill during offseason workouts. At the moment, Jack Westover and rookies Eli Raridon and Tanner Arkin round out the group. Fellow tight end C.J. Dippre is also part of it, but he was placed on the active/PUP list on Tuesday . New England currently has a full roster, but Odukoya’s international status would allow him to join the club as a roster-exempt 92nd player. As such, he would join German-born Lorenz Metz, who currently hold spot No. 91. The Patriots will hold the first practice of this year’s training camp on Saturday at 10:15 a.m. ET.

title: Patriots place 3 on injury lists before training camp
summary: Three members of the New England Patriots are set to begin training camp on the sidelines. Edge defender Harold Landry and tight end C.J. Dippre were both placed on the physically unable to perform list (PUP) on Tuesday, with running back Terrell Jennings moving to the non-football injury/illness list (NFI). Despite those designations, all three […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 06: Linebacker Harold Landry III #2 of the New England Patriots walks to the field during joint training camp between the New England Patriots and Washington Commanders on August 6, 2025 at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Three members of the New England Patriots are set to begin training camp on the sidelines. Edge defender Harold Landry and tight end C.J. Dippre were both placed on the physically unable to perform list (PUP) on Tuesday, with running back Terrell Jennings moving to the non-football injury/illness list (NFI). Despite those designations, all three remain on the Patriots’ active 90-man roster. What those labels do show, however, is that the trio is not yet able to participate in practice. Once their statuses change, they can come off the respective lists at any point and immediately join their teammates on the fields behind Gillette Stadium. Landry, 30, moves to PUP after already sitting out parts of New England’s offseason workout program. A non-participant during last month’s mandatory minicamp, the 2025 free agency pickup was hampered by a nagging knee injury over the second half of his first season with the club. “This is all part of everyone having a little different plan,” head coach Mike Vrabel said about Landry during minicamp. “He is very involved, very heavily involved in the meetings and the workouts and in a leadership role. For him to take reps right now in the spring, I feel like is unnecessary. We will just keep working to make sure that he is ready to go when we need him.” Dippre, 24, arrived in New England as a rookie free agent last season. Initially a practice squad player who finished the year on the active roster without seeing any game action, he did participate in minicamp without any obvious limitation. At points, the sophomore served as the next man up at tight end behind starter Hunter Henry and veteran Jack Westover. Jennings, 25, also did not show any signs of injury during minicamp. In fact, the third-year man saw some reps as a part-time RB3 backing up Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. Unlike Dippre, he did see some game action last year: the former UDFA played in seven games and carried the ball 23 times for 73 yards and a touchdown. Landry, Dippre and Jennings were part of a select group of veterans reporting to the Patriots’ training camp on Tuesday. They were joined by the team’s rookies and quarterbacks. The rest of the team’s roster will have to arrive in Foxborough by Friday. The first practice of this year’s training camp will take place at 10:15 a.m. ET the following day.

title: First players report to 2026 Patriots training camp on Tuesday
summary: Training camp season has arrived in Foxborough, and so has the first group of New England Patriots. Starting on Tuesday, drafted and undrafted rookies as well as select veterans including the team’s quarterbacks have begun reporting to camp. Headlined by starting quarterback Drake Maye and first-round draft pick Caleb Lomu, upwards of 25 players are […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JUNE 02: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots walks on to the field during New England Patriots OTA on June 2, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Training camp season has arrived in Foxborough, and so has the first group of New England Patriots. Starting on Tuesday, drafted and undrafted rookies as well as select veterans including the team’s quarterbacks have begun reporting to camp. Headlined by starting quarterback Drake Maye and first-round draft pick Caleb Lomu, upwards of 25 players are scheduled to report to Gillette Stadium. Rookies reporting 💪 @newbalance | #NEPats pic.twitter.com/wpH094IMJN — New England Patriots (@Patriots) July 21, 2026 The arrivals will go through physical examination and classroom training before hitting the practice fields alongside the rest of the Patriots’ active roster on Saturday. Draft picks The Players listed here were all picked by the Patriots in the 2026 NFL Draft. In total, the team brought in nine players in late April’s selection meeting. OT Caleb Lomu ED Gabe Jacas TE Eli Raridon CB Karon Prunt OT Dametrious Crownover LB Namdi Obiazor QB Behren Morton RB Jam Miller ED Quintayvious Hutchins With the exception of second-rounder Gabe Jacas the entire group has signed its rookie contracts and is therefore eligible to participate in training camp without any restrictions. Jacas, meanwhile, will be in the spotlight the coming days. Under normal circumstances, however, a resolution to his apparent contract stalemate should be expected sooner rather than later — similar to what happened with fellow second-rounder TreVeyon Henderson in 2025. Undrafted free agents The players listed here all signed with the Patriots as rookie free agents. In total, 14 of the UDFAs brought aboard after the draft currently remain on the 90-man roster and will get a chance to prove themselves over the coming weeks. RB Myles Montgomery WR Nick DeGennaro WR Cameron Dorner WR Kyle Dixon WR Jimmy Kibble TE Tanner Arkin OL JonDarius Morgan OL Jacob Rizy DT David Blay Jr. ED Xavier Holmes LB Khalil Jacobs CB Channing Canada CB Kenneth Harris S Peter Manuma Historically, the Patriots have not shied away from giving UDFAs opportunities over the course of the summer. Just last year, two of them — wide receiver Efton Chism and outside linebacker Elijah Ponder — made the team out of training camp. This year, running back Myles Montgomery, tight end Tanner Arkin, offensive linemen JonDarius Morgan and Jacob Rizy, and linebacker Khalil Jacobs look like the most realistic candidates to follow in their footsteps. In total, the Patriots will have four fewer rookies at training camp than last year. Quarterbacks The Patriots have a clear hierarchy at quarterback heading into training camp: QB Drake Maye QB Tommy DeVito QB Behren Morton Drake Maye is the undisputed QB1 coming off an MVP-caliber season that saw him lead the Patriots to the Super Bowl; expectations are high for the third-year man in his second season working alongside offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels. Tommy DeVito was elevated to the top backup spot this offseason in light of Joshua Dobbs getting released, while rookie Behren Morton projects as a camp arm fighting for one of the final spots on the roster. Camp #️⃣3️⃣ for @DrakeMaye2 👏 pic.twitter.com/IAE99mg7Ri — New England Patriots (@Patriots) July 21, 2026 New England’s full roster will have reported at Gillette Stadium by Friday. The Patriots will then hold their first practice of this year’s training camp on Saturday, July 25, at 10:15 a.m. ET.

title: Patriots O-line deep dive: Right guard
summary: When New England Patriots training camp opens at the end of the week, there’s going to be one position group that a lot of eyes are going to be on, and rightfully so. There’s probably not a bigger question mark on the team right now than the offensive line. The possible outcomes for this group […]
full_text: Jun 10, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots guard Mike Onwenu (71) warms up during minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images When New England Patriots training camp opens at the end of the week, there’s going to be one position group that a lot of eyes are going to be on, and rightfully so. There’s probably not a bigger question mark on the team right now than the offensive line. The possible outcomes for this group are wildly different, and, depending on who you ask, people either feel a lot better about last year, about the same, or, in some cases, even worse. In this week leading up to camp, I’m going to do a deep dive into each position along the offensive line and let you know whether I think the Patriots improved, and what to expect from the position as a whole. Today is Day 2, and we’re starting at right guard. Let’s get into it. Right guard deep dive 2025 starter: Mike Onwenu Projected 2026 starter: Mike Onwenu No changes at this position this year: Mike Onwenu is the clear starter, and they didn’t add any backups this offseason, except for undrafted free agent JonDarius Morgan. Onwenu has been one of the best guards in the league the last few years, and the Patriots will be hoping that they can get the same type of performance from him again this year. The big question with this position is what is going to happen in 2027 and beyond. Onwenu is on a reworked one-year deal , and there hasn’t been any word about an extension with the pending unrestricted free agent. The Patriots have extensions coming with Christian Gonzalez and Drake Maye, so they may not be willing to pay Onwenu what he is worth (or at least what he thinks he is worth). If they don’t, there’s no one else to take over, so that would become a sizable hole for the Patriots to fill. Luckily, they still have Big Mike for this season, and they should be solid at right guard once again.

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for OT Caleb Lomu
summary: One year after selecting an offensive tackle in the first round of the NFL Draft, the New England Patriots did it again. Following a short trade-up with the Bills, the reigning AFC champions added Caleb Lomu with the 28th overall pick. Unlike his 2025 counterpart Will Campbell, Lomu did not join the Patriots’ starting lineup […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots tackle Caleb Lomu (74) looks on at minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images One year after selecting an offensive tackle in the first round of the NFL Draft, the New England Patriots did it again. Following a short trade-up with the Bills, the reigning AFC champions added Caleb Lomu with the 28th overall pick. Unlike his 2025 counterpart Will Campbell, Lomu did not join the Patriots’ starting lineup the very moment he set foot in Foxborough. However, the long-term expectation is still the same: like Campbell on the left side, the Utah product was added this year to provide stability on the right — even though his rookie campaign might not look the part. Hard facts Name: Caleb Lomu Position: Offensive tackle Jersey number: 74 Opening day age: 21 (12/23/2004) Measurements : 6’7 1/4”, 313 lbs, 9 1/2” hand size, 33 3/8” arm length, 82 3/4” wingspan, 4.99s 40-yard dash, 32 1/2” vertical jump, 9’5” broad jump, 25 bench press reps, 9.77 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: New England Patriots (2026-) | College: Utah (2023-25) Playing football since his childhood, Lomu attended Highland High School in his hometown of Gilbert, AZ. He saw action at both tackle and guard, and as a senior was named the top offensive lineman in the state. Eventually, he was rated as a four-star recruit and received scholarship offers from multiple high-profile programs such as Michigan, Oregon or USC. However, he opted to join Utah. In three seasons as a Ute, Lomu saw action in 27 games with 24 starts. He redshirted as a freshman after appearing in three games, and from his second season on was a fixture on the team’s offensive line: he started 12 games each in 2024 and 2025, earning freshman All-American and first-team All-Big 12 honors in those respective seasons. Despite having two years of eligibility left, Lomu decided to leave school in 2026. One of the top offensive tackle prospects in the draft, he was selected 28th overall in the first round by the Patriots, as noted above. Scouting report Strengths: Lomu combines good height and adequate length with a buildable frame. He also offers an explosive athletic skillset: he is quick out of his stance and has good foot speed and general range as a pass protector. He has impressive patience in 1-on-1s against pass rushers and the grip strength to keep them engaged throughout his reps. He is nimble on his feet without compromising his balance or foundation, allowing him to mirror defenders and perform quick kickbacks to force them wide. Lomu also also can recover quickly while staying level, and has a good feel for where pressure is coming from; he adjusts his position without much effort. A fluid a athlete, he is an effective second-level blocker who quickly gets to his landmarks in the run game. His quick feet allow him to be used on a variety of reach and pull blocks, and he has the versatility to line up on both the left and the right side of the offensive line. Caleb Lomu | OT | Utah Smooth, athletic mover w/ good frame. Ability to recover w/ feet or hands once behind. Varied hand tech to keep rushers guessing, good mirror once latched. Rangy run blocker on reaches & great framing at 2nd level. Easily works hips around def in space. pic.twitter.com/OGwvcNn9iY — Matt Lane (@Matty_KCSN) April 17, 2026 Weaknesses: More tall than big, Lomu does not stand out from a size perspective and ranks only in the 23rd percentile in arm length and in the 14th percentile in hand size. He has quick feet but oftentimes takes some rather uncoordinated steps, something that is also true for his hand placement. He is a good pass protector, but not on the same level in the run game. His physicality and aggression blocking the run is uneven, and he might have to bulk up and add more core strength in order to consistently move bodies on the ground. 2025 review Stats : 12 games (12 starts) | 823 offensive snaps | 8 QB pressures surrendered (2 hits, 6 hurries) | 4 penalties (incl. 0 declined/offsetting) Season recap: Lomu’s first year as a starter already was a success, but he managed to take his game to another level in his second season as Utah’s left tackle. Not only did he showcase exemplary durability — he was tied for the team lead with 823 offensive snaps before opting out of the Utes’ bowl game against Nebraska — he also performed at a high level as both a pass protector and a run blocker. In 383 pass blocking reps, Lomu surrendered only eight quarterback pressures without a single sack. His pressure rate of 2.1% ranked among the best in the nation among qualifying tackles (i.e. those who played upwards of 325 snaps in pass protection), and he was one of only 20 such OTs at the FBS level not to give up a single sack throughout the season. As a run blocker, meanwhile, Lomu helped Utah gain an average of 7.1 yards per carry to the left side of the formation. Obviously, he alone was not responsible for that number — the run game is a full-team effort — but he did show some strides while also leading the team in YPC when directly ran behind (8.9). With Lomu leading Utah’s O-line, the unit was voted the Big 12 Offensive Line of the Week on four occasions, while he himself was voted first-team all-conference after the year. He subsequently ended his college career early by opting out of his team’s appearance in the Las Vegas Bowl to start his preparation for the NFL. 2026 preview Position: Swing tackle | Ability: Fringe starter/Role player | Contract: Signed through 2029 (2030 UFA) What will be his role? Lomu played left tackle in college, but based on his first offseason in New England he will start his career as a swing tackle behind current Patriots starters Will Campbell and Morgan Moses. As such, he will enter the lineup in case of injury higher up on the depth chart as well as in select packages as a sixth offensive lineman/jumbo tight end. Overall, however, his playing time share will not be on the same level as it was in his final two years at Utah — at least in 2026. By 2027, he realistically could replace Moses as the starting right tackle. What is his growth potential? Lomu has the build and movement skills to become an impact player in the NFL, but he needs to keep filling out his frame and become stronger in the run game. That strength includes physicality; he has to learn to adopt a more aggressive approach in order to compete on a down-by-down basis. If he can do all those things, he has a multi-year career as a starter ahead of him. Does he have positional versatility? Even though he only played a handful of snaps at right tackle and as an inline tight end in college, the Patriots feel strongly about Lomu’s ability to play multiple spots along the offensive line. During the spring, they used him at both tackle positions and also gave him practice reps at left guard. In addition, and despite only playing 24 total special teams snaps over the course of his Utah career (including zero in 2025), Lomu also should be able to serve as a protector on the field goal and extra point blocking units. What is his salary cap situation? Lomu and the Patriots reached an agreement on a four-year rookie contract in early June, and it comes with a $3.44 million salary cap hit in 2026. That number can be broken down into a $885,000 base salary as well as a $2.56 million signing bonus proration, both of which are fully guaranteed. How safe is his roster spot? The Patriots’ first-round pick in this year’s draft, Lomu is a lock to make the team’s roster this season. The bigger question is therefore not whether or not he will be part of the 53-man team or the active game day roster — he will be — but rather how involved he will be in the offensive operation on a week-to-week basis. Summary: Even though offensive tackle was not a major pressing need for the 2026 season, adding a potential future starter at the position early rather than…
author: Taylor Kyles

title: Contract incentives for Mike Onwenu’s new Patriots deal
summary: Earlier this offseason, the New England Patriots and starting right guard Mike Onwenu reached an agreement to revise his contract. After previously being scheduled to count $25 million against the team’s salary cap this season, the number was brought down to $17.5 million. While this $7.5 million decrease can be classified as a pay cut, […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - SEPTEMBER 14: New England Patriots offensive tackle Mike Onwenu (71) leaves the field following the game between the New England Patriots and the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, September 14, 2025 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, Fla. (Photo by Peter Joneleit/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Earlier this offseason, the New England Patriots and starting right guard Mike Onwenu reached an agreement to revise his contract. After previously being scheduled to count $25 million against the team’s salary cap this season, the number was brought down to $17.5 million. While this $7.5 million decrease can be classified as a pay cut, it happened in exchange for a more favorable guarantee structure. As part of it, Onwenu also received $2 million in contract incentives. According to a new report by ESPN’s Mike Reiss, those are structured as follows: RG Mike Onwenu: Contract incentives Maximum incentives: $2,000,000 2026: Up to $2,000,000 $1,000,000: Pro Bowl (original ballot) $1,000,000: First- or second-team All-Pro Both parts of Onwenu’s incentives, which can be earned independently from one another, are considered not likely to be earned and therefore not counted against the Patriots’ salary cap in 2026. The 28-year-old, after all, was neither voted to the Pro Bowl nor a first or second All-Pro team last season. In fact, he has not received recognition at any point in his six-year career in the NFL so far. Should he break this drought and make the Pro Bowl and/or an All-Pro team this coming season, the appropriate amount of $1 million or $2 million would then be counted against New England’s 2027 salary cap. Onwenu is now part of a group of four Patriots with both Pro Bowl and All-Pro incentives in their respective contracts. The others are running back Rhamondre Stevenson, defensive tackle Christian Barmore and special teamer Brenden Schooler. Guard Alijah Vera-Tucker and cornerback Marcus Jones have Pro Bowl incentives only in their respective pacts.

title: Patriots training camp preview 2026: O-line seeks further improvement
summary: Even though the New England Patriots’ offensive line made drastic improvements in 2025 from changes under Mike Vrabel’s first year as head coach, the unit had its drawbacks en route to a Super Bowl appearance Against the Seattle Seahawks, New England’s offensive front struggled to prevent its opponent’s four-man pass rush from reaching quarterback Drake […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JANUARY 11: Jared Wilson #58 of the New England Patriots and Will Campbell #66 of the New England Patriots set up during an AFC Wildcard game between the New England Patriots and the Los Angeles Chargers on January 11, 2025, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Even though the New England Patriots’ offensive line made drastic improvements in 2025 from changes under Mike Vrabel’s first year as head coach, the unit had its drawbacks en route to a Super Bowl appearance Against the Seattle Seahawks, New England’s offensive front struggled to prevent its opponent’s four-man pass rush from reaching quarterback Drake Maye. So, the franchise invested even more resources into the position this offseason. In the next edition of our Patriots training camp preview series, we’ll take a look at New England’s offensive line corps in its entirety and discuss the biggest takeaways heading into the summer practices. Veterans will report to the facility on July 24. *Denotes player on the Pats Pulpit 53-man roster projection Depth chart Starters: LT Will Campbell (22)* , LG Alijah Vera-Tucker (27)*, C Jared Wilson (23)* , RG Mike Onwenu (28)* , RT Morgan Moses (35)* | Backup OTs: Caleb Lomu (21/R)*, Marcus Bryant (24)* , Dametrious Crownover (24/R)* , James Hudson III (27) , Sebastian Gutierrez (27) , Lorenz Metz (29) | Backup IOL: Ben Brown (28)*, Andrew Rupcich (27) , Caedan Wallace (26) , Mehki Butler (25) , Jacob Rizy (24/R) , JonDarius Morgan (23/R) Alijah Vera-Tucker was the lone addition to the starting unit. The former New York Jet slots in at left guard, sliding 2025 third-round pick Jared Wilson back to center after the Garrett Bradbury trade to the Chicago Bears . Wilson played center in college at Georgia. Lining up to the left of Vera-Tucker is Will Campbell, who is also entering his second season in the NFL. And flipping over to the right side of the formation, the veteran tandem of Mike Onwenu and Morgan Moses will look to provide a steady presence once again. Evidently, the Patriots also wanted to improve the depth at tackle, drafting Caleb Lomu in the first round and Dametrious Crownover in the sixth. Lomu spent the spring practicing as the team’s swing tackle and took reps at both guard and tackle spots. Both the Utah product and Crownover are joined by 6-foot-7, 320-pound Marcus Bryant as the leading candidates to earn backup jobs. James Hudson III, who was signed to a one-year deal after one season with the New York Giants, projects as the next man up. On the interior, Ben Brown, who was signed to a two-year contract extension near the end of the 2025 regular season, continues to be the primary center and guard substitute. Former Tennessee Titans guard Andrew Rupcich and 2024 third-round pick under Jerod Mayo, Caedan Wallace, were the two second-team guards during the spring sessions. Rupcich even repped as the starting left guard during OTAs while Vera-Tucker rehabbed from a season-ending torn triceps. Filling out the rest of the depth chart between both tackle and guard are journeyman Sebastian Gutierrez, international tackle Lorenz Metz, 2025 undrafted free agent Mehki Butler and current UDFAs Jacob Rizy and JonDarius Morgan. The coaching staff will eye this group throughout training camp in search of practice squad and mid-season elevation candidates. Key question: How much will the 2025 rookies progress for 2026? Revisiting last season, Campbell received heavy criticism among NFL media and on social media for his postseason struggles after returning from an MCL tear in his knee. The 22-year-old allowed 29 pressures — a 26.4% pressure rate — in the Super Bowl. But before the injury, Campbell was a largely stable presence on Maye’s blind side, logging a 76.1 pass-blocking grade on Pro Football Focus. He said earlier this offseason that he underwent an aggressive physical therapy routine, rehabbing five days a week. As for Wilson, he struggled with snapping to Maye during the summer, and with Bradbury already at center, Vrabel and Co. decided to transition Wilson to left guard, where he won the starting job. Wilson was decent in pass protection and very disciplined as a rookie, only recording three penalties. However, he faced issues moving defensive linemen in the run game, totaling a lackluster 42.8 run-blocking grade (PFF). Nonetheless, his 6-foot-3, 310-pound frame is considered undersized for a left guard, so switching back to center — where his agility and quick feet are better suited — will be a more natural fit for Wilson. Furthermore, his long-term health over the course of 2026 is important to monitor; two ankle sprains and a concussion sidelined Wilson for four contests last season. The potential upside of the offensive line heavily relies on how far those two progress. New England will get a clearer picture of each lineman’s health and state of development when the pads come on in training camp. X-Factor: Alijah Vera-Tucker Partly because of Wilson’s struggles in the run game, the Patriots needed a bigger body with prominent play strength at left guard, and that’s exactly what Alijah Vera-Tucker provides with his power and size (6-foot-4, 308 pounds). Greater push and movement at the point of attack could exceptionally uplift a rushing game that ranked No. 17 in the league with a -0.03 under expected rushing EPA. Vera-Tucker also significantly upgrades the line’s pass protection, with his veteran presence and size alongside Will Campbell supplying more stability on the left side. The pairing of Campbell and Wilson continuously found difficulty picking up stunts and other more complex pass-rush concepts in 2025. The question with Vera-Tucker is whether he can remain healthy next season after suffering three season-ending injuries (two triceps tears and a torn Achilles) throughout his five-year career. If he can, he’ll be an “x-factor” for the offensive line and New England’s ground attack.

summary: Last week, it was announced that the New Orleans Saints and running back Alvin Kamara came to an agreement on a restructured contract which ensures that the 30-year-old will indeed play this season and likely finish his NFL career in the black and gold. However, the Saints also signed former running back Travis Etienne during […]
full_text: Nov 10, 2024; New Orleans, Louisiana, USA; New Orleans Saints running back Alvin Kamara (41) is announced to the fans against the Atlanta Falcons during the first half at Caesars Superdome. Mandatory Credit: Stephen Lew-Imagn Images | Stephen Lew-Imagn Images Last week, it was announced that the New Orleans Saints and running back Alvin Kamara came to an agreement on a restructured contract which ensures that the 30-year-old will indeed play this season and likely finish his NFL career in the black and gold. However, the Saints also signed former running back Travis Etienne during free agency in the offseason. Etienne is expected to do the heavy lifting and take over the starting role but it’s one that Kamara will not walk away from easily. Kamara’s former teammate Terron Armstead revealed on his podcast, “The Set”, that the star running back is “hungry and pissed off,” due his lack of production the past few seasons. So even with Etienne stepping up and getting the bulk of the touches, this will help to keep an aggressive Kamara to stay fresh and make a loud statement with his opportunities on the field. title: What is Kool-Aid McKinstry’s ceiling?
summary: There’s been much to love when it comes to Kool-Aid McKinstry. The Saints’ 2024 second-round pick out of Alabama has already proven to possess elite athleticism, durability, and instincts at the cornerback position. In 17 games last season, McKinstry grabbed three interceptions, had a team-best 17 pass breakups, and managed 76 total tackles in a […]
full_text: Dec 21, 2025; New Orleans, Louisiana, USA; New Orleans Saints cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry (4) smiles as he leaves the field after a game against the New York Jets at Caesars Superdome. Mandatory Credit: Matthew Hinton-Imagn Images | Matthew Hinton-Imagn Images There’s been much to love when it comes to Kool-Aid McKinstry. The Saints’ 2024 second-round pick out of Alabama has already proven to possess elite athleticism, durability, and instincts at the cornerback position. In 17 games last season, McKinstry grabbed three interceptions, had a team-best 17 pass breakups, and managed 76 total tackles in a campaign that saw him make strides in his second year in the league. McKinstry’s aggressive play did leave him susceptible at times to big plays, with opposing quarterbacks punishing him for eight touchdowns. But entering another season with Brandon Staley as defensive coordinator, the former Tide corner looks poised to continue his ascension toward being among the best leaguewide at his position. McKinstry has undeniable talent and shows flashes of brilliance; tidying up the parts of his game that sometimes leave him exposed will only help him become the lockdown corner the Saints drafted him to be. #Saints CB Kool-Aid McKinstry on improving over the offseason: "Never get too satisfied with where I'm at because I feel like I've still got a ceiling to reach … The ceiling is there, my job is to keep my head down till I'm there." pic.twitter.com/MdFWXpUhMl — NOF (@nofnetwork) June 10, 2026 With Alontae Taylor leaving for Tennessee in free agency, the role is McKinstry’s for the taking. What do you expect out of Kool-Aid McKinstry in year three? Can he become a game-changer for Staley’s defense? Give us your thoughts below!
author: Sam Mackenzie

title: Saints can’t afford to wait on Chris Olave’s contract extension
summary: The New Orleans Saints have watched the wide receiver market become significantly more expensive, which makes locking up All-Pro Chris Olave to a long-term extension an absolute must before his price climbs even higher. Over the past year, a number of young star receivers from the 2022 NFL Draft class have reset negotiations across the […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - JUNE 17: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints takes part in drills during mandatory mini camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on June 17, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints have watched the wide receiver market become significantly more expensive, which makes locking up All-Pro Chris Olave to a long-term extension an absolute must before his price climbs even higher. Over the past year, a number of young star receivers from the 2022 NFL Draft class have reset negotiations across the league. In 2025, Garrett Wilson landed a four-year, $130 million deal with the New York Jets and Jameson Williams agreed to a three-year extension worth up to $83 million with the Detroit Lions. While Drake London and the Atlanta Falcons agreed to a four-year, $141 million extension and Christian Watson signed a four-year, $92 million extension with the Green Bay Packers within recent months. Every one of those deals has continued pushing the receiver market upward. For the Saints, the timing couldn’t be more important. New Orleans has already invested heavily in building around its Tyler Shough, and Olave has consistently proven he deserves to be part of the franchise’s long-term future even before Shough arrived. Locking him up long-term as Kellen Moore’s new look offense continues to take shape should be at the top of the Saints’ to-do list. If they wait until after another potential breakout season, Chris Olave’s next contract may look even more expensive than it could today.

full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about today. The Giants’ knucklehead circus is the NFL’s most fascinating powderkeg | SB Nation As much as there is to love, there are two intentionally absent names who are the most critical elements of a successful campaign in 2026: Jaxson Dart and Cam Skattebo, the frat-boy wild cards capable of either ushering in a new era of success in East Rutherford or tanking everything through their own foolishness. It’s unclear how much their penchant for stupidity is real or played up for the camera, but they are exceedingly good at raising eyebrows. To mesh that approach to football with two guys running on vibes is a powder keg. It’s not just simply that they’re willing to hurt themselves, but this loose approach to football is very difficult to manage. Once freedom and personality run supreme, it can be very difficult to pull that all in, and let it fester too long as a team can pull itself apart as everyone is looking out for No. 1 over everything else. John Harbaugh impressed by Jaxson Dart John Harbaugh on if he’s been surprised about anything after getting to work with #Giants QB Jaxson Dart: “I don’t know about surprised, probably just impressed more than anything. I do think he’s obsessed. I believe he really really wants to be good.” (Via Bleav in Giants) pic.twitter.com/WkNrg5ipdG — The Giants Report (@GiantsReport1) July 21, 2026 Giants leaders aren’t just telling Jaxson Dart to run more carefully. They’re showing him | Yahoo Sports So as new Giants staffers settled in, Nagy queued up clips to remind Dart that visits to the blue tent — in the preseason, in his first start and repeatedly through the season — compromise his availability. The goal is not to eliminate Dart’s confidence and swagger. But the Giants are working to hone their young quarterback’s risk-reward calculus. “You can’t just say, ‘Don’t run the football here, because you could get hurt’ — you have to show him the evidence,” said Nagy. ” ‘Where did you take the extra hits? Was it necessary?’ You have to show them clips.” Previewing the top storylines for 2026 NFL training camps | ESPN.com Five injuries to monitor. Malik Nabers, WR, New York Giants. No injury has made more offseason headlines than Nabers’. The Giants’ star receiver tore his right ACL in Week 4 of the 2025 season and underwent surgery to repair the ligament, as well as the damage to his meniscus, a month later. But this past spring, Nabers had to undergo a second procedure on the same knee — a sign that his recovery was likely not going well. Nabers was a highly impactful rookie: 109 catches on 170 targets for 1,204 yards in only 15 games. His evident ascent to the Giants’ No. 1 receiver role was a contributing factor in the team’s willingness to let Wan’Dale Robinson leave in free agency after a strong 2025 season. For depth, the Giants have added tons of veteran dart throws — Calvin Austin III, Darnell Mooney, JuJu Smith-Schuster, Braxton Berrios and even Odell Beckham Jr. — in the hope that someone will be able to fill Robinson’s snaps. If Nabers has to miss regular-season time, the Giants’ receiving core might be one of the oldest and least effective in the league. Assistant coaches who could break out in 2026 for all 32 NFL teams | The Athletic New York Giants: Charlie Bullen, outside linebackers/run game coordinator. John Harbaugh has always had an eye for coaching talent, and it speaks well of Bullen’s potential that he was retained from the previous coaching regime and even got an expanded role as run game coordinator. His position group already featured Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux; the team also drafted versatile defender Arvell Reese in the spring. Bullen will have every opportunity to show his impact on the defense. I really think they can go to the playoffs" @AdamSchefter #PMSLive pic.twitter.com/qrg2e3YG5h — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) July 21, 2026 Giants to play most turf games in NFL in 2026, fueling grass debate | USAToday.com The Giants are set to play 15 games on artificial turf fields next season. The Tennessee Titans are the only other team that will play as many games on turf. The Dallas Cowboys, Minnesota Vikings, and New Orleans Saints will play the second-most games on turf, with 13 each. title: John Harbaugh’s reaction to Cam Skattebo’s failed backflip? ‘Dude, at least stick it’
summary: Did New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh go ballistic when he saw the video of running back Cam Skattebo, coming back from a dislocated ankle, fall while attempting a backflip over the weekend? Not exactly. “My reaction was, dude, at least stick it,” Harbaugh said while appearing on the ‘Bleav in Giants’ podcast with […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo | Getty Images for Fanatics Did New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh go ballistic when he saw the video of running back Cam Skattebo , coming back from a dislocated ankle, fall while attempting a backflip over the weekend? Not exactly. “My reaction was, dude, at least stick it,” Harbaugh said while appearing on the ‘Bleav in Giants’ podcast with Bob Papa and Carl Banks. “Land the thing if you’re gonna do it.” Harbaugh added that “Skat’s gonna be ready to go” training camp. He said he had not spoken to the second-year running back about the incident. “He’s been working super-hard. He’s really been training like crazy, and his mind is on camp,” Harbaugh said. “He’s healthy. He’s ready to roll, and I can’t wait to see him out there at practice.” Skattebo reacted to the furor over his flop by saying “I will not hurt myself before the season.” Skattebo was a fourth-round pick by the Giants in 2025. He averaged 4.1 yards per carry in eight games before being injured. The Giants are anticipating he and Tyrone Tracy will form a solid combination at running back.

title: NY Giants training camp: Will UDFA Ben Mann really be the long-snapper?
summary: Rather than stay for a seventh season with the New York Giants, veteran long-snapper Casey Kreiter signed with the Arizona Cardinals in free agency. He joined former Giants special teams coach Michael Ghobrial there. The Giants brought in two potential replacements. They signed 35-year-old journeyman snapper Zach Triner, who snapped in just four NFL games […]
full_text: Ben Mann with Boston College last season. | Eric Canha-Imagn Images Rather than stay for a seventh season with the New York Giants, veteran long-snapper Casey Kreiter signed with the Arizona Cardinals in free agency. He joined former Giants special teams coach Michael Ghobrial there. The Giants brought in two potential replacements. They signed 35-year-old journeyman snapper Zach Triner , who snapped in just four NFL games over the past two seasons. They also signed undrafted free agent Ben Mann , giving the Boston College long-snapper $10,000 in guaranteed money. The Giants waived Triner on June 1, leaving the 24-year-old Mann as the team’s only long-snapper. They have not added anyone else to compete with Mann. Does that mean Mann will be the snapper for the Giants when the season begins? It sure looks that way. Mann was solid all spring. There were no noticeably bad, or wobbly, snaps. As Chris noted in an earlier profile, the 6-foot-4, 235-pounder is an elite athlete for the long-snapper position . That should translate into having an opportunity to be helpful on punt coverage. Mann spent three seasons at Yale before finishing his college career at Boston College. He is the grandson of Super Bowl champion Chuck Mercein, who played for the Green Bay Packers in the “Ice Bowl.” Have head coach John Harbaugh and special teams coordinator Chris Horton already seen enough from Mann to be comfortable going into the season with him in the critical long-snapping role? We will find out over the next few weeks.
