title: Eagles Rookie Review: Andrew Mukuba is a very important defender entering Year 2
summary: One of my favorite things to do every offseason is to go back and compare my post-draft notes on the Eagles’ rookies with how they actually looked when they got on the field. It’s a fun blend of film study, self-evaluation, and a check on how well certain traits really translate to the NFL. I […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 19: Andrew Mukuba #24 of the Philadelphia Eagles points to fans after an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 19, 2025 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of my favorite things to do every offseason is to go back and compare my post-draft notes on the Eagles’ rookies with how they actually looked when they got on the field. It’s a fun blend of film study, self-evaluation, and a check on how well certain traits really translate to the NFL. I won’t be writing full scouting reports here, as I did that after the draft. This series is more about reviewing last year’s film in comparison to my pre-draft thoughts. Did the player perform as expected? Did anything surprise me? And what do I think comes next? At the end of each article, I’ll give my updated outlook for that player in the future. Previously: Jihaad Campbell Andrew Mukuba Before the draft, I had Andrew Mukuba as my fifth-ranked safety, so I wasn’t as high on him as some. I did think there were better safety prospects, but I still gave Mukuba a second-round grade and thought Pick 64 was about the right range for him. The more I watched him after the draft, the more I liked him. My overall summary before the draft was this: “At worst, Mukuba should be a passing game specialist due to his outstanding ball skills and instincts. He’s a really good football player. He might struggle to be a full-time player due to his size, but he will have a role in the NFL due to his instincts.” I also wrote this after watching even more of his film: “The simple truth is that I do not know if he can play the way he currently does at his size. It’s not simply a case of being undersized. He has small arms too and doesn’t wrap up when he tackles. He hits hard and dominates at the point of attack. The highlight reel hits are great, and I would love to say he can play this way at the next level, but I do not know if he can.” I wasn’t worried about Mukuba because I thought he lacked talent. Quite the opposite. I thought he had some of the best football instincts in the class. 11) The biggest play of the game. The Eagles get a little lucky with the drop, but Mukuba deserves credit for making the mistake count. The Eagles lost a playmaker this offseason in CJGJ, but I think they have a new one in Mukuba. Mukuba is learning and still isn't perfect, but… pic.twitter.com/eXzzNSaWOy — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 16, 2025 My concern was that his physical limitations might eventually stop those instincts from consistently showing up against NFL athletes, and keep him off the field. Which, did eventually happen. One thing I felt strongly about before the season was his fit within Fangio’s defense. I wrote: “He is going to be fantastic as a split-safety in this defense. His recognition of route concepts is outstanding. He already knows how to play many of Fangio’s coverages, and he has an instinctive nature of spacing and where the football is going, which is almost impossible to teach.” Mukuba consistently looked one step ahead of quarterbacks in college. He understood route combinations, recognized concepts developing in front of him, and played with an anticipation that isn’t common coming out of college. As early as week one, look at how fluid he executes a roll turn to cover CeeDee Lamb. Phew. 5) I'll get to Baun more later, but I thought him and Cooper DeJean were fantastic in coverage. Look how fluidly DeJean moves here. Everything he does is effortless. He's such a top athlete. He gets good depth and gets to the flat so quickly that it results in no gain. I had to… pic.twitter.com/CAHuRMUMGC — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 6, 2025 That’s why I expected him to become a useful player immediately, but… “He must change how he plays. I expect him to come downhill quickly in the run game, but he will have to learn to wrap up better and stop flying into offensive players as he did in college. He might need to become a bit more passive in the run game… I can’t see him hitting elite running backs in space like he did in college.” I still feel very much the same about Mukuba after one year. Things I Expected The easiest projection with Andrew Mukuba was never his athleticism. It was his football intelligence. His route recognition, understanding of spacing, and anticipation consistently stood out on film, and those traits were always going to translate. One of the most encouraging parts of Mukuba’s rookie season was how naturally he looked playing from depth. Fangio entrusted him with a proper starting safety role rather than asking him to start out as a role player. The coaching staff clearly believed he could handle the mental demands of playing safety, and I think the film justified that confidence. There were several examples in which he peeled off one receiver to help elsewhere, recognized developing concepts before the quarterback released the football, and simply looked like someone who understood the defense rather than someone who was lost. He wasn’t like this all season. He absolutely improved as the season went on, which is exactly what you want to see from a rookie. He did have some bad moments at the start, but it’s not easy starting in this defense as a rookie. I expected Mukuba to become the Eagles’ starting safety. I think he will become the Eagles’ starting safety and beat out Sydney Brown. I think he will be significantly better in coverage than Brown.” Fangio didn’t ease him into the lineup or protect him with a limited role. He trusted him very early on. As early as week 4, he was playing 100% of the defensive snaps. As early as week 1, he was being used in multiple positions, highlighting his versatility. 10) Drop 8 Tampa-2 from big nickel personnel? Is Fangio going to get funky this year?! Sadly, Mukuba doesn't do as well as Baun/Campbell did and he lets the TE get open. Blankenship does a good job making this a tough catch and although I understand why it's a penalty, I have no… pic.twitter.com/MHxAiBq3bf — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 6, 2025 Another thing that translated immediately was his competitiveness. One concern that’s often raised about lighter defensive backs is whether they’ll shy away from contact against NFL athletes. Mukuba did the opposite. He triggered downhill aggressively throughout the season and never looked reluctant to throw his body into the run game. 8) What an awesome play by Andrew Mukuba. This is the benefit of having a safety with some corner experience! The Eagles often pass off crossing routes, but they don't here, so Mukuba has to fight through traffic and makes the tackle for no gain. This is awesome. There's so much… pic.twitter.com/NFZH1lqnTo — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 16, 2025 Ironically, that willingness is also where one of my biggest pre-draft concerns still exists. Before the draft, I wrote: “He must change how he plays. I expect him to come downhill quickly in the run game, but he will have to learn to wrap up better and stop flying into offensive players as he did in college. He might need to become a bit more passive in the run game… I can’t see him hitting elite running backs in space like he did in college.” After watching his rookie film, I still worry about the way he plays. The missed-tackle numbers themselves aren’t bad, but the film worries me more than the statistics. Mukuba still relies on explosion and timing more than consistently wrapping through tackles, and although that aggressive style produced plenty of big plays in college, I’m not convinced it’s sustainable against NFL athletes over a seventeen-game season. He had some bad moments last year, when he didn’t wrap up. Andrew Makuba with one of the worst reps you’ll ever see: 1) Trips DeJean 2) Completely blows his assignment 3) Late recovery 4) Takes a poor angle 5) Terrible tackle attempt 6) Touchdown Giants pic.twitter.com/0apKWINd6g — Eagles Eric…

With the former first-rounder installed in a premium position in Fangio’s D, Campbell could quickly emerge as a star in his second season. The 2026 Eagles are taking “connection” seriously – BGN “Tough. Detailed. Together.” Since Nick Sirianni was hired as the head coach of the Philadelphia Eagles in 2021, he has doubled down on his core values for the team, with connection being one of the most prominent staples. He’s prioritized this in many ways over the years, but heading in the 2026 season, we’re seeing more of the relationship building that’s happening behind the scenes and ahead of training camp. Not that these opportunities to connect as teammates and friends haven’t existed in the past, but there has seemingly been more cameras around to capture it this year. Whatever your opinion on football players posting their workouts, during a long offseason, it at least gives fans a little hope that the team is focused and building a solid foundation in their time away from the building. If nothing else, the 2026 Eagles roster should be as close as ever as they embark on (another) season with high expectations. NFL fans predict the NFC division winners – SB Nation Eagles overwhelming NFC East favorites. We started our tour of the NFC in the East, where the Philadelphia Eagles were tapped as overwhelming favorites to win the division. Of those who responded, 67% picked Philadelphia to win the division, followed by the Dallas Cowboys with 15%, and the New York Giants with 13%. Washington rounded out the results with 5%. You can see the results, and the full discussion that followed, here. Why Nick Sirianni isn’t concerned handing the keys to inexperienced OC – NBCSP Sirianni likes that story so much because it shows just how hard of a worker Mannion is; how bad he wants it. Sirianni also said that during the spring, there wasn’t a day he beat Mannion to the Jefferson Health Training Complex and there wasn’t a day where Mannion’s car wasn’t still in the parking lot when he left. That work ethic at least partially explains why the Eagles feel like Mannion is ready to be an offensive coordinator in just his third season as a coach at any level. “This dude loves football and he loves to work,” Sirianni said. “I mean I’ve really enjoyed being around him and just his desire. Sometimes we think ‘man he’s talented’ about everybody, ‘man he’s just got it.’ But it doesn’t happen without, whether it’s a player, whether it’s Sean, it doesn’t happen without just this obsession to get better. Assistant coaches who could break out in 2026 for all 32 NFL teams – The Athletic Philadelphia Eagles: Joe Kasper, defensive pass game coordinator. If a young assistant coach can stick around — and even thrive — under top defensive mind Vic Fangio, he is often destined for bigger things. Kasper has worked for Fangio in both Miami and Philadelphia, and is poised for a bigger role now that former colleague Christian Parker (another Fangio disciple) is in Dallas. Nguyen, our senior writer, noted that the “two-high trend will continue to grow and it seems like coaches that can successfully implement some of Fangio’s ideas into their systems take it to another level.” High expectations also surround first-year offensive coordinator Sean Mannion, who is expected to bring elements of Matt LaFleur’s Green Bay/Shanahan-derived system to Philadelphia. 2026 Philadelphia Eagles Fantasy Preview: Can Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley bounce back? – NBC Sports 2026 Philadelphia Eagles Win Total. DraftKings Over/Under: 10.5. Pick: Under (-140). In my heart, I want to pick the over, but -140 for the under is a better price than you can find at most books. It’s easy to see why books think the Eagles aren’t likely to hit 11 wins. They lost several starters in free agency and drafted for the future. Makai Lemon isn’t going to fully replace A.J. Brown as a rookie and none of their subsequent picks are projected to start in 2026. Howie Roseman sacrificed some short-term win probability to build a better team in the long run, and that is enough to convince me to take the value on the under. Eagles 2026 Training Camp Position Preview: Special Teams – PhiladelphiaEagles.com Kicker Jake Elliott enters his 10th season of his storied career with the Eagles. The Illinois native is second all-time in career points for the Eagles (1,007), only behind David Akers (1,323). Elliott owns the record for most 50+ yard field goals (33) in team history. In Super Bowl LIX, he broke the record for most points in a Super Bowl by a kicker with 15, passing 1968 Don Chandler. The 2023 second-team All-Pro ended 2025 with 100% accuracy on field goals on the 39-yard line or closer. On extra points, Elliott had a 97.6% success rate in 2025. The Memphis product did something he had never done in his career in 2025 – record a special teams tackle. [BLG Note: I get that the team’s official website isn’t going to be super critical of Elliott but to not even make the slightest mention of his struggles the past two seasons is kinda wild.] After Asking Steelers For New Home, Kenny Pickett ‘Begged’ Eagles To Trade Him, Says His College Coach – Steelers Depot “The Eagles did not want to trade him,” Narduzzi said recently on 99.9 The Fan’s YouTube channel. “He begged to be traded because he wanted to compete and he felt like he wasn’t going to have a chance to beat out Jalen Hurts. I think there’s some misconceptions about, ‘They just got rid of him.’ No. They wanted him to stay, and they said, ‘We’re not trading you.’ And he begged, and they said, ‘If it’s good for us, we’ll trade you. But if it’s not good for us, we’re not making that move.’” Decoding Jonathan Gannon’s Eagles Defense: What the Coverage Data Reveals – Acme Packing Company Taken together, the data supports a more nuanced read of Gannon than either side of the public debate about him usually allows. He wasn’t simply “too passive,” as some critics argued throughout 2022 — the third-down man-coverage rates and the spikes in blitz aggression in specific weeks show a coordinator capable of asking his defense to take risks when the situation called for it. But he also wasn’t a chess master constantly innovating new wrinkles — the season-long drift toward zone and away from blitzing suggests a defense settling into its most repeatable, lowest-variance version of itself as the year went on, trusting disciplined execution of a smaller menu of calls over an expanding one. How much Cowboys failure belongs to Dak Prescott – Blogging The Boys But he has. That’s because there is another option that remains, and that is for Prescott to be the thing that is elevated. That is not a crazy expectation. Dak is compensated heavily, and it is totally fair to expect a player who commands that type of team resources to make a bigger impact. He has to, at some point, be the guy who punishes aggressive defensive attacks instead of falling victim to them. When the clock is running down, he has to make that throw. He has to be that guy. While Prescott is by no means the problem in Dallas, he has not been the…

title: Steelers WR Roman Wilson listed as player with most on the line in 2026
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers selected wide receiver Roman Wilson out of Michigan in the third round, 84th overall, in the 2024 NFL Draft. Despite this relatively significant investment, the wideout’s career has yet to really get off the ground. Wilson suffered ankle and hamstring injuries that derailed his entire rookie campaign, but still came into 2025 […]
full_text: The Pittsburgh Steelers selected wide receiver Roman Wilson out of Michigan in the third round, 84th overall, in the 2024 NFL Draft. Despite this relatively significant investment, the wideout’s career has yet to really get off the ground. Wilson suffered ankle and hamstring injuries that derailed his entire rookie campaign, but still came into 2025 with optimism that his development was headed in the right direction. After a strong training camp and preseason, Wilson still struggled to find consistent playing time and only recorded 12 catches in his second season. Now entering his third year, this could be Wilson’s last chance to prove himself to the organization that drafted him that he is a starting-caliber NFL wide receiver. The Athletic listed of players — one from each NFL team — with the most on the line in 2026 . Steelers beat writer Mike DeFabo chose Wilson to represent Pittsburgh. “The Steelers had hoped Roman Wilson would take a leap in Year 2 to be part of the answer at WR2. However, his connection with Aaron Rodgers was inconsistent, and by the end of 2025, the former Michigan receiver slid down the depth chart, leapfrogged by late-season additions Marquez Valdes-Scantling and Adam Thielen. Wilson ended 2025 as a healthy scratch in four of the final five games,” Mike DeFabo wrote. “He’s been working hard this offseason to fine-tune his route running and enters a pivotal third season with a prime opportunity. As the Steelers transition from Arthur Smith’s tight end-centric offense to Mike McCarthy’s scheme, the usage of 11 personnel will skyrocket and could turn the WR3 into a starter rather than a rotational piece.” Roman Wilson seems hungry this year. Can’t wait to watch him in a Mike McCarthy offense. pic.twitter.com/PcNd2YROpj — Baku 🐧 (@Mazursky8895) July 20, 2026 DeFabo is absolutely right in his assessment that McCarthy’s offensive system, which tends to feature more receivers, will undoubtedly give Wilson his best opportunity to shine. However, it won’t be an easy road for Wilson to become established in that offense. Pittsburgh made a point to aggressively upgrade their wide receiver room this offseason with the additions of Michael Pittman Jr. and Germie Bernard. Wilson could very well enter training camp as the third wide receiver ahead of Bernard, but holding onto that spot will be a challenge. Earning the trust of an entirely new coaching staff and continuing to develop a more consistent connection with Aaron Rodgers will all be things on Wilson’s plate throughout training camp. 2026 will undoubtedly be the most important of the former Michigan wide receiver’s career. full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Nick Emmanwori #3 of the Seattle Seahawks celebrates after defeating the New England Patriots in the Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s nothing like a training camp jump scare in which a star player is placed on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list. Such was the case for Seattle Seahawks defensive back Nick Emmanwori, who was one of three players put on PUP on Monday . Emmanwori participated throughout minicamp and OTAs, so this undisclosed injury has seemingly come out of nowhere. NFL Network reporter Steve Wyche was on Seattle Sports 710 radio with Michael Bumpus and Stacy Jo Rost on Tuesday, and for any Seahawks fans freaking out over a possible prolonged absence for the second-year player, perhaps this will calm your collective nerves. “I have been told by someone there it’s not something that they’re overly concerned with,” Wyche said. “So I don’t think this is something that’s surgical that’s going to require something that’s going to keep him out for a while.” "I have been told it's not something they are overly concerned with…I don't think it's something that's going to keep him out for a while." NFL Network's Steve Wyche shares what he knows about Nick Emmanwori starting #Seahawks training camp on the PUP list on with… pic.twitter.com/CRoSIFT3xJ — Seattle Sports (@SeattleSports) July 21, 2026 Unlike regular season PUP, which requires a player miss at least the first four games of the year, training camp PUP is easy to come off of. As long as Emmanwori can pass a physical then he can be activated at any time (and, for that matter, the same applies for Tyrone Broden and Kenny McIntosh). We’ve been here before with Emmanwori injury scares. While he missed actual regular season time during his rookie season, the Super Bowl practice scare was quickly eased by Mike Macdonald and Emmanwori himself. If by any chance Emmanwori isn’t on the practice field for Saturday’s opening training camp session, Coach Macdonald will presumably provide some sort of update in his media availability.

summary: The Seattle Seahawks are nearing their first training camp practice of 2026, which means we should expect plenty of roster tinkering over the next several weeks. After bringing in four players for tryouts this week, the Seahawks have turned one tryout into a signing. Former Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Brandon Johnson has been added to the […]
full_text: MADISON, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 16: Defensive back Brandon Johnson (3) of the Oregon Ducks walks in action during a game between the Wisconsin Badgers and the Oregon Ducks at Camp Randall Stadium on November 16, 2024 in Madison, Wisconsin. (Photo by Robin Alam/ISI Photos/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks are nearing their first training camp practice of 2026, which means we should expect plenty of roster tinkering over the next several weeks. After bringing in four players for tryouts this week, the Seahawks have turned one tryout into a signing. Former Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Brandon Johnson has been added to the 90-man roster, while veteran tight end and former John Mackey Award winner Harrison Bryant has been waived. Johnson began his college career at Duke, where he played three seasons and had a couple of All-ACC honorable mentions, before transferring to the Oregon Ducks in 2024. He started eight games and recorded 45 total tackles, 4.5 tackles for loss, and an interception for the eventual Big Ten champions. As a nickel DB, Johnson had a penchant for downhill play, having recorded 5.5 sacks for Duke in the 2022 season. Johnson joined the Philadelphia Eagles as an undrafted free agent last season, appearing in three games as a practice squad elevation. In his limited NFL playing time, he recorded a pass defensed and a solo tackle over 37 snaps (28 defense, 9 special teams). With Nick Emmanwori on the mend with what is seemingly a non-serious injury , this may be an instance of just adding a camp body while Emmanwori recovers and gears up for practice. Otherwise, add Johnson to the list of CBs hoping to stake his claim for either a 53-man or practice squad roster spot.

title: Who are the most intriguing Seahawks players entering training camp?
summary: The wait is nearly over. Seattle Seahawks rookies have reported, veterans are preparing to join them, and Seattle’s 2026 training camp is set to begin. With football returning, so are the questions that could shape the upcoming season. On the latest episode of The Hawks Eye Podcast, I count down my Top 20 Most Intriguing […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 8: Rashid Shaheed #22 of the Seattle Seahawks prepares to receive the punt during the first quarter of the NFL Super Bowl LX football game against the New England Patriots at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The wait is nearly over. Seattle Seahawks rookies have reported, veterans are preparing to join them, and Seattle’s 2026 training camp is set to begin. With football returning, so are the questions that could shape the upcoming season. On the latest episode of The Hawks Eye Podcast, I count down my Top 20 Most Intriguing Seahawks entering training camp. This is not simply a ranking of the best players on Seattle’s roster; being one of the team’s most talented or established players does not automatically make someone one of the most interesting names to follow this summer. Instead, my list focuses on uncertainty, opportunity, development, and overall importance to Seattle’s season. There is second-year quarterback Jalen Milroe, who’s entering a critical stage of his development after barely playing last season, with every training camp rep potentially influencing how Seattle views its future at the position. There’s also a veteran, now two-time Super Bowl champion pass-catcher whose experience is unquestioned, but whose exact role within the offense remains one of the more fascinating questions heading into camp. On defense, I examine second-year d-lineman Rylie Mills, now fully healthy but facing increased expectations after showing signs that he could become a much larger part of Seattle’s front. The rookie class provides another layer of intrigue. Jadarian Price could have an immediate opportunity to earn meaningful touches, while second-round pick Bud Clark will enter a crowded secondary with a chance to carve out a role through his safety/corner versatility and special teams. Those are only a few of the storylines covered during the countdown. Training camp has a way of changing how we view a roster. A strong week of practice can move a young player into the rotation. An impressive preseason performance can turn a roster long shot into a legitimate contributor. A returning veteran can prove that concerns about health, age or role were overstated. Seattle is also entering camp with championship expectations on the back of a magical Lombardi Trophy winning 2025 campaign. The Seahawks are no longer trying to establish themselves as contenders, they are determining which players can help them remain among the NFL’s elite and make another Super Bowl run. title: The 20 new players on the Seahawks roster ahead of training camp
summary: The Seattle Seahawks open their training camp on Saturday. As always, a new season means having to learn a lot of new names and faces before the August preseason opener, and the roster churn will continue over the next several weeks at the bottom-end of the 90-man roster. To get you primed for training camp, […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JUNE 11: Jadarian Price #8 of the Seattle Seahawks looks on during practice at Virginia Mason Athletic Center on June 11, 2026 in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks open their training camp on Saturday. As always, a new season means having to learn a lot of new names and faces before the August preseason opener, and the roster churn will continue over the next several weeks at the bottom-end of the 90-man roster. To get you primed for training camp, we’re providing a quick look at which players are brand new to the squad and thus have no ties to the Super Bowl season. Players like D’Anthony Bell, who spent much of last season with Seattle before getting claimed off waivers by the Carolina Panthers, do not count as “new” upon return. The Seahawks draft class Jadarian Price, running back . Seattle lost Kenneth Walker III in free agency and won’t have Zach Charbonnet for an undetermined length of time after his ACL tear. The Seahawks were destined to take a running back in the draft and they went with Notre Dame’s Price in the first round. He’ll be one of the most watched players throughout the season. Bud Clark, safety . Having lost Coby Bryant in free agency, the Seahawks zeroed in on ball-hawkin’ Bud Clark from TCU. Hard to look away from 15 interceptions over four seasons when trying to find another high-level player in the secondary. Julian Neal, cornerback . With Riq Woolen out of the picture, the Seahawks’ third-rounder was used on Arkansas corner Julian Neal, who possesses the size and length befitting of many Seattle secondaries of yesteryear. Beau Stephens, offensive line . The Iowa guard was so coveted by the Seahawks that John Schneider gave up a 2027 draft pick to move back into the fifth round to take him. Anthony Bradford’s replacement? Not so fast. But he’s an intriguing prospect. Emmanuel Henderson Jr, wide receiver . Seattle’s wide receiver room is crowded already, but the sixth-round pick out of Kansas does have plenty of special teams experience that gives him a fighting chance to make the roster. Andre Fuller, cornerback . Seattle was busy adding corners in the draft, including a seventh-round flyer on Toledo’s Fuller. Just by the very nature of the Seahawks’ current CB room and being a seventh-rounder, he has an uphill battle to make the roster, but by no means should he be counted out. Deven Eastern, nose tackle . It’s an inauspicious start to Eastern’s NFL career, having been placed on PUP to start training camp after missing minicamp and OTAs with an undisclosed injury. The former Minnesota defensive tackle figured to factor into the competition to at least be rotational depth, but that’s up in the air pending any clarity on his injury. Michael Dansby, cornerback . The Seahawks’ final pick was used on another corner, the unheralded Michael Dansby out of Arizona. Treydan Stukes got all the attention among the Arizona DBs, but Dansby wasn’t a bystander on that Wildcats defense. Admittedly, it looks like his best shot to make the roster is as a special teams gunner. The undrafted Seahawks Lance Mason, tight end . Seattle is pretty stacked at tight end with AJ Barner, Elijah Arroyo, Nick Kallerup, and Eric Saubert all set for another season, but the Seahawks still added to the depth chart by signing Harrison Bryant and undrafted rookie Lance Mason. In his transfer year at Wisconsin, Mason earned All-Big Ten Second-Team honors. Uso Seumalo, defensive tackle . The Hawaii native played all of his college football in the state of Kansas, starting in community college before four seasons at K-State. At 330 pounds, Seumalo is one of those big bodies who could be a nose tackle in Mike Macdonald’s defense. Aidan Hubbard, outside linebacker . It was a bit of a surprise that Hubbard went undrafted after 13.5 sacks over his final two seasons at Northwestern, but he represents the biggest edge rushing investment the Seahawks made in the 2026 rookie class. Marvin Jones Jr, outside linebacker . The other UDFA edge option was Marvin Jones Jr, who isn’t related to the former Detroit Lions wide receiver. Jones hopped around from Georgia to Florida State to Oklahoma in his college career, and looks to be more over a “traits over production” signing. Rashad Rochelle, wide receiver . While not part of the Seahawks’ initial UDFA class, Rochelle was brought on in mid-May. His experience as a kick returner may be the selling point more than anything regarding actual wide receiver depth. The Seahawks free agent signings Emanuel Wilson, running back . As part of the makeover of the running back room, Seattle’s first move was to add the ex-Green Bay Packer on a cheap contract . He’s a steady player who won’t light up the box score, and ideally he’s a much better signing than the last ex-Packers running back Seattle picked up. Noah Igbinoghene, cornerback. The former Miami Dolphins first-round pick has bounced around a little bit as a journeyman, finding at least some footing under Dan Quinn and the Washington Commanders. He’ll be in the mix as the third cornerback behind Josh Jobe and Devon Witherspoon. Rodney Thomas II, safety . Much like Wilson was signed before Seattle drafted Price, the Seahawks added Rodney Thomas II from the Indianapolis Colts prior to drafting Bud Clark. Thomas has starting experience and has an extensive special teams background. Dante Fowler Jr, outside linebacker . Seattle skipped out on drafting an edge player in the wake of Boye Mafe’s move to the Cincinnati Bengals, so John Schneider went for the veteran option of Dante Fowler Jr, who was most recently with the Dallas Cowboys. Fowler was teammates with Igbinoghene in their 2024 run to the NFC Championship Game. Bobby Hart, offensive lineman . With Josh Jones on the mend due to a knee injury, Seattle brought in the former Cincinnati Bengals starter during mandatory minicamp as a camp body… maybe competition for Jones, too. I’d sooner believe this competition is over once Jones is on the practice field. Harrison Bryant, tight end . As noted earlier, the Seahawks are well stocked at tight end, but former John Mackey Award winner Harrison Bryant was one of the more interesting adds this offseason. He was an outstanding receiver in college but has been more of a blocking TE in the NFL. The one Seahawks trade Irv Charles, wide receiver/special teams . The only trade the Seahawks made outside of the draft was acquiring special teams standout Irv Charles from the New York Jets for a conditional 2028 pick. He’s never been targeted in the NFL let alone caught a pass, so his chance of getting onto the roster is solely through his role as a gunner.

AFP PHOTO (Photo credit should read JEFF HAYNES/AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images How a gruesome injury helped 49ers leader Fred Warner find his purpose (paywall) “ Warner is convinced his durability is a gift from the heavens. And a DEXA body composition scan taken last year helped him understand, revealing that his bones were six times denser than the average human. “Some guys have a freakish ability to run fast,” he says. “My freakish ability, I guess, is having thick bones to help me stay healthier.” ….This offseason, Warner has been working on taking advantage of one-on-one pass-rush opportunities against running backs, which he hasn’t been asked to do frequently in the past. Holland hopes that Warner will have many more chances to rush against running backs this season. Warner believes he will reach a higher level in 2026 by increasing his competitive intensity, which was already near Goku level. He speaks of becoming more of a “maniac on the field” and breaking through age’s barriers. Thirty, the way he sees it, is an opportunity. So is coming back from injury.” Rams had eyes on De’Zhaun Stribling before 49ers drafted him “What’s interesting about this selection is there was some people that wondered if it was too early for De’Zhaun Stribling to go,” Schefter said on NFL Live . “And there were a couple of teams that I spoke to in the draft process, leading up to the draft, that felt that De’Zhaun Stribling was the best wide receiver in the draft. “Another team, supposedly the Los Angeles Rams, had eyes on him. So, the 49ers didn’t just come up with this pick out of nowhere. They knew that there were other teams that had a very high grade on Stribling when the 49ers declined to trade out the top draft slot in the second round and take him there.” Steve Young reveals how 49ers can help Brock Purdy reach the next level “His game is the first couple seconds,” Young said. “Process, get some protection, have some weapons—as good as it gets. To help him thrive—and every quarterback needs lots of help to thrive—we need some people that can get open quickly,” Young said. “Brandon Aiyuk was somebody who got open on the perimeter quickly—and that’s what his game is. Get open, show up, bam, get the ball to him and go.” “So, Mike, Ricky, they need to be people that can get off the line of scrimmage quickly, get open, get the ball out,” Young added. “That’s when he’s going to be deadly.” 49ers unveil 2026 uniform schedule, including throwbacks and Rivalries look “The 49ers will wear their red throwbacks twice during the regular season—on the road against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 10 and at home against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 17. The white throwbacks will make one appearance in Week 15 against the Los Angeles Chargers, while the black Nike Rivalries uniform will debut in Week 14 against the Los Angeles Rams.” Explaining the biggest difference between the 2025 and 2026 49ers “While that’s partially true — Purdy was under pressure on 39% of his dropbacks — he had plenty of time to throw. On average, Purdy had a whopping 4.24 seconds to throw on 33 dropbacks. He only completed 55.6% of his passes because there was nobody to throw the ball to. I recently rewatched the game. And as someone who appreciates wide receiver play, it was painful. Some of the advanced stats match the eye test. Next Gen Stats has a “catch rate over expected” stat. Across the board, the wideouts were in the negatives. Ricky Pearsall’s numbers seem like they were entered in incorrectly; they were so low. When you’re relying on Jauan Jennings and Kendrick Bourne against an elite secondary, it’s a miracle that the Niners were in this situation to begin with. The wide receiver play for the 49ers will be night and day, and everybody will reap the benefits. Safeties crept closer to the line of scrimmage without fear of one of the Niners’ wideouts running past them. That same issue meant opposing defenses could shrink the field and turn their attention to George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey underneath. The lack of physicality showed up in the running game all too often. Because of that, McCaffrey had to be a magician behind the line of scrimmage. The margin for error in the running game was next to nothing because the receivers didn’t have the necessary passion as blockers. Mike Evans changes everything. He gives the 49ers a weapon on every down, and a go-to target on third down. It also means Pearsall is no longer the focal point and gets the other team’s CB2. When that was the case last season, Pearsall made mincemeat of lesser corners.”

title: Which 49er is under the most pressure in 2026?
summary: It’s becoming clear that the San Francisco 49ers will have a big opportunity to jump back into contention in 2026 after an offseason where they made a number of quality moves in free agency. After a surprise trip to the divisional round last season, the 49ers will look to top that in 2026, but they’ll […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 14: Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers lines up at the line of scrimmage during an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome on September 14, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s becoming clear that the San Francisco 49ers will have a big opportunity to jump back into contention in 2026 after an offseason where they made a number of quality moves in free agency. After a surprise trip to the divisional round last season, the 49ers will look to top that in 2026, but they’ll need several things to go their way. The team’s biggest hindrance over the past few years has been injuries, and the issue arose again in 2025, with George Kittle, Fred Warner, Nick Bosa, Brock Purdy, and others all missing multiple games last season. But the 49ers will also need younger players to step up, wide receivers to be better, and the pass rush to improve after ranking last in sacks in 2025. There are a lot of 49ers looking to take the next step or bounce back in 2026. Who is under the most pressure? The Athletic revealed the player with the most to prove for every NFL team ahead of training camp, and the 49ers’ candidate was defensive end Nick Bosa, who is coming off a torn ACL. “Bosa is coming off his third knee surgery — and the second ACL injury to the same knee — and is being asked to carry the 49ers’ pass rush while mentoring young players Mykel Williams and Romello Height,” The Athletic’s Vic Tafur wrote. “It seems like the 49ers will still add a veteran edge player to help Bosa (after Bryce Huff suddenly retired). “The return of Bosa, linebacker Fred Warner and tight end George Kittle from injuries is a big reason this team has Super Bowl aspirations. Bosa, who turns 29 in October, is also going to need a new contract after this season, as the five-year deal he signed in 2023 has a $54.9 million salary-cap hit in 2027. If Bosa can show that he is still one of the best speed-to-power rushers in the NFL, the 49ers will be in for a successful season and Bosa in for another huge payday.” While there are several 49ers returning from injury, Bosa’s return could be the most important of them all. Bosa was playing at an extremely high level in a short sample size last offseason before suffering the injury. And the 49ers clearly struggled without him, ranking last in sacks. The 49ers didn’t do much with their pass rush in the offseason, with the main addition being Texas Tech’s Romello Height in the draft. That adds more pressure on Bosa to contribute and fast.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 49ers roster preview: Why Carver Willis needs a redshirt year
summary: The San Francisco 49ers knew they needed to get younger and more athletic along the offensive line. Center Jake Brendel enters the final year of his contract, while Dominick Puni and Connor Colby were the only other players on rookie contracts heading into the NFL Draft. The Niners ended up drafting 24-year-old Carver Willis in […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - MARCH 01: Carver Willis #OL54 of Washington participates in a drill during the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine at Lucas Oil Stadium on March 1, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers knew they needed to get younger and more athletic along the offensive line. Center Jake Brendel enters the final year of his contract, while Dominick Puni and Connor Colby were the only other players on rookie contracts heading into the NFL Draft. The Niners ended up drafting 24-year-old Carver Willis in the fourth round, a tackle who they view as an interior lineman out of Washington. Carver’s 40-time was in the 78th percentile. That speed shows up when he’s on the move, whether working laterally or climbing to the second level. However, despite a 6’5″ frame, Willis is a few pounds over 300, with smaller hands than De’Zhaun Stribling and arms slightly longer than the receiver the 49ers drafted at the top of the second round. You’re not going to last on the edge with that body type in the NFL. Most of Willis’s athletic comparisons on Mockdraftable ended up playing center. The more you watched Willis at Washington, despite playing tackle, the more it seemed like he was destined to snap the ball in the NFL. Basic Info Age: 24 Experience: Rookie Height: 6’5 Weight: 303 pounds Cap Status Willis has a base salary of $885,000 in 2026 and a prorated signing bonus of $267,498. His cap number in 2026 is $1.15 million. He’s not going anywhere, as it would cost more to cut Willis than to keep him. He’ll be relatively cheap for the duration of his rookie deal, as is the case with most fourth-rounders. Free agency additions were telling The 49ers struck gold with Dominick Puni in the third round of the 2024 NFL Draft. Like Willis, Puni was a tackle convert. He’s also a sixth-year senior who played in 45 games. Eighteen of Willis’s starts came at right tackle, with 10 coming at left tackle. The 49ers likely admired Willis for playing through pain for the final six games of the season after being sidelined for three games after tearing his right MCL in 2025. Toughness aside, there are only Senior Bowl reps of Willis at guard. He played both right and left guard, but a week’s sample isn’t much to go off. Chris Foerster said he believes Willis is a starting-level NFL player this offseason. That can be true, but expecting him to pick up guard over a few months and hit the ground running feels like a leap a playoff team should not be willing to take — unless Willis blows them away during training camp. The 49ers signing veterans Robert Jones and Brett Toth this offseason, in my mind, was them telling us they want a veteran to win the job. They want experience on the field and to avoid another Spencer Burford situation like last season. Willis will get a fair shot to win the job, but he’d need to impress the way Puni did as a rookie. Puni took advantage of an injury and never looked back. Puni also came into the league with a wingspan, vertical, and broad jumps in the mid-70th percentiles, whereas Willis’s vertical jump was in the 31st percentile. Which leads us to our next point… Why Willis will likely need to redshirt I believe the offensive line is the most difficult position to translate to the NFL as a rookie, even for fifth- and sixth-year seniors. You cannot simulate the strength and athleticism these defensive lines have nowadays in college. Puni had both of those traits, which is why he was and remains an outlier. Watching Willis against collegiate programs with NFL prospects, Ohio State and Oregon, he did not look like the kind of prospect who would be ready to play as a rookie. When I referenced Willis’s vertical jump, that kind of lower-body explosion shows up when it’s time to be an anchor as a blocker. There are plenty of traits to like about Willis. His hand placement and punch timing are above average, even if his hands can occasionally get a little wide — likely Willis overcompensating. He does a great job on combo blocks, can easily redirect, and moves more like a second-rounder than a fourth-rounder. Best of all, Willis competes through the whistle and will look to finish whoever he is blocking. He stays engaged, which is a valuable trait to have. Some things happen to Willis that he cannot control. I saw one of the Ohio State players forklift him off the ground. Too often, his lack of length was problematic. And while changing directions isn’t an issue, the shorter arms allow defenders to close space on him, knowing that Willis won’t affect them. This is a three-out-of-four play sequence below. Watch the left tackle, No. 50: No. 1 on Oregon will be a 1st-rounder next year. He appears in the second clip. Those are the types of defensive tackles Willis will face this season as a rookie. When I watched him, Willis looked like a player who needed more sand in his pants to hold up in pass protection. Now, the 49ers could do different things upfront to hide him or minimize the number of 1-on-1s Willis gets. He was at his best when he was uncovered. When he could help somebody else out, or had help on combination blocks. That’s a center. Foerster is probably correct in viewing Willis as a starter, but that’s likely in 2027 to replace Brendel and become the 49ers’ center of the future. As a rookie, Willis should take advantage of a professional strength & conditioning program, as well as all of the nutrition that comes with being a pro. He’ll learn the ins and outs of playing a new position while going against NFL-quality linemen on the scout team.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Explaining the biggest difference between the 2025 and 2026 49ers
summary: The San Francisco 49ers head into training camp without any contract drama or holdouts. They’ll need to sort out a couple of positions, but heading into the 2026 season, there will be zero mentions of the words “rebuild” or “retool,” which felt like that was the narrative heading into last season. The team that is […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JUNE 03: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers looks on during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on June 3, 2026 in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers head into training camp without any contract drama or holdouts. They’ll need to sort out a couple of positions, but heading into the 2026 season, there will be zero mentions of the words “rebuild” or “retool,” which felt like that was the narrative heading into last season. The team that is built on the backs of its All-Pros will look different with those All-Pros on the field. Getting back Fred Warner and Nick Bosa on one side of the ball will make a world of difference. Role players won’t have to play starter snaps. And depth pieces will benefit from that. Defensive coordinator Raheem Morris will have complements to his stars that Robert Saleh didn’t have a year ago. Morris will get the second-year versions of Mykel Williams and Alfred Collins. His secondary pass rushers will be rookies Romello Height and Gracen Halton, as opposed to Kalia Davis and Clelin Ferrell. But the biggest difference that’ll help raise the ceiling will happen on the other side of the ball. What will be the biggest difference between the 2025 and 2026 49ers? My answer: When the 49ers got trounced in the NFC Divisional round, Brock Purdy completed three passes to wide receivers. Three. The prevailing thought was that Purdy didn’t have enough time to throw and the offensive line got their butts kicked. While that’s partially true — Purdy was under pressure on 39% of his dropbacks — he had plenty of time to throw. On average, Purdy had a whopping 4.24 seconds to throw on 33 dropbacks. He only completed 55.6% of his passes because there was nobody to throw the ball to. I recently rewatched the game. And as someone who appreciates wide receiver play, it was painful. Some of the advanced stats match the eye test. Next Gen Stats has a “catch rate over expected” stat. Across the board, the wideouts were in the negatives. Ricky Pearsall’s numbers seem like they were entered in incorrectly; they were so low. When you’re relying on Jauan Jennings and Kendrick Bourne against an elite secondary, it’s a miracle that the Niners were in this situation to begin with. The wide receiver play for the 49ers will be night and day, and everybody will reap the benefits. Safeties crept closer to the line of scrimmage without fear of one of the Niners’ wideouts running past them. That same issue meant opposing defenses could shrink the field and turn their attention to George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey underneath. The lack of physicality showed up in the running game all too often. Because of that, McCaffrey had to be a magician behind the line of scrimmage. The margin for error in the running game was next to nothing because the receivers didn’t have the necessary passion as blockers. Mike Evans changes everything. He gives the 49ers a weapon on every down, and a go-to target on third down. It also means Pearsall is no longer the focal point and gets the other team’s CB2. When that was the case last season, Pearsall made mincemeat of lesser corners. Rookie De’Zhaun Stribling adds a much-needed speed element, but in the form of a 6’2” and 200+ pounder. That body type can win over the middle, after the catch, and block the type of players the Niners couldn’t last year, like linebackers and safeties. Whether it’s Christian Kirk, Jacob Cowing, or Jordan Watkins, the smaller, shiftier types will allow Shanahan to run coverage off and stretch the field horizontally. Those are the kind of receivers who will complement the top three, allowing them to stay healthy for the season. It all circles back to Evans, and the domino effect that comes with having a player who you cannot afford to leave 1-on-1 on the field. It’s why the 49ers offense is in a prime position to return to an elite unit because of their Jimmys and Joes, and not with Shanahan needing to use smoke and mirrors.

title: Is age really that much of a concern for the 49ers?
summary: We’ve been going all over this for the last few months: the 49ers are getting older. And while we discuss it in the comments, everyone else mentions that they are getting too old and beat up. Is that much of an issue? It will be in a year or two if these last couple of […]
full_text: Dec 10, 2023; Santa Clara, California, USA; San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle (85) celebrates with running back Christian McCaffrey (23) after scoring a touchdown against the Seattle Seahawks during the fourth quarter at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images We’ve been going all over this for the last few months: the 49ers are getting older. And while we discuss it in the comments, everyone else mentions that they are getting too old and beat up. Is that much of an issue? It will be in a year or two if these last couple of draft picks don’t work out. I’ve been harping about finding a replacement for Trent Williams, even though that’s not exactly the way things work in the NFL. Can it be done currently? Well, if the last two seasons are any indication, yeah, maybe. In both seasons, the 49ers were inundated with injuries, and how they won the wild card game against the Philadelphia Eagles last season is still something I’m trying to figure out (oh, but its awesomeness can’t be argued). Albert Breer mentioned the age as something interesting to watch in his latest column on SI.com . The 49ers’ age is notable, and makes them as all in as their NFC West rivals in Los Angeles. Trent Williams is 38, Kyle Juszczyk is 35, George Kittle and Mike Evans are 32, Christian McCaffrey is 30, Fred Warner is 29 and Nick Bosa is 28. Can all those guys stay healthy? Do the Niners have a big swing left in them before the trade deadline to give them their best shot? It’s an interesting circumstance. Do older players get injured? Sure. But that’s really the main thing: if they don’t get injured (and that might happen), then I don’t think anyone will care about how old the roster is. If they make another NFC Championship this season, age really wasn’t an issue, and this season was a success. But going into the season? Same applies. I don’t really care how old the roster is as long as they are winning. The injury concerns are real, but it’s not like only the old players got sidelined last year and the year before that. At the end of the day, it’s a question of whether the age of the 49ers is really that much of an issue or just a talking point for everyone talking about the 49ers. Only time will tell, I suppose. Are you that concerned about their age, or is that just a number at this point?
author: Patrick Holloway

title: 49ers’ rookie De’Zhaun Stribling is getting more respect by the week
summary: Stop me if you’ve heard this before: The 49ers made a polarizing draft pick. Well, in the case of their most recent one, 2026’s De’Zhaun Stribling, the pick itself seemed to be an absolute mixed bag when it comes to fans’ reactions. Most called it a reach—at best. And then he came to OTAs, and […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - MAY 8: De'Zhaun Stribling #15 of the San Francisco 49ers poses for a photo during Rookie Minicamp at SAP Performance Facility on May 8, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Stop me if you’ve heard this before: The 49ers made a polarizing draft pick. Well, in the case of their most recent one, 2026’s De’Zhaun Stribling, the pick itself seemed to be an absolute mixed bag when it comes to fans’ reactions. Most called it a reach—at best. And then he came to OTAs, and after everyone was done blasting the pick, reports came that he may have been off the board a couple picks later anyway . Now we have comparisons of Stribling to the likes of Chris Godwin Jr., and that an NFL team had him ranked higher than Philadelphia Eagles first-round pick Makai Lemon . Stribling’s stock continues to rise, and he hasn’t even played a snap yet. Add him as a sleeper to a rookie offensive player of the year list—a list from CBS Sports’ Jordan Dajani who gave four sleepers to consider . Stribling is known for his blocking ability and physicality, but he also ran a 4.36 40-yard dash at the combine at 6-foot-2. He caught 55 passes for 811 yards last season for the Ole Miss Rebels and led the team with six receiving touchdowns. He also caught seven passes for 122 yards in the College Football Playoff Quarterfinal upset against Georgia. Surely he can find a role in this efficient San Francisco 49ers offensive attack — and should have the opportunity, too. Really, his blocking ability and speed are enough for me and scream Kyle Shanahan offense. Like many, I wondered what the hell the 49ers were doing when his name was called. After I did a bit of research on someone I knew nothing about , I walked away saying this might end up being a steal. Kyle Shanahan is not one to throw his rookies into the fire unless absolutely necessary (and they are absolutely ready). Dajani makes a good point about injuries and the presence of Mike Evans at wide receiver. I wouldn’t be surprised if Evans is at least out for a good portion of a game or two during the season—which would open the door for Stribling. Plus, we don’t know who will fill the Kendrick Bourne/Jauan Jennings role this year, with both out of the mix. If Stribling is that guy, he’d be the highest pick spent on the role for Shanahan. It’s funny how on draft day many of us (myself included) were wondering what the 49ers were doing, but now, I, for one, am excited to see what this guy does in Kyle Shanahan’s offense. He could be the sleeper pick for Offensive Rookie of the Year. I just hope if he does win it, it’s by ability and production, not because of injuries and attrition.

title: PFF doesn’t know who the Titans’ WR1 is
summary: The Tennessee Titans worked hard to revamp the wide receiver position this offseason. They drafted Carnell Tate at No. 4 overall and also signed Wan’Dale Robinson to a four-year, $70 million contract in free agency. Everyone expects Tate and Robinson to be the Titans’ top two receivers for quarterback Cam Ward in 2026. Well, everyone […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans wide receiver Calvin Ridley (0) makes a catch during organized team activities at Vanderbilt Health Football Center Friday, May 29, 2026. | DENNY SIMMONS / THE TENNESSEAN / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans worked hard to revamp the wide receiver position this offseason . They drafted Carnell Tate at No. 4 overall and also signed Wan’Dale Robinson to a four-year , $70 million contract in free agency. Everyone expects Tate and Robinson to be the Titans’ top two receivers for quarterback Cam Ward in 2026. Well, everyone but Pro Football Focus, apparently. PFF recently ranked all 32 starting wide receivers (WR1) in the league. For the Titans, they… chose Calvin Ridley and ranked him dead last at No. 32 overall. In what universe is Ridley still the Titans’ WR1 after the Tate and Robinson offseason acquisitions? “ Ridley’s 2025 season was cut short by injury, but he is expected to return as Tennessee’s top target in 2026 ,” Dalton Wasserman and Max Chadwick wrote . “ He recorded 1,000-yard seasons in both 2023 and 2024. Before the injury, Ridley was averaging a career-high 17.8 yards per reception, which ranked fourth among wide receivers with at least 30 targets last season. Flanked by free-agent addition Wan’Dale Robinson and first-round pick Carnell Tate, Ridley should see more favorable matchups on the outside in 2026 .” Wasserman and Chadwick are talented writers, but this feels like a whiff. A lack of knowledge surrounding the Titans by mainstream media members isn’t new for this fanbase. A 32-year-old Ridley coming off a serious injury won’t be the Titans’ WR1 in 2026. In fact, Ridley is likely competing for the WR3 role with both Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike. Ayomanor and Dike had impressive rookie seasons, and should be better as sophomores. Ayomanor is a bigger bodied outside receiver with blocking capabilities. Like Ridley, Dike is flexible enough to play multiple receiving positions, both inside and outside. Ridley won’t be handed reps by Brian Daboll. Expect Tate and Robinson to be the Titans’ preferred receivers.
author: Justin Melo

title: Explaining why every Commanders training-camp roster battle matters
summary: In a little over a week, Hogs Haven will be buzzing with news about new Commanders additions in training camp. Naturally, the spotlight will focus the most on returning stars like QB Jayden Daniels, high-profile free agent additions such as OLB Odafe Oweh and TE Chig Okonkwo, and early-round NFL draft picks LB Sonny Styles […]
full_text: In a little over a week, Hogs Haven will be buzzing with news about new Commanders additions in training camp. Naturally, the spotlight will focus the most on returning stars like QB Jayden Daniels, high-profile free agent additions such as OLB Odafe Oweh and TE Chig Okonkwo, and early-round NFL draft picks LB Sonny Styles and WR Antonio Williams. For some fans, however, the more interesting camp stories are annual battles waged by players on the fringe, fighting their way onto the final 53-man roster and keeping their NFL dreams alive. Over the years, Washington football fans have witnessed some great camp and preseason stories of underdogs beating the odds, like Alfred Morris, Kyshoen Jarrett, Chase Roullier, Jeremy Reaves and Kam Curl. Each year at Hogs Haven we celebrate the efforts of early-career roster-fringe players to earn a place on the team – or at least convince us that they will – with the Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Award . This year a new crop or fringe hopefuls will try to make their case, along with a host of returning players. I highlighted the Mason/Brennan-eligible candidates among them in a three-part preview ( Front Runners , Chasing Pack , Dark Horses and Long Shots ) ahead of OTAs. This year’s camp promises some interesting position battles at kicker , center , wide receiver and defensive back, with opportunities for fringe-players to earn playing time. Names to watch at those positions include Drew Stevens, Matt Gulbin, Jaden Bradley, Chris Hilton, Malik Spencer, and Fred Davis II. But the real excitement of training camp and pre-season is that you never really know who might emerge from obscurity to claim a position on the final 53. While most Day 3 draft picks, UDFAs and other players on reserve/futures contracts will never make it as major contributors on an NFL team, it is a lazy take to dismiss their chances. The numbers are stacked against them. But every preseason we see players emerge from the bottom of depth charts to claim roster spots, and sometimes become starters and even stars in the NFL. To illustrate why every preseason battle deserves attention, this article diverts the spotlight for a moment from the early roster locks to focus attention on players who began their NFL journeys on the fringes, fighting for positions in camp, and went on to earn significant playing time on Super Bowl rosters. As the Commanders seek to return to the big stage, GM Adam Peters will need to fill out the roster with 53 competitors. As the data in my most recent article revealed, he is unlikely to do that entirely with early-round draft picks, marquee free agents, and trade acquisitions. He will most likely need some help from players who faced an uphill battle to earn their place on the team. To set the stage for battles for the last few places on the roster in camp, let’s take a moment to reflect on the contributions and journeys of former roster-fringe hopefuls to Super Bowl rosters. Former Roster-Fringe Players on Super Bowl Teams – 2020 to 2025 This piece took its inspiration from the analysis I did for my recent article on how Super Bowl teams acquired their players . One thing which really stood out as I was tracing the players’ journeys was the number of players acquired by Super Bowl teams as late-round NFL draft picks, UDFAs, waiver and practice squad claim, and as fringe free agent signings. The proportion of former roster-fringe players was particularly enriched among the special teams players. However, most Super Bowl teams had more of these players than I had expected on offense and defense. And the two teams which had made repeat Super Bowl appearances in the sample seemed to be particularly stacked. To confirm that impression, I broke down the Super Bowl roster data into “Mainstream” and “Roster-Fringe” acquisitions, on offense and defense. As in the previous article, I only included “major contributors” who played 20% or more of offensive or defensive snaps in the Super Bowl. “Mainstream” acquisitions included players drafted in rounds 1-6, veteran free agents and players acquired by trade. “Roster-Fringe” acquisitions included seventh-round draft picks, undrafted free agents acquired in their draft year, players claimed off waivers or another team’s practice squad, and “fringe free agent” signings. The last category was included to capture players signed as free agents in the first three years of their careers with negligible game experience on other teams. Fringe FA is a major acquisition route for special teams players. But only two players made it onto offensive or defensive Super Bowl rosters in this way: DL Cory Durden (Patriots, 2025) and OL Andrew Wylie, (Chiefs, 2020 and 2022). The following table shows the complete breakdown: In the six Super Bowls from 2020 through 2025, 48/353 (13.6%) of the major contributors on offense and defense initially made their way onto their team from the roster fringes. The average Super Bowl roster contained four former roster-fringe players on offense or defense. The maximum number was eight (2020 Chiefs) and the minimum was two (2025 Patriots, 2020 Buccaneers). It is worth noting that the decision to only count seventh-round draft picks as roster-fringe was arbitrary. Had I included sixth-round picks, the percentage of former roster-fringe players would have been even larger. The takeaway message from this analysis is, before anyone dismisses the chances of a seventh-round pick or UDFA making the final 53-man roster, remember, every one of the past 12 Super Bowl teams had at least two players who started out the same way making significant contributions on offense or defense. Two of the roster-fringe players who made good during this period went on to become stars in the league. Several became starters or major contributors on offense or defense. Even more became important rotational players, backups or special teams contributors. To weather a 17-game season and emerge as a championship contender, an NFL team needs all of the above. Now, let’s take a look at the journeys of a selection of these players from camp hopeful to the Super Bowl. We’ll end with five players who got their start with the Redskins or ended up on the Commanders’ roster. Impact Players QB Brock Purdy, 49ers – The last player drafted in 2022 began his rookie season as an afterthought, buried on the depth chart behind first-round trade target Trey Lance and veteran Jimmy Garoppolo. Following season-ending injuries to Lance in Week 2 and Garoppolo in Week 13, Purdy was named the starter. He led the 49ers to the NFC Championship game, where his season ended with an elbow injury. The following season he led the 49ers back to the big stage, becoming the lowest drafted QB to start in a Super Bowl. Purdy earned a Pro Bowl nomination that season and finished 4 th in AP MVP voting . LT Jordan Mailata, Eagles – Hailing from the Bankstown suburb of Sydney, Australia, Mailata made the jump from the South Sydney Rabbitohs NRL under-20’s team to the NFL International Player Pathway Program . After a summer at the IMG Academy, and despite never having played a down of American Football, he was selected 233 rd overall by the Eagles in the seventh round of the 2018 draft. Mailata took his first regular-season snap in Week 1 of 2020. He got his first start at left tackle in Week 4, filling in for injured starter Jason Peters, and went on to start 10 games until his season was ended by a concussion. The following season he signed a four-year, $64 million contract as the Eagles’ starting left tackle, allowing Peters to leave in free agency. Mailata has become one of the NFL’s best at his position, earning second team All-Pro honors in 2024, when he started in the Eagles’ Super Bowl win over the Chiefs. title: Will edge rusher Odafe Oweh be worth his $96m deal this season? – Survey
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Commanders fans and fans across the country. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys. Last month, Hogs Haven listed Odafeh Oweh at #4 in our list of the top-ten Commanders […]
full_text: Oct 12, 2025; Miami Gardens, Florida, USA; Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Odafe Oweh (98) celebrates with fans after the game against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Sam Navarro-Imagn Images | Sam Navarro-Imagn Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Commanders fans and fans across the country. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys. Last month, Hogs Haven listed Odafeh Oweh at #4 in our list of the top-ten Commanders for 2026. Here’s what Scott Bair said about Oweh in that article: He’s an intriguing talent with the size you want at 6-foot-5 and 251 pounds, with the speed and power you need to excel off the edge in new coordinator Daronte Jones’ system. His relative athletic score was super high – catching a trend among big Adam Peters investments? – with solid combine numbers in all the right places. Oweh gets to the quarterback a ton. Translating that to sacks and errant throws and turnovers is the key. He’s clearly capable of creating havoc, but how will Oweh fare without expert pass rushers around him. He hasn’t been the alpha to this point, and he’ll be counted on to be one in 2026. His response to that expectation will be a major factor in how the Commanders fare defensively in 2026. Oweh doesn’t just need to be a double-digit sacks guy. He needs to make game-changing plays and lead the defensive line. Washington’s biggest free agent commitment this offseason came early in the March free agency period when Adam Peters inked Odafe Oweh to a 4-yr, $96m contract as the first of several moves intended to fix what was wrong with Washington’s pass rush in 2025. Some people were critical of the contract as an overpay for a player who hasn’t earned this kind of payday while others viewed it as a savvy move to sign an ascending 27-yr-old player. Bleacher Report called the signing of edge rusher Odafe Oweh one of the 10 worst free agent signings of the offseason: [T]he fact that Baltimore gave up on a 10-sack player and flipped him for a so-so defensive back and a Day 3 pick says something—and that something isn’t great. Oweh had just 13 sacks over the first three seasons of his career combined. He has never been much of a factor against the run—he has hit the 40-tackle mark just once. His 47 pressures and 16.4 percent pass-rush win rate last year per PFF were good, but not great. Oweh’s average annual salary ranks among the 12 best edge-rushers in the game. His production and talent does not. A to Z Sports , on the other hand, praised the signing of Oweh: The Commanders bringing in Oweh checks off a lot of boxes, and he showed so many flashes when he joined the Chargers. Eight sacks and 35 pressures in 12 games on a new defense isn’t something to just overlook. He also had the sixth-highest pressure rate in the NFL at 17.3% after he joined the Chargers in Week 6. Oweh also only missed two tackles in those 12 games with the Charges, which is insane when you think about it. He’s also very stout in the run game at 6-5, 260 pounds, and he’ll bring power and speed off the EDGE in Washington. This is a franchise player to build around, who is hitting his prime as he turned 27 two months ago. It’s impossible not to love this move The question Today, we’re asking you to assess how confident you are that Oweh will live up to his contract this season. Comments & Results Of course, we invite you to answer the survey question below, but also feel free to expand on your answer and provide nuance in the comments section. While you are certainly free to simply share which choice you made on the survey question, the most interesting comments will explain why you answered the way you did. I rely on those comments when discussing the results of the survey when they are posted in a separate article the next few days. POLL QUESTION

full_text: The Daily Slop – 21 July 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Will Commanders implement a three safety package? Looking at how the Vikings used a three safety package and how Washington could look to use one One of the key parts of the Vikings defense under Flores and Jones last year was the use of a three safety package. The Vikings were one of the few teams that stayed in their base defense most of the time, but when they did go to a sub-package, they typically went for a big nickel, three safety package rather than a typical slot corner. There’s a few reasons for doing that. The first is personnel. The Vikings had three safeties that they wanted on the field, so it makes sense to build a package around that personnel. But the Vikings had other reasons too. Going with a third safety over a slot corner is a way of matching up against the modern trend of offense. Many NFL offenses are looking to run the ball a lot more often and one of the best ways to run the ball right now is to get the defense into a nickel package and force the slot corner into the run fit as a linebacker. We’ve seen this with the Commanders in recent years when a smaller corner like Mike Sainristil goes into the slot and then the offense lines up their slot receiver tight to the formation, forcing Sainristil to play almost as a linebacker, where his size is attacked. To counteract that trend, the Vikings use a bigger body instead of a typical slot corner. They put one of their bigger safeties in the slot, giving them the flexibility to fit the run better than a slot corner, but still drop into coverage better than a typical linebacker. The Vikings also protect that third safety by using a lot of zone coverage. So instead of having a third safety have to match up against some of the league’s best receivers in the slot, they drop into zone coverage instead. So what exactly does this look like and how might Jones look to implement it in Washington? Let’s dive into it. Quick video on why Nick Cross is among the top players to watch at Commanders' training camp https://t.co/Jwye7sQqA8 — John Keim (@john_keim) July 20, 2026 One of the unique things the Vikings did with their three safety package was change up who was being substituted off the field for the third safety. The Vikings ran a base 3-4, which we’re expecting Jones to run in Washington too. In a 3-4, typically the defense would take off one of their three interior defensive lineman when they switch to a nickel sub-package, but not the Vikings. The Vikings liked to keep all three interior defensive lineman on the field as much as possible to help them control the run game. So instead of taking off an interior defensive lineman, the Vikings had to substitute one of the four linebackers. The Vikings would often switch up which of the four linebackers they would substitute for the third safety. They had two main variations; a 4-2-5 package and a 5-1-5 package. They often looked very similar, as you’ll soon see, but there are some subtle differences. When new Commanders DC Daronte Jones was in Minnesota, the Vikings often prefered to use a 3rd safety instead of a slot corner in their nickel packages. Will Jones look to do the same in Washington? I took a closer look: https://t.co/1SJ8RuEZJb pic.twitter.com/ue0S6LsukP — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) July 21, 2026 To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com PHOTOS | Nick Cross distributes backpacks to Washington youth Commanders safety Nick Cross spent the day at the Boys and Girls Club of Greater Washington where he played games with kids and distributed backpacks View Link View Link View Link View Link View Link View Link Heavy.com Commanders new blitzing defense made the decision to sign with Washington a ‘no brainer’ for Leo Chenal Daronte Jones comes from Minnesota, where he spent five seasons with the Vikings. He has worked under their defensive coordinator Brian Flores since 2023 and is expected to implement a similar system in Washington. As Chenal alluded to, Jones’ defense will rely on the linebacker position much like Flores’ defense does. The Vikings defense blitzed more than any other team last season, a league-high 44.3%. Chenal appears up to the task as he labeled his decision to join Washington, “A no-brainer.” Chenal revealed in an interview on NFL Network’s The Insiders that he chose the Commanders over other potential suitors because of their scheme under new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. “It really involves the linebackers,” Chenal said last Thursday. “It involves guys playing to their skill set. It’s really cool being able to walk through different things with coaches and having feedback, feedback to the coaches, them talking to us, they really want to have us take advantage of what we’re really good at. We kind of developed the scheme more and more, and we’re going to continue to mold that around the guys that we have. It’s really cool how personalized it is. As a Mike linebacker, being in the middle, you go each way, come downhill, you’ve got so much flexibility as a linebacker in this defense.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE WUSA9 Should the Commanders trade for Patriots receiver Kayshon Boutte? I don’t believe the Commanders would be asking Boutte to become a featured part of the offense. They would be asking him to become a complementary veteran vertical receiver. He could play a high number of snaps without commanding a particularly high number of targets. Terry McLaurin would remain the No. 1 option. Chig Okonkwo could frequently function as the second option, with Boutte and rookie receiver Antonio Williams potentially rotating behind them in the progression. And don’t forget the presence of running back Rachaad White as a receiver and others like Dyami Brown, Van Jefferson, Treylon Burks, Luke McCaffrey, and Jaylin Lane who would also like to have a say in target distribution this season. Looking at his three years with the Patriots so far, Boutte plays as a field-stretching X receiver, not a traditional boundary X. As long as Washington defines the job that way, the fit could work. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Commanders 2026 opponent breakdown | Minnesota Vikings Can the Kyler Murray experiment work in Minnesota? Murray didn’t have to wait long to find a new home after the Arizona Cardinals released him. It was widely believed that the Vikings were interested in the former No. 1 overall pick, and all it took was one visit for Murray to sign a one-year deal with them. Now comes the big question: is this marriage going to work? The pieces are certainly there for it to be a successful partnership. The Vikings had one of the best defenses in the league last year, and they already have an offense with solid foundational pieces like Jefferson. Additionally, head coach Kevin O’Connell has shown that when he has competent quarterback play, like he did with Sam Darnold in 2024, that his scheme can be a potent one. But can Murray be competent? There are arguments to be made for and against him in that regard. Although he himself has been mostly efficient with a completion rate of 67.1%, the Cardinals have not been as successful, which could be more on the Cardinals than Murray. He’s also struggled with injuries over the last four seasons, which has caused him to miss 27 games in that span. Still, there’s no doubt that this is the best team Murray has been on in several years, so assuming he wins the job over McCarthy, which he is expected to do, then he’ll have a good opportunity to succeed.
