title: The truth about Commanders QB Jayden Daniels’ NFL MVP chances in 2026
summary: Following an excellent rookie season, Jayden Daniels looked like the future of the NFL. One injury-plagued season later, he’s entering 2026 with more to prove than almost any quarterback in football. If he can answer a handful of critical questions, Daniels has a legitimate path back into the NFL MVP conversation. “I’m done talking about […]
full_text: Following an excellent rookie season, Jayden Daniels looked like the future of the NFL. One injury-plagued season later , he’s entering 2026 with more to prove than almost any quarterback in football. If he can answer a handful of critical questions, Daniels has a legitimate path back into the NFL MVP conversation. “I’m done talking about last year. Last year is last year.” That’s what Daniels said during minicamp availability , when asked about his thoughts on the 2025 season. Nobody can blame him. It left a sour taste in the mouths of so many people. But Daniels, who played just four full games for Washington last season , has an opportunity to put his name back in the upper echelon of quarterbacks this year. Jayden had his name mixed into the MVP race as a rookie two seasons ago, and to repeat that level of success depends on how several questions get answered this year. Mastering David Blough’s offense David Blough is a new offensive coordinator with limited coaching experience before being promoted from assistant quarterbacks coach. Daniels’ relationship with Blough is essential to the baseline success of the quarterback and the offense. Daniels’ accuracy is up there with the best quarterbacks, but athleticism and scrambling ability are his most dynamic assets. We know he can break a defense down with that threat alone but, in a new scheme, he has to be able to keep the offense ahead of schedule with his decision-making and timing as a passer first. Staying healthy for an entire season The biggest question isn’t talent — it’s durability. Daniels proved during his rookie campaign that he can play through a full season, but injuries limited him to just four complete games in 2025. Until he strings together another healthy 17-game season, durability will remain part of the conversation surrounding his long-term ceiling. We don’t have the answer now, but this season will bring more clarity. Elevating Washington in big games In the 2024 and 2025 regular seasons with Jayden Daniels starting, Washington has a 2-9 record against teams above .500. I believe this record is more of an indictment on the makeup of the roster than it is directly reflective of Daniels himself. Washington’s receiver and tight end production were lackluster in 2025 and struggled to provide an explosive pass game for any Washington quarterback. Additionally, the defense in both seasons was abysmal, forcing the offense to play perfect football to keep them in games essentially. What makes this record more critical moving forward, though, is the complete roster overhaul GM Adam Peters has done this offseason . On paper, this team has filled plenty of holes that have plagued the team over the last two seasons, and it should give Daniels more of a chance to influence the game in a major way. Leading the Commanders to an NFC East title Another element we should also pay attention to this season is how he performs in NFC East matchups . Daniels still has to prove he can consistently outperform established veterans like Dak Prescott, especially in division games that often shape the NFC East race. Being able to go toe-to-toe with Prescott, as well as winning the division, is an easy way to place a legitimate bid for the MVP. In the end, Jayden has a real shot, albeit a long shot(+2500) , at the MVP this year. It will always come down to how many wins your team accumulates, elite numbers in a top-5 offense, signature wins, and memorable moments, all things that voters will be paying attention to. Daniels has already shown he possesses MVP-level talent. The question entering 2026 isn’t whether he can make spectacular plays—we’ve already seen that. It’s whether he can stay healthy, master a new offense, consistently beat quality opponents, and lead Washington to the top of the NFC East. If he checks those boxes, don’t be surprised if his name finds its way back into the MVP conversation by December. I break down each of those questions in detail in the video below. Make sure you subscribe to the channel and comment your thoughts on Jayden’s MVP chances this season in the article comments below.

title: Washington Commanders hidden gems: 3 secret superstars for the 2026 roster
summary: The 2024 Washington Commanders made the NFC Championship game for the first time since 1991, which is also the last time the franchise won a Super Bowl. The 55-23 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles in the 2024 conference title game was a heartbreaker, but expecting that to happen in the first place for a franchise […]
full_text: The 2024 Washington Commanders made the NFC Championship game for the first time since 1991, which is also the last time the franchise won a Super Bowl. The 55-23 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles in the 2024 conference title game was a heartbreaker, but expecting that to happen in the first place for a franchise that hadn’t even had a winning season since 2015? Well, Commanders fans could be forgiven for being happy with what they had and severely excited for the future. Unfortunately for the Commanders, every season tells its own story and, for the 2025 team, it was back to a harsher reality. This team inverted its previous 12-5 record to 5-12. The defense fell apart, dropping from 23rd to 28th in DVOA . The offense experienced a more drastic downturn, from sixth to 23rd . Jayden Daniels, who may have had the best rookie season any quarterback has ever had , missed 10 games with multiple injuries, and the coaching on both sides of the ball was more suspect than expected. Offseason turnaround was as severe as one might imagine. Offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury was replaced by former assistant quarterbacks coach David Blough and defensive coordinator Joe Whitt Jr. (who was stripped of play-calling duties at midseason in favor of head coach Dan Quinn) was replaced by former Minnesota Vikings defensive backs coach & pass game coordinator Daronte Jones. So now, the optimism is back! “I feel like this is an elevated group with a lot of versatility,” Quinn said at the owners meetings in March . “I like the speed that we added to the team and for me, the thing I love the most is the competition that comes with putting a good group together. When you look at some of our positions… man, that is going to be a battle. And the thing that comes from that is where everyone lifts up and goes. So, having the new players in the building, we’ve had a lot of the current guys, so I get to see them on a pretty regular basis, but having the new guys in for their days when they signed, I enjoyed that. Because after a tough end of season into January and February, to get some of these guys in here to see their enthusiasm doing it all together, that was really cool.” To take that cool into the new season, Quinn will need serious contributions from everyone on the roster — not just the obvious stars. So, here’s three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Commanders — one underrated veteran, one underrated free-agent signing, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: Safety Jeremy Reaves A primary reason the team replaced Whitt with Jones was the pass defense. Which was… well, let’s be diplomatic. It sucked. The 2025 Commanders allowed 350 completions on 540 attempts (64.8%) for 4,400 yards (8.1 YPA), 33 touchdowns, eight interceptions, and an opponent passer rating of 104.2, which was the NFL’s fifth-worst. Blown assignments were the norm as opposed to the exception, and the only guy in that secondary who seemed to be able to transcend it was safety Jeremy Reaves. In 2025, Reaves allowed 22 catches on 34 targets for 211 yards, 134 yards after the catch, one touchdown, one interception, seven pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 79.4. He also had 58 solo tackles, 18 stops, five tackles for loss, and three pressures on just eight pass-rushing snaps. The @Commanders ' secondary was a disaster in 2025. Except for safety Jeremy Reaves. Guy to watch in 2026. pic.twitter.com/mxwdszGmN5 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 14, 2026 The undrafted free agent out of South Alabama bounced around for a good long time. The Philadelphia Eagles signed him in 2018, but he didn’t make final cuts. Washington signed Reaves off the street, but bounced him off and on their practice squad over the next few years enough to give the guy whiplash. He didn’t make the final roster out of camp until 2022, and that was the year he made the Pro Bowl and First-Team All-Pro as a special teamer. The Commanders signed him to a two-year, $6 million deal in 2024, and bumped that up to a new one-year, $3.5 million deal in 2025. Based on Reaves’ development and how things might go with better coaching, this may be the last time he’ll be talking about smaller contracts. “I think the biggest thing for me is that the game has just slowed down so much, even in from last year to this year,” Reaves said in Aug. 2025. “I was coming off a knee injury, and everything was just kind of going really fast. I was trying to prove myself to a new staff and a new front office. And this year I just came in with the confidence that all I have to do is be me, and at the end of the day this is a game. I get to come out here and have fun every day and compete. And so, I’ve just been out here flying around, looking at the different things that offenses are showing formation-wise, split-wise — okay, who’s on the ball? Where are my deep threats when I’m at safety? “Just going out there and just trusting what I see. I think that’s the big thing with guys, they might see something, but they don’t necessarily trust what they’re seeing. You got the instincts for a reason, so you gotta use them.” Reaves has the instincts, and he’s learned how to use them. He’ll be a crucial part of the Commanders’ defensive turnaround, assuming everything clicks with the guys around him. Underrated free agent: EDGE K’Lavon Chaisson The 2025 Commanders did get to the quarterback at a pretty decent rate; their 42 regular-season quarterback takedowns were slightly above league average . But their pressure rate of 19.6% was the NFL’s seventh-lowest, and the front office went after that problem with gusto in the offseason. They signed former Baltimore Ravens and Los Angeles Chargers edge rusher Odafe Oweh to a four-year, $96 million contract with $68 million guaranteed. They also penned former New England Patriots edge defender K’Lavon Chaisson to a one-year, $11 million contract with $10.3 million guaranteed. Based on last season’s production, those contracts should have been closer together. And Chaisson had a legitimate case to take the lead. In 2025 with the Ravens and Chargers, Oweh had 7.5 sacks and 51 total pressures, while Chaisson had 7.5 sacks and 52 pressures with the AFC champions during the regular season and was a menace in the playoffs. Now, this was Chaisson’s latest turn after an underwhelming four seasons with the Jacksonville Jaguars, the team that took him with the 20th overall pick out of LSU in the 2020 draft. The Carolina Panthers signed him in March 2024, but he didn’t make final cuts. The Las Vegas Raiders took their shot by signing Chaisson to their practice squad on Sept. 10, promoted him to the active roster on Oct. 5, and were rewarded with Chaisson’s six sacks and 29 pressures — his best NFL season to date. This prompted the Patriots to sign Chaisson to a one-year, $3 million contract, which he more than maxed out . Chaisson was a Secret Superstar at the start and at the end of the 2025 season, because the tape did not lie. In four seasons with the Jaguars, K'Lavon Chaisson did very little to validate his 20th overall selection in the 2020 draft. One season with the Raiders turned things around, and now, the Patriots will look to put the cherry on top. pic.twitter.com/eCODMkKm8H — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 14, 2025 Like just about everyone on the @Patriots ' defense, K'Lavon Chaisson has gone from very good to thermonuclear in the postseason. pic.twitter.com/LUoGr2LWiJ — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) January 22, 2026 Putting Chaisson and Oweh on the same defensive line should increase Washington’s pass-rush possibilities to an extreme degree. “Man, just continue to believe,” Chaisson said in his first Commanders press conference, when asked about his specific NFL path. “That’s it. Continue to believe. Everybody’s story is not the same. Everybody’s journey is not the same. “Comparison is the biggest thief of joy. So the best thing I loved about all this is the journey. Everything that I learned, the lessons…

title: Commanders-Vikings Week 16; can Daronte Jones outdo his mentor Brian Flores?
summary: It’s 5 o’clock somewhere… The 5 O’Clock Club The 5 o’clock club is published from time to time during the season, and aims to provide a forum for reader-driven discussion at a time of day when there isn’t much NFL news being published. Feel free to introduce topics that interest you in the comments below. […]
full_text: Dec 7, 2025; Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA; Washington Commanders running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt (22) rushes the ball against Minnesota Vikings linebacker Gabriel Murphy (59) during the second half at U.S. Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brad Rempel-Imagn Images | Brad Rempel-Imagn Images It’s 5 o’clock somewhere… The 5 O’Clock Club The 5 o’clock club is published from time to time during the season, and aims to provide a forum for reader-driven discussion at a time of day when there isn’t much NFL news being published. CLICK HERE to see the full 5 o’clock club archive 2026 opponent preview series: Wk 1 Eagles | Wk 2 Cowboys | Wk 3 Seahawks | Wk 4 Colts | Wk 5 Giants | Wk 6 49ers | Wk 9 Rams | Wk 11 Bengals | Wk 12 Cardinals | Wk 13 Titans | Wk 14 Texans | Wk 15 Falcons Previewing Washington’s 14 opponents of the ‘26 season — one at a time In 2026, the Commanders will, like every other team in the NFL, play 17 games against 14 opponents. With the amount of roster change that NFL teams undergo annually along with the unusually large number of head coach and coordinator changes in 2026, it seems useful to spend some time to review each of Washington’s regular season opponents. VIKINGS The Commanders complete the trifecta of 2026 games played against teams whose head coaches were once offensive coordinators in Washington by taking on Kevin O’Connell after having gone head-to-head against Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers in Week 6 and Sean McVay’s Rams in Week 9. Week 16 Preview: Washington Commanders at Minnesota Vikings Date: Date & Time TBD Location: US Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Minnesota The Vikings had a very successful regular season in 2024, winning 14 games behind Sam Darnold before ultimately losing to the Rams on the opening weekend of the playoffs. It may have been the failure in that playoff game that led to Darnold’s departure to the Seahawks, where he led his team to a Super Bowl championship in February. The Vikings entered the 2025 season with sky-high expectations that did not come to fruition as the team stumbled to a 9-8 regular season 3rd place finish in the NFC North, missing the playoffs. They now find themselves caught between two timelines: trying to win right now with veteran Kyler Murray, who has durability concerns, while simultaneously sheltering a young quarterback, JJ McCarthy, whose developmental timeline may have stalled. "Justin Jefferson should never have a season like the one we saw last year." @minakimes needs to see better QB play from the Vikings this season ✍️ pic.twitter.com/ONFoZppIGW — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) July 10, 2026 The Commanders and Vikings will both enter the 2026 season with memories of magical 2024 seasons that ended in ultimate playoff disappointment followed by more or less forgettable 2025 seasons. The Commanders have re-tooled the coaching staff and are running it back with Jayden Daniels. The Vikings appear to be flailing about a bit at quarterback, but have stood firm with their coaching staff. Dan Patrick wasn’t having any of Kevin O’Connell’s coachspeak on QB1 pic.twitter.com/JAgCXyT0mT — The Coachspeak Index (@CoachspeakIndex) July 10, 2026 By the time the game is played in Week 16, all the questions about these two rosters and coaching staffs are likely to have been answered, but right now, in mid-July, those questions abound. Will this be a matchup between two NFC powerhouses jockeying for better playoff seeding? Will it, rather, be a meaningless game between two teams suffering through another disappointing season? Or will it end up being a painful, one-sided affair akin to last year’s contest, with one team trying to secure a playoff berth while the other team’s fan base is thinking primarily on the game’s effect on draft position? The All-Time Series Numbers Recently Washington heads to Minnesota trying to break a long losing streak on the road. The burgundy & gold has lost four straight games in the Twin Cities, with its last victory there coming back in 2007. Dan Quinn’s roster now faces the challenge of winning inside U.S. Bank Stadium to erase nearly two decades of road struggles against the Vikings. The most recent game (which I referenced in the introduction above) was a 31-0 shellacking put on the Commanders in December 2025. Many fans feel as if Kliff Kingsbury sealed his doom in DC with a series of 3 incomplete passes after the Commanders faced 2nd & goal at the Vikings 2 yard line on Washington’s first possession of the game. Washington turned the ball over to the Vikings just before the end of the 1st quarter, then the defense allowed a 98-yard TD drive to make the game 14-0 and the rout was on. Washington’s subsequent offensive drives comprised 3 punts, 2 interceptions, and a fumble — with Vikings QB JJ McCarthy taking a knee on the final 3 snaps of the game to run off the final 2 minutes in a humiliating Week 14 defeat of Dan Quinn’s team. Historical series Although the Vikings inaugural season was 1961, they didn’t play the Redskins until November 1968. The Vikings got off to a hot start, winning the first two games in the series, and 5 of the first 7 before the Redskins turned things around with 7 straight wins — including a pair of overtime games and 3 playoff victories — from the 1982 postseason to the 1992 postseason. It’s been mostly downhill since that time, however, as the Vikings have won 11 of 15 games played since ‘93, and 8 of 10 since 2010. The Vikings lead the all-time series 16-13, though Washington won 3 of 5 playoff games between the two teams in the 20-year stretch from the ‘73 season to the ‘92 season. Vikings Coaching Staff While there were some staff changes, the Vikings coaching staff returns for the 2026 season substantially the same as it was in 2025, with the same head coach and coordinators. Perhaps the most significant coaching staff change was the hiring of Assistant Head Coach Frank Smith to replace Mike Pettine, who retired. Head Coach : Kevin O’Connell Offensive Coordinator : Wes Phillips Defensive Coordinator : Brian Flores Special Teams Coordinator : Matt Daniels Washington & Minnesota: Contrasting offensive philosophies While Minnesota’s offensive designer — head coach Kevin O’Connell — and Washington’s new OC David Blough are both seen as young, creative and intelligent former players and offensive innovators (and Blough was in Minnesota briefly as a player under KOC), they take different approaches to offensive design. O’Connell, who had a successful 3-year stint in Washington that saw him rise in 3 seasons from QB coach to offensive coordinator, is a direct branch of the dominant Sean McVay coaching tree. His foundational philosophy was cemented while working under Jay Gruden in Washington and later as Sean McVay’s offensive coordinator with the Los Angeles Rams. His system relies heavily on West Coast timing, mid-zone/outside-zone run principles, and a heavy volume of 11-personnel groupings to stress the defense through the air. Like KOC, David Blough has risen rapidly through Washington’s offensive coaching ranks, moving from Assistant QB coach to OC, also in 3 years. While both O’Connell and Blough trace elements of their offensive identity to the same schematic roots, they prioritize entirely different mechanics. Because Blough spent time as a practice squad player directly under O’Connell in Minnesota in 2022, the foundational DNA of the two systems shares a heavy West Coast influence, but his — that is Blough’s — implementation of that system for the 2026 season is expected to differ significantly from that of his old coach. In fact, many people expect his years playing under Ben Johnson in Detroit and working for Kliff Kingsbury in Washington to heavily influence the Washington offensive philosophy, making it a hybrid of multiple successful offensive philosophies.
